title: What the Alabama Act Covers
bodyText: Alabama's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies statewide to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Alabama, including a rented manufactured home, with no county, city or unit-count exception, and it is the exclusive remedy for rights under the rental agreement. It does not cover: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious services; occupancy under a contract to buy the home; fraternity or similar organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings; an employee whose housing depends on employment on the premises; a condominium or cooperative owner; agricultural rentals; and a seller (or the seller's family) staying up to 36 months after selling. It also does not cover squatters. The Act applies to agreements made, extended or renewed on or after January 1, 2007. It is liberally construed, creates no new tort duties, and every duty and remedy carries an obligation of good faith. Days are calendar days, but a statutory period that ends on a weekend or official holiday runs to the next business day the court is open.

title: Local Ordinances and Rent Control
bodyText: Alabama counties and cities may not enact or enforce any resolution or ordinance about residential landlords, rental housing codes, or landlord-tenant rights and obligations; the state Act supersedes them, including ones passed before 2007. Local governments may still enforce building codes, health codes and other general laws that affect rental property, but only if those codes apply equally to similar owner-occupied homes. Separately, no local government may enact, keep or enforce any rule that controls the amount of rent charged for private property. Local building, health and code-enforcement rules (for example in Birmingham, Huntsville, Mobile and Montgomery) are outside this library's scope, and a 2026 law lets Class 1 cities adopt vacant-property registration.

title: Lease Terms Alabama Prohibits
bodyText: An Alabama lease may not make the tenant: waive rights under the landlord's maintenance duty, the tenant's remedies for the landlord's noncompliance or for loss of essential services, the security deposit rules, or the law of unlawful detainer; confess judgment; pay the landlord's attorney's fees or costs of collection; or release, limit or indemnify the landlord's liability arising under law. These terms are unenforceable, and a landlord who tries to enforce a term it knows is prohibited owes the tenant actual damages plus up to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. A lease lien on the tenant's household goods is unenforceable (unless perfected before 2007), and distress for rent is abolished. A tenant in possession may not withhold rent to enforce the tenant's rights.

title: Alabama Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Alabama limits security to one month's periodic rent, except for additional security for pets, changes to the property, or increased liability risk. There is no interest, separate-account or escrow requirement. At the end of the tenancy the landlord may keep only accrued rent and damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties, and must mail the refund or an itemized list of deductions with any balance within 60 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives up possession. The tenant must give a forwarding address in writing; without one, the landlord mails to the last known address or the rental address. A landlord who misses the 60-day deadline owes the tenant double the original deposit. A refund the tenant does not claim within 90 days is forfeited under the Act. Whoever owns the property when the tenancy ends is bound, and a seller stays liable for the deposit and prepaid rent.

title: Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: An Alabama landlord must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, make repairs to keep the premises habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances (including elevators), provide garbage receptacles and removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat (unless the tenant controls a separately metered installation). These duties do not arise for a condition the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused. If the landlord materially fails, the tenant may give written notice ending the lease in not less than 14 days unless the landlord fixes the problem, and may recover actual damages, attorney's fees and an injunction. If the landlord willfully or negligently fails to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service after notice, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' written notice or recover the lost rental value. There is no repair-and-deduct remedy, and the tenant may not withhold rent while in possession.

title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: In Alabama, a landlord's rules about common areas or tenant conduct bind a tenant only if they promote tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abuse or fairly distribute services; are reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; are explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; are not meant to evade the landlord's duties; and the tenant had notice of them at signing or when adopted. A rule adopted after signing that substantially changes the tenant's use is not valid unless the tenant consents in writing, and where a rule and the lease differ, the lease wins.

title: Entry and Access
bodyText: Alabama requires at least two days' notice before a landlord enters to show or service the unit, at reasonable times; a note posted on the main entry door is enough. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, repair, provide services or show the unit, and a repair request is consent to enter to do that repair. A general notice or schedule of more than two days for repairs, maintenance, pest control or health and safety services, given separately from the lease, covers those entries. The landlord may enter without consent only in an emergency, by court order, to do maintenance the tenant failed to do after notice, during an absence over 14 days, on reasonable belief of abandonment, or to show the unit in the last four months before the lease expires if the tenant signed a separate general notice. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy has no fixed expiration date and the Act does not say how the four months apply to one, so rely on this showing right only after a termination notice has set an end date. If the tenant refuses lawful access the landlord may seek an injunction or end the lease; if the landlord enters unlawfully or harasses the tenant, the tenant may seek an injunction or end the lease, and either side may recover actual damages.

title: Eviction (Unlawful Detainer) Process
bodyText: For unpaid rent, an Alabama landlord gives a written notice stating the rent and any late fees owed and that the lease will end on a date at least seven business days after the tenant receives it; if the tenant does not pay within that time, the lease ends. For other material breaches, or an intentional material misrepresentation in the lease or application, the notice gives at least seven business days, and a curable breach that is fixed in time does not end the lease. Some breaches cannot be cured (illegal drugs, illegal firearm use or criminal assault on the premises, a repeat of the same breach within six months, and intentional misrepresentation), and no breach may be cured more than twice in 12 months without the landlord's written consent. Eviction is a civil action in district or circuit court, heard ahead of other civil cases; if personal service fails, papers may be left with a resident or posted on the door and mailed. In district court the tenant must answer within seven calendar days after service, and court time periods in eviction cases run in calendar days. Either side may appeal within seven days, but a tenant's appeal does not stop the writ unless the tenant pays all rent since filing into court and keeps paying. The writ of possession is automatically stayed for seven days after judgment. The landlord may recover rent, actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees by statute. Default and eviction notices are outside Alabama's electronic-transactions law, so give them on paper. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: An Alabama landlord may not take back a rental by lockout, removing the tenant, or willfully cutting off heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except where the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit or the Act permits. A tenant who is unlawfully removed, locked out or has services willfully interrupted may recover possession or end the lease and, either way, recover the greater of three months' rent or actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees, and the return of the deposit and unearned prepaid rent. Liens on a tenant's household goods are unenforceable and distress for rent is abolished.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: An Alabama landlord may not retaliate by discriminatorily raising rent, reducing services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because the tenant complained to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to the landlord about the landlord's maintenance duties, or organized or joined a tenants' union. A tenant who is retaliated against has the same remedies as for an unlawful ouster (the greater of three months' rent or actual damages, plus attorney's fees) and a defense to eviction. The landlord may still evict where the tenant or household caused the violation, the tenant is behind on rent, compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit, or for other material lease violations. Alabama sets no presumption period.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Unless the lease sets a definite term, an Alabama tenancy is week-to-week for weekly rent and otherwise month-to-month. Either side may end a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least seven days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice. A fixed-term lease ends on its own terms. If the landlord consents to the tenant staying after the term, the tenancy becomes periodic.

title: Holdover Remedies
bodyText: If an Alabama tenant stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent, the landlord may sue for possession and, if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, recover the greater of three months' rent or actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees. If the landlord consents, the tenancy becomes week-to-week or month-to-month. Two older Alabama statutes also speak of double rent for tenants who hold over after written demand or notice; whether they still apply to tenancies under the Act has not been settled by statute.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Since 2024, an Alabama property owner or agent can have a squatter removed without an eviction case. The owner gives notice at the dwelling that the person has no right to be there and must leave immediately, then files a sworn affidavit in the statutory form with local law enforcement, which verifies ownership and, after at least 24 hours, serves a notice to vacate immediately; the agency may charge up to $50. The procedure does not apply to a tenant, a holdover tenant, an immediate family member of the owner, or where litigation over the dwelling is pending. A false affidavit is a crime, and a person wrongfully removed may recover possession, actual damages, punitive damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney's fees. Entering or staying unlawfully in a dwelling and causing $1,000 or more in damage is third-degree burglary, and renting out property one has no authority to lease is a crime (a felony from October 1, 2026).

title: Selling or Changing Management of a Rented Property
bodyText: Unless the parties agree otherwise, an Alabama landlord who sells a rented property in a good-faith sale is relieved of liability for events after written notice of the sale to the tenant, but stays liable for the tenant's security deposit and prepaid rent. A manager is relieved for events after written notice to the tenant that its management ended. The owner and manager disclosure must be kept current by any successor. The new owner holds the landlord's interest and is bound by the deposit rules when the tenancy ends. In a court receivership started after 2024, a receiver generally may not reject a lease of a tenant's primary residence. There is no state rule on tenants' rights in foreclosure; federal law applies.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: A declarant converting an Alabama building to condominiums must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession at least 60 days' notice before they must vacate, by hand delivery to the unit or prepaid mail, describing their rights. No tenant may be required to vacate on less than 60 days' notice, except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct disturbing other tenants, and the tenancy terms may not change during that period. Missing notice is a defense to eviction. The conversion notice can also serve as the Act's termination notice, but it does not let the declarant end a lease early.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: Alabama has no separate state statute letting servicemembers end residential leases; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs. Alabama extends the federal SCRA to members of the Alabama National Guard (and guard members of other states employed in Alabama) called to state active duty or federally funded duty other than training in a proclaimed emergency, for the same periods the federal law requires.

title: Alabama Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Alabama's Fair Housing Law bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or handicap, including refusing reasonable accommodations or reasonable modifications for a disability. It tracks the federal classes and adds none. Exemptions: owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, and single-family houses rented by a private owner of no more than three houses without a broker or discriminatory advertising (the advertising ban still applies). A landlord may refuse an applicant convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance, may ask about it on the application, and may set reasonable occupancy standards. Housing need not be provided to someone whose occupancy is a direct threat or would cause substantial physical damage.

title: Service Animal and Assistance Animal Law
bodyText: Alabama gives a person with a disability who uses a service animal full and equal access to rental housing, with no extra charge; the tenant is liable for damage the animal causes, and the landlord may ask for proof of vaccinations. For other assistance animals, including qualifying emotional support animals, a landlord may require reliable documentation from the person's medical provider of the disability and the disability-related need only when they are not readily apparent or known, and must keep it confidential. Misrepresenting a disability or need, or creating or providing a false document or vest for an animal in housing, carries a $500 civil penalty or a Class C misdemeanor, and a Class B misdemeanor for a repeat. Knowingly misrepresenting oneself as using a service animal is also a Class C misdemeanor with 100 hours of community service.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: Alabama's electronic-transactions law does not apply to notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a person's primary residence, or to utility cutoff notices. Deliver those notices on paper (in hand, by mail, or by posting on the primary entry door where the Act allows). Electronic signatures on the lease itself are valid.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: An Alabama property owner or lessee (or its agent) may have a vehicle that has become unclaimed on the property under the state's unclaimed-vehicle procedure removed to a secure place; the tow company gets a lien for reasonable removal and storage fees, and the owner, lessee and tower are liable to the vehicle's owner only for gross negligence. Law enforcement may remove vehicles left 48 hours or more. Alabama has no statute requiring tow-away signs on private residential lots. Class 1 and Class 5 cities may set up procedures to remove inoperable vehicles from private property as nuisances.

title: Bounced Checks
bodyText: Alabama's bad-check charge statute lets lenders, creditors and merchants charge the greater of $30 or the bank's actual return charge for a dishonored check; whether it covers a residential landlord collecting rent is not settled by the text, so keep any returned-payment fee at or below $30 unless the lease and a court say otherwise. Writing a check knowing it will not be honored is a Class A misdemeanor; to use the statutory presumption, the holder sends the statutory notice by certified or registered mail and the drawer has 10 days to pay the amount plus the service charge.

title: Utility Accounts
bodyText: An Alabama landlord is not responsible for paying utilities unless the lease says so. A sewer bill in a tenant's name is the tenant's sole responsibility and is not a lien on the property, and a provider of goods or services may not make a landlord pay a tenant's delinquent bill for an account in the tenant's name or claim a lien on the property for it. Tampering with a meter to divert gas, electricity or water is a crime. A utility may rely on a writ of possession when deciding whether to disconnect service.

title: Lead Hazards
bodyText: Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to Alabama rentals built before 1978. Alabama adds its Lead Reduction Act: people doing lead-based paint inspections, risk assessments, abatement and similar activities must be accredited, and anyone paid to renovate target housing must give the owner and occupants a lead hazard information pamphlet before starting work. Alabama has no separate state lead disclosure form for leases.

title: Drug-Related Nuisance Actions
bodyText: In Alabama, the attorney general, a district attorney, a county or city attorney, a county resident (including a tenant) or a community group may sue in circuit court to abate a drug-related nuisance at a property. If a nuisance is found, the court may award damages of $300 to $40,000 per plaintiff, fines when a government sues, and attorney's fees, and may order the owner to clean up and repair, add locks, lighting, security or cameras, pay rent into court for up to 90 days, turn rents over to a trustee, suspend housing subsidies to the owner, or seal the property. A non-resident owner's criminal culpability must be shown by clear and convincing evidence. Illegal drug activity by a tenant is also a noncurable lease default.

title: Rental Agreements and Immigration Status
bodyText: Alabama's Code still contains a 2012 provision making it unlawful to harbor a person unlawfully present in the United States by entering into a rental agreement with that person, if the landlord knows or recklessly disregards that the person is unlawfully present. Parts of Alabama's 2011-2012 immigration laws were challenged in federal court and the separate harboring section was repealed in 2025, so whether this rental provision can be enforced should be checked with a lawyer before relying on it either way. Alabama law does not require or forbid asking applicants about immigration status. Fair-housing law still bars national-origin discrimination.

title: Registered Offenders in Birmingham, Jefferson County and Morgan County Rentals
bodyText: In a Class 1 Alabama city (Birmingham), a registered sex offender may not live in a residence where another registered sex offender on the Jefferson County Sheriff's list lives, and an owner or lessee who knowingly permits it is fined $5,000 per violation. The owner is protected if the rental application or the lease contains the tenant's signed statement that the tenant is not a convicted sex offender. A sex offender who is the spouse or child of the owner or lessee is excepted. The same rule, $5,000 owner penalty and lease-statement protection apply throughout Jefferson County, which adds that only one adult offender on the Sheriff's list may live in an apartment complex unless they are at least 100 yards apart, and in Morgan County, where offenders on the Sheriff's list must live at least 100 yards apart (see `edu-sex-offender-disclosure-al`). Statewide, registrants may not live within 2,000 feet of a school, childcare facility or resident camp, but that duty is on the registrant, not the landlord.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid into Court
bodyText: In an Alabama eviction or rent action while the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, but must pay accrued rent into court and keep paying as it comes due; the court decides whether the tenant stays and pays the net amount to whichever side is owed. If no rent remains due, judgment for possession goes to the tenant. A landlord may recover attorney's fees if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit and not in good faith. A tenant not in possession may counterclaim without paying rent into court.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Alabama does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in a separate or interest-bearing account.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Alabama does not cap residential late fees or require a grace period. Late fees may be included in the seven-business-day nonpayment notice. Courts may still refuse to enforce a fee that operates as a penalty.

title: No Application Fee Limit
bodyText: Alabama does not limit rental application or screening fees or require them to be refunded.

title: No Rent Increase Notice Rule
bodyText: Alabama sets no advance-notice period or limit for rent increases. Rent may change by agreement, at renewal, or on a new periodic term after proper termination notice, but not as retaliation.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Alabama law does not require landlords to accept housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income and does not make source of income a protected class. Local governments cannot add landlord-tenant rules of their own.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no radon disclosure or testing requirement for rentals.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment statute for rentals. The general duty to keep the premises habitable and meet housing codes still applies.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no mold disclosure, inspection or treatment statute for rentals. The general duty to keep the premises habitable and meet housing codes still applies.

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Duty
bodyText: Alabama statutes do not require carbon monoxide alarms in rental housing.

title: No Statutory Smoke Alarm Duty for Rentals
bodyText: Alabama statutes do not require landlords to install or maintain smoke alarms in rental homes or apartments; the only statutory smoke detector duty is for hotel guest rooms. Building and fire codes adopted locally or by rule may still require them.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no flood-history or flood-zone disclosure requirement for rentals.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Alabama gives tenants no statutory right to install electric vehicle charging equipment.

title: No Rent Receipt Duty
bodyText: Alabama does not require landlords to give receipts for rent, including cash rent.

title: No Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Alabama has no statute protecting a tenant from eviction or penalties for calling police or emergency services.

title: No Lease Termination on a Tenant's Death
bodyText: Alabama has no statute ending a residential lease or setting a special procedure when a tenant dies; the lease and general estate law govern.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Alabama does not require a move-in inspection, condition checklist or inventory. A signed move-in report is still good evidence in a deposit dispute.

title: No Drug Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental was used as a methamphetamine or other drug lab.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right
bodyText: Alabama has no statute letting a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking end a residential lease early, change locks, or have an abuser removed from the lease. A court's protection-from-abuse order can, however, remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns or leases it (see `edu-dv-eviction-protection-al`). Federal VAWA protections apply in covered federally assisted housing.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Alabama has no statute sealing, expunging or limiting public access to eviction (unlawful detainer) case records. Alabama's court rules let a court seal any civil record only after a hearing and a written finding, on clear and convincing evidence, that it falls in one of six narrow categories (such as a serious threat of harassment or other particularized harm to a party); there is no eviction-specific sealing rule.

title: Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Alabama lets a person waive, in a written contract such as a lease, the exemption that protects up to $7,500 of personal property (adjusted every three years) from collection of a judgment. The waiver can never reach cooking utensils and stoves, table, tableware, chairs, beds and bedding in use by the family, clothing, the family library, or a vehicle or tools personally essential to the debtor's business, and it works only if it is pleaded in the lawsuit and declared in the judgment. A homestead waiver needs a separate signed and witnessed document. The library offers an optional waiver clause (`exemption-waiver-al`), off by default. It is a collection term aimed at the tenant that many residential leases leave out, so use it only as a deliberate choice.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease by written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and security within five days, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If a person's failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover from that person up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-402)

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If fire or casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs their enjoyment of the property, the tenant may move out immediately and tell you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value (Ala. Code § 35-9A-406). The exception names only damage caused by 'the tenant', not by the tenant's family or guests (see `edu-tenant-caused-damage-al`). If the lease ends, return the recoverable deposit and all unearned prepaid rent, accounting for rent as of the date of the casualty.

title: After the Eviction Judgment
bodyText: After an Alabama eviction judgment for the landlord, the writ of possession issues on the landlord's application once the automatic seven-day stay ends. A sheriff or constable who neglects or refuses to execute the writ owes the landlord $200. A tenant who comes back in without just cause after being removed can be held in contempt, and further writs may issue; going back into possession after being put out under court process is also a crime, punished by a fine of $200 to $1,000 (half paid to the landlord) and at least six months in jail. No Alabama statute sets duties for a tenant's belongings or animals when the writ is executed, or gives landlords immunity for it. The Act lets a landlord dispose of property left in the unit more than 14 days after a lawful termination, with no duty to store or protect it. Removing belongings or changing the locks before the writ is executed is self-help the Act forbids.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: Alabama has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy by written notice (at least 7 or 30 days) and may decline to renew a fixed-term lease when it ends, without giving a reason, however long the tenant has lived there. Situational limits still apply: a landlord may not bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint to a government agency, a repair complaint to the landlord, or organizing or joining a tenants' union; a declarant converting a building to condominiums must give tenants at least 60 days' notice and may not require them to leave sooner except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants; and in a possession case the tenant may counterclaim, paying rent into court, and wins possession if no rent remains due. Federal rules for subsidized housing are not covered here.

title: Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act defines 'goods' to include real property and 'sale' and 'buying' to include leasing and renting, so on its face it reaches a residential lease with a tenant renting for personal, family or household use. Its list of unlawful practices includes misrepresenting what is offered (its characteristics, benefits, standard or quality), advertising with intent not to rent as advertised, and false statements about the need for repairs, plus a catch-all for any other unconscionable, false, misleading or deceptive act. The list does not name leaving blanks to be filled in after signing or failing to give a copy at signing. A consumer may recover actual damages or $100, whichever is greater, up to three times actual damages at the court's discretion, and attorney's fees, after a written demand at least 15 days before suing; consumers may not sue as a class. Whether the Landlord and Tenant Act's statement that it is the exclusive remedy for rights under a rental agreement limits these claims is not settled by statute.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases, and no statute requiring a lease to list the tenant's waivers or to use a particular type size. A court may still refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If an Alabama tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or someone on the property with the tenant's consent deliberately or negligently causes a condition, the tenant's repair, termination and essential-service remedies do not arise for it. A fire or casualty caused by the tenant gives the tenant no right to end the lease or pay reduced rent; that exception names only 'the tenant', so a fire caused by a guest may still give the tenant those rights. The tenant must not damage the property, or knowingly, recklessly or negligently let anyone else do so. The landlord may recover actual damages and apply the deposit, and for a health or safety problem that repair, replacement or cleaning can fix, may do the work after seven days' written notice and bill it as rent. The tenant may not withhold rent. If the landlord ends the lease for the breach, the landlord has a claim for rent and actual damages, subject to a duty to mitigate. How Alabama courts measure lost future rent is case law not read here. The library offers an optional clause (`tenant-caused-damage-al`).

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data. Federal antitrust law and Alabama's general laws still apply.

title: Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: Under Alabama's Act, 'rent' means all payments the tenant is to make to or for the landlord under the rental agreement, so late fees and other lease charges count as rent without any special wording. The nonpayment notice may include late fees, and the cost of repairs the landlord makes after the tenant fails to fix a health or safety problem is billed as rent. This library's default clause still says an unpaid late fee alone will not support ending the lease; that is a library choice, not a legal limit.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If an Alabama tenant breaks the tenant's statutory upkeep duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and the problem can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, the landlord may give written notice describing it and asking the tenant to fix it within seven days (or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency). If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and bill the tenant for the actual and reasonable cost (or its fair and reasonable value) as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. No lease clause is needed for this right, and because the bill is rent it can go in a nonpayment notice once it is due.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach, and its consumer protection act does not list blanks left to be filled after signing. Complete every blank before signing anyway: a blank leaves the term unclear, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No Alabama statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential leases; the covenant Alabama law reads into the words 'grant, bargain, sell' applies to conveyances of ownership in fee, not to leases. The Act does protect the tenant against unlawful or harassing entry, lockout and service cutoffs, and requires the tenant to respect the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. Whether Alabama courts imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment into a lease is case law not read here.

title: Forms Alabama Law Supplies
bodyText: Alabama supplies no statutory lease form and no form for the Act's nonpayment or breach notice, which must be in writing, give at least seven business days and, for unpaid rent, state the rent and late fees owed. Forms the law does supply: the owner's sworn affidavit to have a squatter removed, which must be substantially in the statutory form with the notice given at the dwelling attached; the notice the court issues in an eviction case, and optional judgment and writ forms; and a 10-day notice to quit for default under the older general landlord-tenant chapter, which serves only tenancies outside the Act.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Alabama statute addresses whether a tenant may install security cameras or video doorbells, so the lease controls, including its rules on alterations. Alabama crimes still apply: using a device to record a private conversation without the consent of at least one person in it is criminal eavesdropping; secretly watching someone while trespassing in a private place is criminal surveillance; and secretly watching someone where they expect privacy, for sexual gratification, is a felony. A camera or doorbell that records the audio of conversations its owner is not part of can raise the eavesdropping issue.

title: Abandonment and Your Duty to Re-Rent in Alabama
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental, but that duty does not come ahead of your right to rent your other vacant units first. The tenant's leaving does not by itself end the lease; if you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease expires, the old lease ends on the date the new tenancy begins. You may also end it with the act's written notice if rent goes unpaid. Until then rent keeps accruing, and you have a claim for rent and for actual damages, reduced by what reasonable re-letting brings in. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the remaining term for this purpose is one month or one week. Alabama treats a unit as abandoned, in addition to any other evidence you have, when the electric service has been off for seven consecutive days. You may enter when you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. Property left more than 14 days after termination may be disposed of without any duty to store it (see `abandoned-property-al`). Keep records of your advertising and showings, since your recovery depends on reasonable efforts.

title: Attorney Fees Come From the Statute, Not the Lease
bodyText: An Alabama lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney's fees or your costs of collection. Such a term is unenforceable, and enforcing a lease you know contains it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. You still recover fees in the cases the law itself allows. A court may award you actual damages and reasonable attorney fees for the tenant's noncompliance with the lease or with the tenant's statutory duties; after the lease ends you have a separate claim for actual damages for breach and reasonable attorney's fees; you may recover reasonable attorney's fees if a tenant's counterclaim in a possession or rent case is without merit and not raised in good faith; and you may recover them for a willful, bad-faith holdover. The tenant has matching statutory rights against you, so no reciprocity clause is needed or allowed. Leave any attorney-fee or collection-cost term out of the lease and ask the court for fees under the statute. One practical limit: on the district court's small-claims docket (claims up to $6,000), no party may recover attorney fees unless represented by a licensed attorney.

title: Arbitration Clauses in an Alabama Lease: Not Offered
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that authorizes or regulates arbitration clauses in residential leases. Its general arbitration statutes are old: parties may refer a dispute to arbitrators they choose and the award can be entered as a judgment, but Alabama law also says an agreement to submit a controversy to arbitration cannot be specifically enforced. The Federal Arbitration Act makes a written arbitration clause in a contract involving interstate commerce valid and enforceable, save on grounds that exist for revoking any contract; whether a particular residential lease falls under it is case law this library has not reviewed. The bigger problem is Alabama's landlord-tenant act. A lease may not have the tenant give up the remedies tied to your repair duty, your noncompliance or essential services, the deposit rules, or the law of unlawful detainer, and enforcing a lease you know contains a prohibited term carries a penalty of actual damages plus up to one month's rent and attorney's fees. Whether an arbitration clause that sends those claims away from the courts is such a waiver is unsettled. For that reason the library's shared arbitration clause does not carry Alabama, and the library offers no arbitration clause here. Cautious course: do not require arbitration. If you use one anyway, take advice first, limit it to money claims, keep eviction, deposit, repair and essential-service claims and injury claims in court, and preserve every statutory remedy.

title: Waiving Casualty Rights or the Duty to Mitigate: Not Offered in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's casualty rule is in the landlord-tenant act: if fire or casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs the home, the tenant may move out and terminate on written notice within 14 days, or keep living in the usable part and pay reduced rent. No other Alabama statute, inside or outside the act, lets an express agreement override that right, and none deals with an untenantable building generally. The act's list of terms a lease may not waive does not name the casualty section or the duty to mitigate damages, so a waiver of either is not expressly prohibited. But whether a court would enforce one, or treat it as unconscionable or as limiting your liability under law, is case law this library has not reviewed. The library does not offer a casualty-waiver or no-mitigation clause. Use `casualty-landlord-termination-al`, which adds your own right to end the lease after a casualty without reducing the tenant's, and handle tenant-caused damage through `tenant-caused-damage-al`.

title: No Collection Fee in an Alabama Lease
bodyText: An Alabama lease may not make the tenant pay your costs of collection, so a lease charge for sending an account to collections, a collection-agency percentage, or a fee for your own collection work is prohibited, and enforcing a lease you know contains such a term exposes you to actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and attorney's fees. This also matters if you hand a former tenant's balance to a collection agency: under federal law a third-party debt collector may not collect any interest, fee, charge or expense on top of the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law permits it, and an Alabama lease cannot authorize it. Recover collection costs only where a court awards them, for example reasonable attorney's fees under the landlord-tenant act.

title: No Confession-of-Judgment Clause in an Alabama Lease
bodyText: An Alabama lease cannot have the tenant authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you try to enforce a lease that you know contains a prohibited term, the tenant can recover actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. A second, general statute reaches every contract, not only leases: any agreement made before a lawsuit starts to confess judgment, or to authorize someone else to confess judgment, in an Alabama court is void, and a judgment taken that way must be set aside on a motion made within six months after it is entered. The same statute also voids an advance agreement to be sued in a county other than the one the venue statutes fix, so do not put a venue-shifting term in the lease either; eviction venue is the county where the property is. Alabama has no lease bond or other route that lets a tenant agree in advance to a judgment for possession: recover possession only through the court eviction process. A tenant may still agree to a judgment after a case is filed, for example in a settlement entered with the court.

title: Checks Outside the Landlord-Tenant Title for Alabama
bodyText: Three questions are often answered outside a state's landlord-tenant law. Squatters: Alabama has a specific procedure, outside the main act, for asking law enforcement to remove an unauthorized person from a dwelling (see `edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-al`). Cash rent receipts: no Alabama statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for cash rent (see `edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-al`). Registration as a condition of an eviction: Alabama has no landlord or rental registration, so registration is not a condition of a possession judgment, with one important exception for companies. An LLC, corporation, limited partnership or other entity formed outside Alabama that limits any owner's liability and transacts business here must register with the Secretary of State, and until it does it may not maintain any lawsuit in an Alabama court, which includes filing an eviction. Register a foreign entity before you file.

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges or Cleaning Schedule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute letting a lease pre-set charges against the deposit, such as a fixed carpet-cleaning or move-out cleaning fee, and none prescribing a notice for one. At the end of the tenancy you may apply the deposit only to accrued rent and to the damages you suffered because the tenant failed to meet the tenant's statutory duties: keeping the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits, disposing of waste properly, using fixtures and appliances reasonably, and not destroying, defacing or damaging the property. A flat cleaning or carpet charge taken from every deposit, whatever the unit's condition, is not a measured loss from a breach of those duties, and the deposit rules cannot be waived in the lease. So itemize actual costs, unit by unit: deduct cleaning or carpet work only where the tenant left the unit dirtier or more damaged than its condition allowed, and keep invoices and before-and-after photos. A schedule of typical charges can still help you itemize consistently, as long as each deduction is tied to the actual condition. The library does not offer a pre-set cleaning-fee clause for Alabama (see the decision on `carpet-cleaning`).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds: Two Alabama Statutes Point Different Ways
bodyText: Two Alabama statutes speak to a deposit refund the tenant never collects, and they do not fit together. The landlord-tenant act says a deposit unclaimed by the tenant, and any refund check left outstanding, is forfeited by the tenant after 90 days; it does not say who then owns the money. The unclaimed property act lists a security deposit as property, makes the business holding it a holder, and presumes property of this kind abandoned three years after the owner could first demand it; a holder must then report it to the State Treasurer before November 1 each year (covering the year to June 30), send the owner a written notice at least 60 days before reporting if the amount is $50 or more and an address is on file, keep records for 10 years, and pay a civil penalty of $100 a business day (up to $5,000), or $500 a day (up to $25,000) if the failure is willful, for not reporting. Which statute controls a forfeited deposit is unsettled. Cautious course: after 90 days stop owing the tenant a mailing, but do not treat the money as yours; keep it identified, and if it is still unclaimed after three years, report and remit it under the unclaimed property act. The Treasurer must waive the penalty for a holder who acted in good faith. Do not add a lease clause that forfeits unclaimed refunds to you or deducts a dormancy charge from them: the deposit rules cannot be waived, and the library offers neither.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama gives tenants no right to pay a security deposit in installments, and no statute requires you to offer one. You may agree to installments if you choose. If you do, put the schedule in writing, say what happens if an installment is missed, and remember that the whole deposit, however collected, may not exceed one month's periodic rent plus any additional security for pets, changes to the premises or increased liability risks.

title: Last Month's Rent in Alabama: Keep It Separate From the Deposit
bodyText: No Alabama statute restricts how last month's rent paid in advance may be applied. (A real estate broker who manages the property must keep it in a separate, federally insured account and account for prepaid rents when management ends or the property is sold; see `edu-security-deposit-holding-al`.) The deposit section is headed "Security Deposits; Prepaid Rent" but deals only with security; prepaid rent appears elsewhere in the act as money you must return, unearned, when the tenancy ends early because of your breach, a casualty or an unlawful ouster, and as a liability a seller keeps after selling. Whether money labeled last month's rent counts toward the one-month cap on security is not settled by the text. The library treats rent paid in advance for a specific rental period as prepaid rent, not security (see `security-deposit-cap-al`). To keep it that way, label the payment as rent for a named month, apply it to that month, and do not use it to cover damages; money you may apply to damages is security and counts toward the cap.

title: No Deposit Notice at Move-Out in Alabama, but Ask for the Forwarding Address
bodyText: Alabama requires no notice from you to the tenant at move-out about the deposit, such as a notice of a right to a pre-move-out inspection or of how the deposit will be handled. The duty runs the other way: when the tenant vacates, the tenant must give you a valid forwarding address in writing. If the tenant does not, you mail the refund or itemized accounting by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address or, if none, to the rental property's address. Your 60 days start when the tenancy has ended and possession has been delivered. A short written reminder at move-out asking for the forwarding address costs nothing and protects your 60-day mailing.

title: Repair Contacts and Approved Repairers in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act does not require you to name a repair contact or approved repairers, and no Alabama statute lets a tenant hire a repairer and send you the bill or deduct repair costs from rent; a tenant in possession may not withhold rent to enforce the tenant's rights. So the lease can decide who receives repair requests and require your written approval, naming the contractor and any cost limit, before a tenant arranges work at your expense (the optional clause `designated-repairer-al`). Keep the clause from reaching the tenant's statutory remedies, which a lease cannot waive: the 14-day notice to terminate for your material noncompliance, damages and an injunction, and the essential-services remedies. When a tenant requests a repair, the tenant is treated as consenting to your entry to make it. You must also disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, who manages the premises and who receives notices (see `landlord-disclosure-al`).

title: Keeping a Victim's Information Confidential: Federal Rule in Covered Housing; No Alabama Program
bodyText: Alabama has no address-confidentiality program and no statute requiring a landlord to keep a tenant's domestic-violence status or new address confidential. In federally covered housing (public housing, Section 8, low-income housing tax credit and other covered programs), federal law is strict: any information a tenant or applicant gives you to claim protection, including the fact that they are a victim, must be kept in confidence, may not be entered into any shared database, and may not be disclosed except with the person's written request or consent, for use in an eviction proceeding on that ground, or as other law requires. Good practice everywhere: store such documents separately, limit who can see them, and never tell an abuser where a victim has moved.

title: No Special Deposit Timing After a Domestic-Violence Move-Out in Alabama
bodyText: Because Alabama has no domestic-violence lease-termination right, it has no special rule on when the deposit clock starts after a victim leaves. The ordinary rule applies: you return the deposit, with an itemized list of anything withheld, within 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered. If a victim moves out but a co-tenant stays, the tenancy has not ended and there is no deposit to settle yet, unless you and the tenants agree to release the departing tenant and divide the deposit. If a court order removes an abusive co-tenant, the lease, and both tenants' obligations under it, continue, and the deposit stays in place. Put any agreement to release one tenant in writing, signed by every tenant on the lease.

title: No Alabama Eviction Protection for Domestic-Violence Victims; Federal Rules in Assisted Housing
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act has no rule protecting a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking from eviction, and no state statute bars evicting a tenant because of abuse they suffered. Two things still limit you. First, if the home is in a federally covered housing program (public housing, a Section 8 voucher or project-based unit, a low-income housing tax credit property, HOME, rural housing and others), federal law forbids denying or evicting an applicant or tenant on the basis of being a victim; an incident of actual or threatened violence is not a serious or repeated lease violation or good cause to end the victim's tenancy; and criminal activity directly relating to the abuse, committed by a household member or guest against the tenant, is not grounds to evict the victim. You may instead bifurcate the lease and evict only the abuser. Second, an Alabama court issuing a protection order may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it, and after a hearing, where the abuser has a duty to support the victim or children living in the home and is the sole owner or lessee, may give the victim possession by evicting the abuser. Comply with any such order you are notified of. Be careful with the act's noncurable default for criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property: it targets the person who committed the assault, and using it against the victim in covered housing would violate federal law. Outside covered housing, treating victims more harshly than other tenants can also raise fair-housing sex-discrimination issues.

title: No Domestic-Violence Lock-Change Right in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama gives a domestic-violence victim no statutory right to have the locks changed or to change them, and no statute voids a lease term on the subject or creates a damages claim for refusing. A protection order is the route Alabama provides: the court may order the abuser removed and excluded from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it, and may direct law enforcement to accompany the victim. If you receive a protection order that excludes a co-tenant or occupant, comply with it. Changing the locks at the victim's request then is a sensible step, at the victim's cost unless you agree otherwise, and you should keep a key for the access the law gives you. Do not lock out a tenant whom no court order excludes: Alabama bars a landlord from taking possession except through the courts, and an abuser who is a tenant keeps their tenancy until a court orders otherwise. In federally covered housing, follow your program's emergency-transfer plan as well.

title: Where Alabama's Protection-Order Law Is
bodyText: Alabama's domestic-violence protection orders are issued under the Protection From Abuse Act, Title 30, Chapter 5 of the Code of Alabama. The relief that matters to a landlord is in section 30-5-7: the court may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of ownership, order possession of a vehicle and essential personal effects, and, after a hearing, where the abuser has a duty to support the victim or children living in the home and is the sole owner or lessee, give the victim possession by evicting the abuser. An order does not affect title to real property. The chapter has not moved; its relief section, 30-5-7, was last amended in 2015. Orders from other states are enforced in Alabama under the Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act, Title 30, Chapter 5B. Ask for a copy of any order a tenant relies on, and follow its terms.

title: Documents a Victim May Give You: Federal List Only
bodyText: Alabama has no landlord-tenant provision for domestic-violence victims, so it has no state list of qualifying documents and no state time limits. The only list that applies to an Alabama landlord is federal, and only in covered housing (public housing, Section 8, low-income housing tax credit and other covered programs). There, if a tenant or applicant claims protection, you may ask in writing for documentation, and the person may provide one of four forms: a certification form approved by the program's federal agency; a document signed by the person and by a victim-service provider, attorney, medical or mental-health professional stating under penalty of perjury that the incident qualifies; a record of a law-enforcement agency, court or administrative agency; or, at your discretion, a statement or other evidence. The person has 14 business days after receiving your written request, which you may extend. You do not have to ask for documentation at all. If documents conflict, you may require third-party documentation. A protection order issued by an Alabama court under the Protection From Abuse Act is a court record within that list.

title: No Eviction Fee or Collection Charge in an Alabama Lease
bodyText: An Alabama lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees or costs of collection. An eviction fee, a filing or processing charge, or a lease fee for sending a demand is a cost of collecting what the tenant owes, so do not put one in the lease; enforcing a lease you know contains a prohibited term exposes you to actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and attorney's fees. Recover what the law gives you instead: possession, rent, actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees through the court, which also decides court costs. A fixed charge dressed as liquidated damages is no safer; whether it is an unenforceable penalty is case law (see `edu-liquidated-damages-al`). Late fees are different: Alabama sets no cap and lets you include them in the nonpayment notice (see `edu-no-late-fee-cap-al`).

title: No Waiver or Indemnity of the Landlord’s Legal Liability
bodyText: An Alabama lease may not have the tenant agree to excuse or limit any liability you have under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its costs. A release, hold-harmless, waiver-of-claims or indemnity clause covering your own legal liability is unenforceable, and enforcing a lease you know contains one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. The ban covers liability 'arising under law', so it reaches your statutory duties and ordinary negligence claims alike. What you may still do: make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, the tenant's family or guests cause; require renters insurance for the tenant's own belongings and liability; and state that the tenant is responsible for the tenant's own property. The landlord-tenant act itself does not create or remove tort claims, so injury claims run under the general law.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no faster or special deposit procedure for abandonment, a short tenancy, an eviction or a tenant who disappears. The single rule applies: within 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered, mail the refund, or an itemized list of amounts withheld with any balance, to the forwarding address the tenant gave in writing, or else to the last known address or the property. For an abandoned unit, the tenancy ends when you re-rent it for a term starting before the old lease expires, and you may treat the unit as abandoned if the electric service has been off for seven consecutive days; possession is delivered when you regain it. Mail on time even when the tenant has left no address: missing the 60 days costs double the original deposit.

title: Deposit Alternatives in Alabama: No Statute
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on deposit-alternative programs, fees in lieu of a security deposit, or surety bonds sold to tenants, so there is no required notice, no right to switch to a deposit, and no credit-reporting rule specific to them. The general rules still apply. Alabama's cap reaches money you demand or receive as security for the tenant's obligations, so a refundable payment that secures performance is security however it is labeled; a genuine nonrefundable fee for a third-party product is not security, but every payment due under the lease counts as rent. If you offer an alternative, make it optional, say plainly that the fee is not a deposit and will not be refunded, that it does not limit what the tenant owes you for damage or unpaid rent, and that the provider may pursue the tenant for amounts it pays you; never charge it in addition to a full deposit for the same risk without saying so. A provider collecting from the tenant may be a debt collector under federal law.

title: No Relief From Forfeiture After the Notice Runs, Except the Court Payment Routes
bodyText: Once your seven-business-day notice for unpaid rent runs without payment, the Alabama lease terminates. Apart from the two court routes below, no statute lets the tenant undo that termination by paying the arrears and your costs later, lets a court relieve the tenant from the forfeiture on equitable grounds, or keeps the lease alive for rent while the tenant loses possession. After termination you have a claim for possession and for rent, and a separate claim for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. But if you accept rent knowing of the default, you waive your right to terminate for that breach unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach. Two payment routes remain in court. In the possession case a tenant who counterclaims must pay accrued and accruing rent into court; the court decides whether the tenant stays in possession, and if no rent remains due once the court has applied the money paid in and netted the claims, judgment for possession goes to the tenant. And a tenant who appeals keeps possession only by paying into court all rent payable under the lease since the eviction was filed and staying current. A lease clause declaring a forfeiture or a right of re-entry adds nothing, and you may not act on one yourself: possession comes only through the court.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction or Cause Notice in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no just-cause eviction rule, so a termination notice does not have to state a cause except where the act requires it: a notice for a breach must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach, and a nonpayment notice must state the rent and late fees owed. A periodic tenancy may be ended without cause by written notice given at least seven days before the termination date (weekly) or at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (monthly), and a fixed term simply ends. Local governments may not adopt just-cause or rent-control rules: the landlord-tenant act bars local ordinances on landlord-tenant rights and obligations, and a separate statute bars any local rule that would have the effect of controlling rent. Two limits remain: you may not end a tenancy in retaliation for a code complaint, a repair complaint or joining a tenants' union, and in federally assisted housing, check the program's own termination rules (not read for this row).

title: What Parts of the Habitability Duty Can Shift: Garbage, Water, Hot Water and Heat
bodyText: Two parts of your maintenance duty bend. First, the duty to supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or where the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Second, in a single-family residence (one that has direct access to a street and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility with another unit), you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant takes over garbage removal and the supply of water, hot water and heat. That written agreement may be part of the lease. For every other dwelling those duties stay with you unless a separate signed agreement under the library's `tenant-repair-agreement-al` covers specified work. Nothing lets the lease remove the running-water duty where the property has a well rather than utility water; if the tenant is to maintain a well in a single-family home, put that in writing as a specified maintenance task. You are not responsible for paying for utility services unless the lease says so.

title: The Habitability Duty Cannot Be Waived, Only Reassigned in Narrow Cases
bodyText: A lease may not have the tenant waive the tenant's rights under your duty to maintain the premises, so no clause can remove a habitability requirement or accept the home "as is" in place of it. Alabama allows only reassignment of who does certain work, never removal of the standard itself. In a single-family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant handles garbage removal and the supply of water, hot water and heat, and specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling. In any other dwelling the tenant may take on specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration, never for work needed to meet the building and housing codes, never in a way that reduces your duties to other tenants, and never as a condition of the lease (use the library's separate agreement, `tenant-repair-agreement-al`). Where a building or housing code imposes a greater duty than the act's own list, the code duty governs. The tenant's repair rights do not arise for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family, a licensee or a guest caused willfully or negligently.

title: No Health-District Rental Regulations in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute creates health-district rental regulations, requires you to give tenants local health rules on request, or directs tenants to a health district (the State Board of Health's own rules were not searched for a rental-housing chapter). What exists instead: you must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and counties and cities may adopt and enforce health codes that apply to rental property if those codes apply equally to similar owner-occupied homes. A tenant who complains to a code-enforcement agency about a violation affecting health and safety is protected from retaliation.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed. The deposit section governs money held as security for a tenant's obligations under a rental agreement, so whether it reaches money taken before any agreement exists is not settled. Treat a holding deposit cautiously: put its terms in writing before you take it, say how long you will hold the unit, whether the money becomes part of the first month's rent or the security deposit if the lease is signed, and whether any of it is kept if the applicant backs out. Refund it promptly if you decline the applicant or cannot deliver the unit. Once it is credited to the deposit, the total security counts toward the one-month cap. If a licensed real estate broker takes the money, the Real Estate Commission's rules require it to be held in the broker's trust account.

title: Jury Waivers in an Alabama Lease: Not Offered
bodyText: Alabama's constitution says the right of trial by jury 'shall remain inviolate'. No Alabama statute addresses a jury waiver in a residential lease, either to allow it or to forbid it, and the landlord-tenant act's list of prohibited terms does not mention juries. In practice an eviction starts in district court, and a jury matters mainly if the case is appealed: an appeal from the district court goes to the circuit court for a new trial, and a jury is available there only if the party appealing demands it in the notice of appeal, or the other side files a written demand within 14 days after being served with the notice. Whether a jury waiver signed in a lease before any dispute is enforceable against a residential tenant is case law this library has not reviewed. The library therefore offers no jury-waiver clause for Alabama. If you want one, take advice first, make it conspicuous and separately acknowledged, and do not combine it with any term that limits the tenant's statutory remedies.

title: Penalty for Enforcing a Lease You Know Contains a Prohibited Term
bodyText: Four kinds of lease terms are prohibited in Alabama: waiving the tenant's rights under your repair duty, the tenant's remedies for your noncompliance or for loss of heat, water or other essential services, the security-deposit rules or the law of unlawful detainer; letting anyone confess judgment; making the tenant pay your attorney's fees or costs of collection; and excusing, limiting or indemnifying your legal liability. A prohibited term is simply unenforceable. The penalty comes in when you seek to enforce a lease that contains a term you know is prohibited: the tenant may then recover actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. Read literally, the text reaches seeking to enforce any provision of a lease that contains a term you know is prohibited, not only the bad term itself, so remove any prohibited term before you sign; do not rely on a severability clause to protect you. The penalty has applied since January 1, 2008, a year after the rest of the act took effect. Alabama has no later-added section with its own voidness rule that displaces this penalty.

title: What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama gives tenants a set menu of remedies. (1) Material noncompliance with the lease, or noncompliance with your maintenance duty that materially affects health and safety: the tenant may give written notice naming the breach and a termination date at least 14 days after you receive it; if you fix it in time, the lease continues. The tenant may also recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees and get an injunction. (2) Willful or negligent failure to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service after notice: the tenant may end the lease on at least 14 days' written notice, or recover damages for the drop in rental value; electing this route rules out the general remedy for the same breach. (3) Failure to deliver possession at the start: rent abates and the tenant may terminate or sue for possession; a willful failure not in good faith costs up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. (4) Unlawful ouster or willfully cutting services: the tenant may recover possession or terminate, plus up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney's fees. (5) Fire or casualty not caused by the tenant: move out and terminate, or prorate rent. (6) Unlawful or harassing entry: injunction or termination, plus damages. A tenant in possession may not withhold rent to enforce these rights, but may counterclaim in a rent or possession case and pay the rent into court. The tenant's rights do not arise for conditions the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused. On termination you must return the recoverable deposit and unearned prepaid rent.

title: Landlord Registration in Alabama: None for Rentals, but Register Your Company
bodyText: Alabama has no statewide landlord or rental-property registration or licensing, and counties and cities may not adopt landlord registration ordinances, since the landlord-tenant act bars local ordinances relative to residential landlords. One local exception exists for vacant buildings: a Class 1 municipality may require owners of vacant residential or commercial buildings to register them, with an annual fee of up to $250 rising to a $1,000 cap, an in-state agent for an out-of-state owner, and inspections; a commonly owned multi-unit building with an occupied unit showing utility use, or a multi-unit building actively marketed for sale or lease, is not vacant, and the ordinance must exempt, for periods it sets, any vacant property advertised in good faith for sale or lease on commercially reasonable terms. The registration that matters most is your business's: an LLC, corporation, limited partnership or other entity formed outside Alabama that limits any owner's liability and transacts business here, which on the cautious reading includes owning and renting out property, must register with the Secretary of State, and until it does it may not maintain any lawsuit in an Alabama court, including an eviction or a suit for rent. It can still defend a suit, and its leases stay valid. Alabama has no assumed-name filing that a landlord must make. You must also give tenants the owner's or agent's name and address in writing (see `landlord-disclosure-al`).

title: Your Remedies When an Alabama Lease Ends for the Tenant's Breach
bodyText: When a lease ends because of the tenant's breach, you have a claim for possession and for rent, and a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the lease and reasonable attorney's fees. Before termination you may also sue for actual damages, reasonable attorney fees and an injunction for the tenant's noncompliance with the lease or the tenant's statutory duties, without ending the tenancy. You may not take possession yourself, by lockout or by cutting heat, water, electricity or gas, except where the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. Eviction cases go to the district or circuit court in the county where the property is and take priority on the court's calendar. A money claim alone of up to $6,000 (not counting interest and costs) belongs in district court, on its small-claims docket. A company may appear there through an officer or a full-time employee, but no party may recover attorney fees on the small-claims docket unless represented by a licensed attorney. You must make reasonable efforts to re-rent an abandoned unit, and any amount owed is reduced by what you recover.

title: No General Duty to Cooperate With or Report to Police in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a residential landlord, as a landlord, to cooperate with law enforcement, report crimes or suspicious activity by tenants, or join a crime-free housing program, and landlords are not on the state's mandatory lists for reporting child abuse or the abuse of protected adults. Duties that reach anyone still apply to you. In Baldwin, Escambia and Mobile counties, local acts make it the duty of any person who knows of a death in the categories those acts define to report it promptly to the coroner or medical examiner or to law enforcement, and not to disturb the body; in Escambia and Mobile a knowing failure is a Class B misdemeanor. Statewide, you may ask law enforcement to remove an unauthorized person under the unauthorized-occupant procedure (see `edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-al`), and a drug-related nuisance at your property can lead to a court action (see `edu-drug-nuisance-al`).

title: Recording an Alabama Lease: Only Over 20 Years
bodyText: Alabama does not require residential leases to be registered or recorded, and recording does not change any right under the landlord-tenant act. One rule matters for long leases: no leasehold may run longer than 99 years, and a lease for more than 20 years is void for the excess over 20 years unless the lease or a memorandum of it is acknowledged like a deed and recorded in the probate office of the county where the property is within one year after it is signed. An ordinary one-year or month-to-month residential lease needs no recording.

title: Liquidated Damages in an Alabama Lease: A Case-Law Question
bodyText: No Alabama statute sets a test for liquidated damages or penalty clauses in a residential lease. The Uniform Commercial Code's rules, which allow agreed damages only at a reasonable amount and void an unreasonably large figure as a penalty, cover sales and leases of goods, not dwellings. For a home, whether a fixed charge for a breach (an early-termination fee, a set cleaning charge, a fee for breaking the lease) is an enforceable estimate of your loss or an unenforceable penalty is decided by Alabama case law, which this library has not reviewed. The landlord-tenant act's own rule is that you recover appropriate damages and must mitigate them. So any fixed figure in an Alabama lease should be a reasonable estimate of the loss you expect, should not be charged on top of the actual loss it is meant to replace, and should never be labeled a penalty. The library's early-termination and other clauses are drafted to work if a court treats the figure as a cap on your actual damages.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant in Alabama: Two Routes, Depending on the Home
bodyText: Alabama lets you shift maintenance to a tenant only in two defined ways, and which one applies depends on the kind of home. A single-family residence is a structure used as one dwelling unit that has direct access to a street and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility with another unit (sharing a wall is allowed). For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, and the lease can be that writing, that the tenant handles garbage removal and the supply of water, hot water and heat, plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling. For every other dwelling (apartments, duplexes that share a water heater, rooms), the tenant may take on specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, such as a rent credit or payment; never work needed to meet the building and housing codes; never in a way that reduces your duties to other tenants; and you may not make signing or performing that agreement a condition of the lease. In neither case may the lease remove the habitability standard itself. Use `tenant-repair-agreement-al` for the separate agreement; do not put a duty shift for a multi-unit property in the lease.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and the Alabama Deposit Cap
bodyText: Alabama does not forbid nonrefundable fees, such as a pet fee or a move-in fee, and does not require any special notice for them. What matters is substance. Money you take as security for the tenant's obligations is a security deposit whatever you call it: it counts toward the one-month cap (plus any additional security for pets, changes to the premises or increased liability risks), and it must be returned or itemized within 60 days after the tenancy ends. A payment labeled a nonrefundable "deposit" invites a court to treat it as security. So name a true fee as a fee, state its amount and what it pays for, and do not use it to cover damage or unpaid rent at move-out. All lease charges count as rent under Alabama law. The library's optional clause `nonrefundable-fees-wv` lists the fees and sends any other security into the deposit.

title: No Separate Notice Required for Nonrefundable Fees in Alabama
