bodyText: Alabama does not require a separate notice, signature or acknowledgment for nonrefundable fees or nonrefundable deposits. Stating each fee, its amount and its purpose in the lease is enough as far as Alabama statute goes (see `edu-nonrefundable-fees-al`). Keep any money that secures the tenant's obligations inside the security deposit.

title: Out-of-State Owners in Alabama: Agents and Service of Process
bodyText: Alabama does not require an out-of-state owner to hire an Alabama manager or name an in-state agent in every lease, and no statute requires tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. What applies instead: at or before the start of every tenancy you must disclose in writing the name and business address of the person managing the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and for receiving notices, and keep that current; if you do not, the person who signed the lease for you becomes your agent for those purposes. A landlord who is not an Alabama resident, or a business entity not authorized to do business here, can be sued in Alabama over the rental and served as the court rules allow. An unregistered out-of-state entity is treated as consenting to service of process for claims arising from its Alabama business. In a Class 1 municipality with a vacant property ordinance, an out-of-state owner of a vacant building may be required to name an Alabama agent.

title: No Waiver or Shortening of the Notice to Terminate in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute lets a lease waive or shorten the notice a landlord must give before terminating a residential tenancy. Under the landlord-tenant act you terminate for a breach or for unpaid rent by written notice giving at least seven business days, and a periodic tenancy by written notice at least seven days before the termination date (weekly) or at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (monthly). A lease may not have the tenant give up rights under the law of unlawful detainer, and enforcing a lease you know contains a prohibited term carries a penalty, so the library offers no clause shortening or waiving these notices. Two situations need no notice at all. A tenancy for a fixed term ends when the term expires, and a tenant who stays on without your consent is holding over; you may sue for possession. Also, an older statute outside the act lets a landlord end a tenancy of less than a year on 10 days' written notice where the tenant holds over without a special agreement, and terminate for a default on a 10-day notice to quit, but those apply only to tenancies the act does not govern (see `edu-scope-exclusions-al`).

title: Which Alabama Tenant Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act names what a lease cannot take away. A lease may not have the tenant waive or give up: (1) the rights and remedies tied to your duty to maintain the premises; (2) the tenant's remedies when you materially fail to comply with the lease or the maintenance duty (the 14-day notice to terminate, damages, attorney fees and injunctions); (3) the tenant's remedies when you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service; (4) the security-deposit requirements; or (5) the law of unlawful detainer. Separately, a lease may not authorize a confession of judgment, make the tenant pay your attorney's fees or collection costs, or excuse or indemnify your legal liability. Rights outside that list are not protected by this section, but a court can still refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and a claim or right disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement, unless the settlement is unconscionable. Waiving a rule Alabama does not have is meaningless, so check that a right exists before drafting around it.

title: Paying to Stay in Alabama: The Notice Period, the Counterclaim and the Appeal
bodyText: Alabama gives a tenant three payment routes and no general right to redeem the tenancy. First, the nonpayment notice: it must state the rent and any late fees owed, and if the tenant pays within seven business days after receiving it, the lease does not end. A tenant may cure breaches only twice in any 12 months without your written consent. Second, an appeal: a tenant who appeals an eviction judgment can stop the writ of possession only by paying into court all rent payable under the lease since the case was filed and keeping current while the appeal is pending; a missed payment lets you get the writ. Third, in the possession case a tenant who counterclaims must pay accrued and accruing rent into court; the court decides whether the tenant stays in possession, and if no rent remains due once the counterclaim and payments are applied, judgment in the possession action is entered for the tenant. Outside those routes, no statute lets a tenant reinstate the lease simply by paying after the notice period ends or after judgment, and nothing requires you to accept partial rent or a payment from a charity or agency. If you do accept rent after a default and still want to evict, remember that accepting rent with knowledge of the default waives your right to terminate for it unless the tenant agrees in writing, after the breach, that it does not (see `edu-waiver-by-acceptance-al`). Alabama prescribes no reservation wording for partial payments.

title: Rental Inspections in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no state rental-inspection program and no statute letting a lease authorize a government inspector to enter without the tenant's consent at the time. Counties and cities may not adopt rental housing codes or ordinances aimed at landlords, but they may enforce building codes, health codes and other general laws against rental property if those laws apply equally to similar owner-occupied homes; an inspection under such a code can reach your property. In a Class 1 municipality that adopts a vacant property registration ordinance, the ordinance may let the program administrator inspect the interior and exterior of a vacant property on at least 10 days' prior notice to the owner once registration is made or required, and yearly while it stays registered; a commonly owned multi-unit building with at least one unit occupied with evidence of utility use, or a multi-unit building actively marketed for sale or lease, is not "vacant", and the ordinance must exempt, for periods it sets, any vacant property advertised in good faith for sale or lease on commercially reasonable terms. Your own access to the unit follows the act's entry rules. The library's optional clause `rental-inspection-cooperation-mn` asks the tenant to cooperate with code inspections without treating the lease as the tenant's consent for an inspector to enter.

title: How You Hold a Deposit in Alabama: No Rule for Owners; Trust Accounts for Brokers
bodyText: Alabama does not tell a landlord where or how to hold a security deposit. There is no escrow, separate-account, bank-disclosure, bond or interest requirement for an owner managing their own property (see `edu-no-deposit-interest-al`). A licensed real estate broker or agent who holds deposits for an owner is different: real estate licensees must deposit and account for all money belonging to or held for others in a separate, federally insured account at an Alabama financial institution, may not commingle it with their own funds, and must keep records of it for at least three years. The Real Estate Commission's rules make the qualifying broker who provides the management services responsible for the deposits, require residential deposits to be handled under the landlord-tenant act, and require an accounting and transfer of all deposits and prepaid rent within seven business days after a management agreement ends or the property is sold. Even if you self-manage, keeping deposits in a separate account makes the 60-day refund and itemization easier to prove.

title: The Deposit Rules Cannot Be Waived in the Lease
bodyText: A lease may not have the tenant waive or give up the requirements of security deposits set by Alabama's landlord-tenant act. So a lease cannot raise the one-month cap (outside the act's own exceptions for pets, changes to the premises and increased liability risks), stretch the 60-day refund and itemization deadline, drop the itemized list, waive the double-deposit penalty for a missed deadline, or make the tenant forfeit the deposit on terms the act does not allow. Such a term is unenforceable, and enforcing a lease you know contains it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. The library's deposit clauses are drafted to the statutory terms; see `security-deposit-return-al` and `security-deposit-cap-al`.

title: Deposits When an Alabama Rental Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell a rental in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, you are relieved of liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless you agree otherwise, but you stay liable to the tenant for all security the tenant can recover and all prepaid rent. Separately, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules, so the buyer must refund or itemize within 60 days even if you never handed the deposit over. In practice: transfer the deposits and prepaid rent to the buyer at closing, get the buyer's written assumption, and send the tenants written notice of the sale and the new owner's or manager's name and address (the owner-identity disclosure must be kept current). If a licensed broker holds the deposits, the broker must account for them and transfer them to the buyer within seven business days after closing, unless the closing documents already moved them.

title: The Penalty for a Late Deposit Refund in Alabama: Double the Original Deposit
bodyText: If you fail to mail a timely refund or itemized accounting within 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered, you must pay the tenant double the amount of the tenant's original deposit, not double the amount withheld. The penalty turns only on timeliness: Alabama has no separate forfeiture for a missing bank notice, an escrow failure or an incomplete damage list, and no rule that a late list forfeits your right to sue for damage. Mailing by first-class mail within the 60 days, to the address the tenant gave in writing, is sufficient compliance. Either side may still recover other damages it is owed, so a landlord who pays the penalty can still sue for unpaid rent or damage beyond the deposit. Separately, a lease term waiving the deposit rules is unenforceable, and enforcing a lease you know contains one costs actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and attorney's fees.

title: No Rule on Posting Deposit Standards in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule requiring you to post, publish or give tenants the standards you use to calculate deposit deductions, whatever the size of your property. Deductions must still be limited to accrued rent and damages from the tenant's breach of the tenant's statutory duties, and itemized in writing within 60 days. Applying the same written standards to every unit is good practice and supports your itemized lists if a tenant disputes them.

title: No State Limit on Renting Single-Family Homes in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or restricts short-term renting of residential property at the state level. Local zoning still applies to land use. Whether a county or city ordinance that singles out rental homes (for example, an owner-occupancy requirement) survives the landlord-tenant act's ban on local laws aimed at residential landlords is unsettled: the act keeps only building codes, health codes and other general laws that apply equally to similar owner-occupied property, and a rule that applies only to rentals does not. Check your city's zoning code before buying a property to rent, and take advice if an ordinance treats rentals differently. Homeowners' association covenants can also restrict leasing (see `hoa-compliance-al`).

title: The Dollar Limits in Alabama Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: Alabama sets few figures. The security deposit may not exceed one month's periodic rent, except for pets, changes to the premises or increased liability risks. Missing the 60-day deposit refund or accounting costs you double the original deposit. Enforcing a lease you know contains a prohibited term costs actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and attorney's fees. Some wrongs carry up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees: your willful, bad-faith failure to deliver possession, an unlawful lockout or a willful cutoff of essential services, retaliation, and, on your side, a tenant's willful, bad-faith holdover. During a declared state of emergency, a rent 25 percent or more above the area's average in the 30 days before the emergency, not explained by reasonable costs, is prima facie unconscionable. Alabama has no statutory cap on rent, rent increases, late fees, application fees, pet fees or other charges, and local governments may not set one.

title: The Tenant's Duties Under Alabama Law
bodyText: Every Alabama tenant has seven duties whether or not the lease repeats them. The tenant must: comply with the obligations building and housing codes place primarily on tenants that materially affect health and safety; keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste in a clean and safe manner; keep plumbing fixtures as clear as their condition permits; use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably; not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly, recklessly or negligently let anyone else do so; and behave, and require guests to behave, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. The tenant must also occupy the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise, follow valid rules, and not unreasonably refuse you access. If a breach of these duties materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, and the tenant does not fix it within seven days after your written notice (or promptly in an emergency), you may do the work and bill the reasonable cost as rent. A material breach also supports a seven-business-day notice to terminate. The library's `tenant-maintenance` clause states these duties in the lease.

title: No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no tenant protection act like California's: no statewide cap on rent increases, no just-cause rule, and so no required notice telling tenants about one, no exemption notice for properties outside it, and no sunset date to track. Local governments may not fill the gap: no county or city may enact or enforce an ordinance that would have the effect of controlling the rent charged for private property, or any ordinance on landlord-tenant rights and obligations. There is nothing to be exempt from, so no exemption statement belongs in an Alabama lease.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no tenant protection act like California's: no statewide cap on rent increases, no just-cause rule, and so no required notice telling tenants about one, no exemption notice for properties outside it, and no sunset date to track. Local governments may not fill the gap: no county or city may enact or enforce an ordinance that would have the effect of controlling the rent charged for private property, or any ordinance on landlord-tenant rights and obligations. Do not copy California's rent-cap notice into an Alabama lease; it would describe rights your tenants do not have.

title: No Tenant-Protection Sunset to Track in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no tenant protection act like California's: no statewide cap on rent increases, no just-cause rule, and so no required notice telling tenants about one, no exemption notice for properties outside it, and no sunset date to track. Local governments may not fill the gap: no county or city may enact or enforce an ordinance that would have the effect of controlling the rent charged for private property, or any ordinance on landlord-tenant rights and obligations. Alabama's landlord-tenant act has no expiry date; it applies to rental agreements entered into, extended or renewed on or after January 1, 2007.

title: A Court May Refuse to Enforce an Unconscionable Lease Term
bodyText: If a court finds, as a matter of law, that a lease or any term in it was unconscionable when it was made, the court may refuse to enforce the lease, enforce the rest of it without the unconscionable term, or limit the term to avoid an unconscionable result. The same applies to a settlement in which a party gave up a claim or right under the landlord-tenant act or the lease. When unconscionability is raised, each side gets a chance to present evidence about the setting, purpose and effect of the lease. Alabama's statutes do not define unconscionability for leases; what counts is case law. One related statute applies to rent itself: during a declared state of emergency, renting a dwelling house at an unconscionable price is unlawful, and a price 25 percent or more above the area's average in the 30 days before the emergency, not explained by reasonable costs, is prima facie unconscionable. Alabama has no statute that declares any particular lease clause enforceable despite unconscionability, and none that lets a court revise a running lease because performance has become excessively burdensome.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach Waives Your Right to Terminate for It
bodyText: In Alabama, accepting rent while you know the tenant is in default, or accepting performance that varies from the lease, waives your right to terminate the lease for that breach. The only exception is an agreement made after the breach has occurred. That timing matters: a standard non-waiver clause signed with the lease, before any breach, does not by itself stop the waiver. Cautious course once a breach has happened and you intend to terminate: refuse or promptly return rent you do not want to count as a waiver, or get the tenant's written agreement, made after the breach, that your acceptance of a payment does not waive the breach or any notice you have given. Accepting a full cure of unpaid rent within the notice period ends that default anyway. Remember that a tenant may cure a breach only twice in any 12-month period without your written consent, and some breaches cannot be cured at all. No Alabama statute addresses accepting rent after an eviction case is filed; that is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: No Alarm-Tampering Fee in Alabama: Charge Your Actual Cost
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that sets or allows a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm in a rental. The only alarm-tampering offense in Alabama law is for smoke detectors in hotel guest rooms, which does not cover apartments or houses rented to tenants. What you can do instead: the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, so you can charge the tenant the actual, reasonable cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant or the tenant's guests disabled, collect it from the security deposit at move-out, or sue for it. If a disabled alarm is a health or safety problem that a repair or replacement can fix and the tenant does not fix it within seven days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, do the work, and bill the actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date. Do not put a flat tampering fee in the lease: no Alabama statute allows one, and whether a fixed charge is an unenforceable penalty is a question for the courts. The library's optional clause `detector-care-la` covers this by charging the reasonable cost only.

title: No Alternate Housing Duty in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama law does not require you to provide or pay for substitute, alternate or temporary housing while repairs are made, whether or not the tenant asks. The tenant's remedies for a repair failure are to end the lease after a 14-day written notice, to sue for actual damages and attorney's fees, or, for a loss of heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, to end the lease or recover the reduced rental value. After a fire or casualty the tenant may move out and end the lease or pay reduced rent for the part still usable. If you choose to put a tenant up elsewhere during major repairs, agree the terms in writing, including how rent is handled.

title: Excluding Appliances in an Alabama Lease
bodyText: Alabama has no rule that appliances found in a rental are presumed to be supplied by the landlord, and no list of appliances that cannot be excluded. Your maintenance duty covers facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply. You may therefore state in the lease that an item left at the property is not supplied and will not be maintained, using the optional clause `appliances-excluded-al`. Whether an item you leave in the unit for the tenant's use counts as supplied by you is not settled by the statute; if it does, a no-repair term waives a duty the lease cannot waive. The cautious course is to offer to remove each listed item before the tenancy starts and list only items the tenant chooses to keep. Do not list anything that a building or housing code requires you to provide, anything needed to keep the unit habitable, or anything needed for heat, running water or hot water, since those duties cannot be waived; and do not list an item whose failure could seriously affect health or safety, such as a gas appliance or water heater. For a home that is not a single-family residence, do not use this clause to move repair work you do owe to the tenant; that takes a separate signed agreement (`tenant-repair-agreement-al`).

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairways or other elevated exterior elements of rental buildings, and no inspection report to give tenants. You must still make repairs needed to keep the premises habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, and comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety. Inspect balconies, decks and railings yourself on a regular schedule and repair them promptly.

title: No Bed Bug Statute in Alabama: Cooperation by Lease
bodyText: Alabama has no bed bug statute: no disclosure, inspection, treatment or cooperation rule. The tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits, must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect or make repairs. If the tenant does not fix a tenant-caused health or safety problem within seven days after your written notice, you may do the work and bill the reasonable cost as rent. The library's optional clause `pest-cooperation-pr` asks the tenant to report infestations, allow treatment and follow preparation instructions, and charges treatment to the tenant only where the tenant's side caused it. See also `edu-no-bed-bug-disclosure-al`.

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Statute in Alabama: Deduct Only Tenant-Caused Costs
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out and no age or condition test for carpet or paint deductions. The deposit rule is narrow: at the end of the tenancy you may apply the deposit only to unpaid rent and to damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties, such as keeping the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits and not deliberately or negligently damaging it, itemized in writing within 60 days. So you may deduct the reasonable cost of cleaning carpets the tenant left dirtier than the tenant's cleaning duty allows, or of repairing carpet the tenant damaged. The library does not offer an Alabama clause requiring professional cleaning in every case, because a flat cleaning charge that does not rest on the tenant's own failure may not fit the deposit rule. Take dated photos of the carpets at move-in and move-out.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no specific rule on lighting common areas, and no rule on whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own meter. You must keep common areas clean and safe, and adequate lighting of stairs, halls and entrances is part of that. You are not responsible for paying utilities unless the lease says so, so utility payment is set by the lease; but do not use the lease to make a tenant in a multi-unit building responsible for keeping common areas safe, which stays your duty. If a tenant's meter serves common-area lights, say so in the lease before the tenancy starts and adjust the rent or reimburse the cost.

title: No Statutory Rent Bar After Condemnation in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that bars you from collecting rent after a building is condemned or ordered vacated. Cities may adopt housing ordinances that prohibit occupancy of an unsafe or insanitary dwelling until it is brought up to code, and cities and counties can order unsafe buildings repaired or demolished. If an order stops lawful occupancy, the tenant's statutory remedies apply: after a fire or casualty the tenant may move out and end the lease or pay reduced rent for the usable part; for a failure to keep the unit habitable, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' written notice and recover actual damages. Whether rent is owed at all for a period when occupancy was unlawful is not settled by statute. The cautious course: do not charge rent for any period in which an official order bars occupancy, and refund unearned prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit if the lease ends.

title: Habitability Rules Alabama Does Not Have
bodyText: Searches of all Alabama statutes and recent acts found none of the following habitability rules that some other states have: a repair-and-deduct remedy or rent escrow (the tenant may not withhold rent while in possession); a presumption of habitability or uninhabitability; a required lease statement that the unit is fit; a duty to provide alternate housing during repairs; a minimum heat temperature; a water heater temperature setting; a duty to supply a stove or refrigerator; a radiator cover rule; window guard or security bar rules; balcony inspections; deadbolt, peephole or rekeying requirements; a statewide housing code; and a bar on rent after condemnation. What does apply: your statutory duties to comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, keep the premises habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain supplied facilities and appliances, provide garbage removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, with the tenant's notice, termination, damages and essential-services remedies. Local building, fire and housing codes may add requirements. Each item has its own note in the library.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no law on letting a tenant house friends or family displaced by a disaster, and no rule that suspends a lease's guest or occupancy limits after a disaster. The lease's guest and occupancy terms apply as written, and fair housing law still applies to how you treat household members. If a tenant asks to take in displaced people, agree any temporary change in writing, with an end date. Displaced-person relocation rules in Alabama law cover people moved by state acquisitions of property, not disaster guests.

title: Disasters: Casualty Rules and Emergency Rent Pricing in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that ends a tenancy or suspends rent because of a declared natural disaster. If a fire, storm or other casualty you did not cause substantially impairs use of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay in the usable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty. The optional clause `casualty-landlord-termination-al` gives you a matching right to end the lease. During a declared state of emergency, Alabama's price-gouging law bars unconscionable prices for the rental of any facility in the affected area; a price 25 percent or more above the average of the prior 30 days is presumed unconscionable unless your added costs explain it. The cautious course is not to raise rent on new or renewing leases in an affected area during the emergency period beyond your documented added costs.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama gives a landlord no statutory right to end a lease because of an environmental event such as contamination, a chemical release, mold or a sinkhole. If the event is a casualty that substantially impairs use of the unit, the tenant has the casualty rights, and the library's optional clause `casualty-landlord-termination-al` gives you a right to end the lease after a fire or other casualty you did not cause. The library does not offer a separate environmental-event termination clause for Alabama: the casualty clause covers sudden physical damage, and for other conditions you keep your duty to repair and keep the premises habitable, and may end a periodic tenancy with the normal written notice.

title: Fire and Building Codes That Reach Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no statewide housing or property-maintenance code for rentals, but fire and building codes still reach your property in three ways. First, the State Fire Marshal has adopted the 2021 International Fire Code, with some appendices, effective January 1, 2025; the rule says it is used for projects whose architect contract is dated on or after that date, and the Fire Marshal's fuel gas, mechanical and existing-buildings codes are older 2015 editions. Second, the Fire Marshal or a local fire official may inspect any building on a written complaint and order you, as owner, or the occupant to fix a fire hazard right away, such as missing repairs, fire escapes, alarms or extinguishing equipment; ignoring the order is a misdemeanor. Third, cities and counties may adopt building, fire-prevention and housing codes, and from January 1, 2027 builders and remodelers of homes and buildings of up to four units must work to the Alabama Residential Building Code or the local residential code. The state building code itself covers only state buildings, schools, hotels and theaters, not ordinary rentals. Whatever building and housing codes apply to your property are part of your repair duty under the landlord-tenant act. A local code can apply to rentals only if it applies equally to similar owner-occupied homes. Check with the local building official and fire department for the code and edition in force where the property is.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit Duty for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in a rental home or apartment. The State Fire Marshal may not require sprinklers in a single-family dwelling, and since October 1, 2024 no state board, city or county may adopt a code that requires a residential fire sprinkler system in a home or in a building of up to four units; a local ordinance on residential sprinklers adopted on or before March 9, 2010 may still be enforced. Larger apartment buildings can still need sprinklers under the State Fire Marshal's fire code or a local building or fire code, mainly for new construction and major work. The State Fire Marshal's rule is unclear on whether the fire code's appendix on adding sprinklers to existing high-rise buildings is adopted, so if you own a high-rise, take the cautious course and ask the State Fire Marshal's office. If the property has a sprinkler system, keep it in good and safe working order as part of your repair duty, and use a permitted fire sprinkler contractor for installation, repair, maintenance and inspection unless your own trained employees do the work on your own system. A fire official may also order you to fix a lack of fire extinguishing equipment that makes the building especially liable to fire.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama statutes and rules incorporate model codes and standards in two different ways, and it matters which edition applies to your property. Some statutes adopt a standard as it changes: the fire sprinkler law refers to the latest edition of the NFPA sprinkler standards, and the fire alarm law requires systems installed after August 1, 2009 to follow the latest edition of NFPA 72. Others adopt one fixed edition: the State Fire Marshal's rule adopts the 2021 International Fire Code, and its fuel gas, mechanical and existing-buildings codes are 2015 editions, with later editions allowed only on request for a project. The Alabama Residential Building Code is whatever edition the Home Builders Licensure Board adopts, based on a published edition of the International Residential Code. Local codes are whatever edition the city or county adopted by ordinance or resolution. Ask the local building official which edition applied when your building was built or renovated.

title: When a Repair Problem Is Serious Enough for Tenant Remedies
bodyText: Alabama's tenant remedies turn on two different tests. To start the 14-day cure-or-terminate process, the tenant needs either a material breach of the lease, or a breach of your statutory maintenance duties that materially affects health and safety. A minor or cosmetic defect does not qualify. The statute does not define "material" or list qualifying conditions, so whether a defect qualifies is decided case by case. The tenant's essential-services remedy has its own test: it applies when, after notice, you willfully or negligently fail to promptly supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service. A retaliation claim based on a complaint to a code agency also requires a code violation materially affecting health and safety. None of these remedies arises for a condition the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused. Treat any condition that threatens health or safety, or any failure of an essential service, as material and fix it promptly.

title: No Habitability Presumption in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama law sets no presumption about habitability. No statute says that a code violation, an inspector's finding or a missing service is presumed to make a unit uninhabitable, and none presumes that a unit is habitable because the tenant moved in or did not complain. Whether a condition breaches your duty to keep the premises habitable, or materially affects health and safety, is proved like any other fact. Your duties still apply in full: comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, make all repairs needed to keep the premises habitable, and keep supplied facilities and appliances working. Keep records of inspections, repair requests and repairs, since they are your evidence if a dispute arises.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in Alabama Leases
bodyText: Alabama does not require the lease to say that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation. The duty exists anyway: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the lease and your statutory maintenance duties, including keeping the premises habitable. A lease cannot waive those duties. The library's maintenance clause states your repair duty in the lease for clarity; it is optional, not required.

title: Heat in Alabama Rentals
bodyText: You must supply reasonable heat at all times, and keep heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order. The heat duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for heat, or where the unit's heat comes from equipment the tenant alone controls on a direct utility connection. Alabama sets no minimum indoor temperature or heating season. You are not responsible for paying utilities, including heating fuel or power, unless the lease says so. For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant supplies heat; for any other dwelling, a shift of heat or heating-equipment work to the tenant needs the separate signed agreement described in `tenant-repair-agreement-al`, never a lease clause. If, after notice, you willfully or negligently fail to make heat available, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' written notice or recover the reduced rental value; cutting off heat to force a tenant out is unlawful and costs up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is more, plus attorney's fees. Heating boilers in apartment houses of six or more units need state boiler inspection certificates.

title: Remedies for Unlawful Entry in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama sets no fixed penalty for entering a rental without proper notice, but the tenant has remedies. If you make an unlawful entry, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant, the tenant may get a court order to stop it or end the lease under the 14-day breach procedure, and in either case recover actual damages. You must not abuse your right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in an emergency, by court order, after abandonment, or under the other listed exceptions, give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable times; posting a note on the main entry door stating the time and purpose is allowed. A tenant who unreasonably refuses lawful access gives you the same remedies in reverse.

title: No Key-Control Mandate in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring a key-control policy, key logs, or background checks for employees who hold keys, at any size of complex. Keep keys and codes secure anyway: you may enter only as the landlord-tenant act allows, and your staff's misuse of keys can expose you to negligence claims.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate that you must get for a rental or attach to the lease. Alabama law also does not require you to remove or abate existing lead-based paint. For a home built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet still apply; use the library's lead disclosure. What Alabama does certify is people and firms: anyone doing lead inspections, risk assessments, abatement or renovation that disturbs paint in pre-1978 housing must be accredited and certified. The state statute exempts an owner renovating his or her own residential property, but the Department of Public Health's rule treats an owner working in a dwelling occupied by others, such as a rented unit, as covered. The cautious course is to use a certified firm and accredited renovator for paint-disturbing work in an occupied pre-1978 rental, unless the work is minor repair and maintenance or the components have been tested lead-free.

title: No Alabama Lead Notice With the Lease; Renovation Pamphlet Only
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet, Alabama requires no state lead notice, certificate or packet to be delivered with the lease. Alabama has one lead notice of its own, and it comes with renovation, not with the lease: before renovation that disturbs paint in a pre-1978 rental unit, the firm doing the work must give the owner the federal Renovate Right pamphlet and also give it to an adult occupant if the owner does not live there, getting a signed acknowledgment or a certificate of mailing. For work in common areas of a multi-unit building, the firm must notify each affected unit in writing or post signs. If you or your staff do the renovation yourselves in an occupied rental, treat yourselves as the firm and follow these steps. Emergency repairs are exempt from the advance pamphlet. A water system may also send its customers notices about lead in drinking water; that is the water supplier's duty, not yours. See also the library's lead disclosure and lead hazards rows.

title: Elevators, Boilers and Other Building Facilities in Alabama
bodyText: Two Alabama safety laws put duties on owners of building facilities that rental buildings often have. Elevators, platform lifts, stairway chairlifts, escalators and dumbwaiters must be registered with the state, inspected every year by a licensed elevator inspector, and tested on schedule by a licensed elevator mechanic; you have 30 days from the inspection report to correct violations. Boilers and pressure vessels need state inspection certificates, though heating boilers in private homes and in apartment houses with fewer than six units are exempt from the inspection and certificate rules, and small water heaters fall outside the boiler law. Alabama has no rule on garage door openers or other consumer-product facilities in rentals. Whatever facilities you supply, you must keep in good and safe working order.

title: No Pesticide Notice Rule for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring you to notify tenants before pesticide application or pest control treatment, beyond the ordinary notice to enter. You need the tenant's consent or at least two days' notice before entering for pest control, unless you have given the tenant, separately from the lease, a general notice or advance schedule for pest control service, in which case no further notice is needed; posting a note on the main entry door is an allowed way to give notice. Pest control companies are licensed by the state. Pest problems that affect habitability are part of your repair duty.

title: No State Pool Safety Rule for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no state statute or state health rule setting pool fence, barrier, lifeguard or safety-notice duties for pools at apartments or rental homes. The State Board of Health's pool standards apply to hotel pools, and the hotel rules exclude apartments that do not offer single-night stays. County health departments may have their own swimming pool rules, and cities may adopt swimming pool codes by ordinance, so check with the county health department and the local building official before opening a pool to tenants. Your duty to keep common areas clean and safe covers a pool held out for tenants' use.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to test a private well that serves a rental or to give test results to tenants (state agency well rules were not read). Well construction is regulated through the licensing of water well drillers, not through the landlord-tenant act. If a well supplies the unit, it is part of your duty to supply running water and to keep plumbing and sanitary facilities in good and safe working order, and water that is unsafe to drink can breach your habitability duty. Testing the well before each tenancy, and keeping the results, is the cautious course.

title: Promises to Repair in Alabama Leases
bodyText: Alabama does not require your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. But a promise you make in the lease, or one the tenant can prove you made, is part of the rental agreement, which includes oral agreements. If you materially fail to keep it, the tenant may end the lease after a 14-day written notice unless you cure, and may recover actual damages and attorney's fees. Put every promised repair in the lease or a signed addendum with a completion date, so both sides know what was agreed. The tenant must not unreasonably refuse you entry to make agreed repairs.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination Right in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that lets you end a lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or more than the property is worth. After a fire or other casualty that you did not cause and that substantially impairs use of the property, the library's optional clause `casualty-landlord-termination-al` lets you end the lease by written notice; that clause rests on the lease, not on a cost test. Otherwise, you must make the repairs needed to keep the premises habitable, and you may end a periodic tenancy only with the normal written notice. The tenant has the casualty and repair termination rights described in `edu-casualty-termination-al` and `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-al`.

title: No Rent Escrow or Escrow Exemption in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rent escrow or repair escrow program, so there is no exemption from one and no exemption notice to give tenants. A tenant may not withhold rent while in possession. The only time rent goes to the court is when you sue a tenant in possession for possession or rent and the tenant counterclaims; the tenant then pays the rent as it comes due into court. See `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-al`.

title: Repair Notices in Alabama
bodyText: To start the 14-day cure-or-terminate process for a repair problem, the tenant must give you written notice describing the problem. For a failure to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the remedy starts once you have received notice of the breach; that notice need not be written, and under the act you have notice of a fact you actually know, have been told, or have reason to know from the circumstances. Your repair duties themselves do not depend on any notice from the tenant. A lease may ask tenants to report repairs in writing, and the library's maintenance clause does, but it cannot take away the tenant's statutory rights: if you actually knew of the problem, a missing written request does not excuse you. Alabama has no rule that a lease allowing verbal requests waives your right to written notice; the termination notice is always in writing. A tenant's request for a repair counts as consent for you to enter and make it.

title: No Code Variance Notice Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statewide housing or sanitary code for rentals and no rule that a code variance, waiver or exception for a rental must be given to tenants or attached to the lease. If a local building or housing code official grants you a variance, keep a copy; tell tenants about it if it affects their safety or use of the unit. The state boiler board may allow variations in boiler inspection schedules, and some statutes exempt certain buildings from building codes, but none requires notice to tenants.

title: No Lock or Security Device Statute in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or other security devices in rentals, and no duty to rekey locks between tenants. Two rules still matter. You may not change the locks or otherwise exclude a tenant from the unit except through the court eviction process or after abandonment or surrender; if you do, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is more, plus attorney's fees. And you must keep the premises habitable, keep common areas safe, and maintain facilities you supply, which includes locks you provide. Rekeying between tenants is good practice. Whether a security failure makes you liable for a crime against a tenant is a negligence question for the courts, not a statutory duty; the landlord-tenant act neither creates nor removes tort duties.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no law that delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for federal or state employees during a government shutdown or furlough. The lease's rent and late-fee terms and the normal notice rules apply; for nonpayment you must give written notice of at least seven business days stating the rent and late fees owed before ending the lease. Any payment plan you agree with a furloughed tenant should be in writing.

title: No Smart Access Statute in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on smart locks, keypads, app-based entry or other smart access systems in rentals, and no law letting a domestic-violence survivor ask a device account manager to cut off another person's access. If you use such a system, the ordinary rules apply: you may enter only as the landlord-tenant act allows, you may not use the system to lock a tenant out, and you must keep it, as a facility you supply, in good working order. Companies that install electronic security systems for others are licensed by the state; that licensing does not regulate you as the user. Spell out in the lease how credentials are issued, replaced and returned.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure or Retrofit Aid in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no law requiring you to tell a tenant, in the lease or anywhere else, whether the building has fire sprinklers. Alabama also has no state grant, loan or tax credit for adding sprinklers to an existing rental building. You may describe the building's fire protection in the lease if you choose; if you do, keep it accurate. For whether a sprinkler system is required at all, see the separate note on sprinkler duties.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule requiring radiator covers, on request or otherwise, and no lease rider about them. If the property has steam or hot-water heat, keep the heating system in good and safe working order and supply reasonable heat. In an apartment house of six or more units, a heating boiler is subject to the state boiler law's periodic certificate inspections; boilers in private residences and smaller apartment houses are exempt from those inspections. If young children live in a unit with exposed hot radiators, consider covers as a safety measure.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to supply a stove or refrigerator in a rental (local housing codes were not read and may). If you do supply them, or any other appliance, you must keep it in good and safe working order, unless the problem was caused willfully or negligently by the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or someone else on the premises with the tenant's consent. Whether a unit is a roomer's unit also turns on these items: under the landlord-tenant act a roomer occupies a unit that lacks a toilet, refrigerator, stove, kitchen sink and a bathtub or shower all provided by the landlord, where one or more of them are shared. Say in the lease which appliances you supply. To list items left at the property that you will not maintain, see `appliances-excluded-al`.

title: No State Rule on Refused Subsidy Inspections in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama law has no rule on a landlord's or tenant's refusal of a housing inspection in a subsidized tenancy. Inspections in voucher and other assisted tenancies are governed by the federal program rules, the housing assistance payments contract and the lease addendum, not by Alabama statute. Under Alabama law the tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect or repair, and you may enter without consent only in the listed cases, so coordinate housing-authority inspection dates with the tenant and give the normal notice. Read the housing authority's rules on missed or refused inspections before signing a voucher lease.

title: No State Subsidy Proration Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule on how a subsidized tenant's share of rent is prorated or abated when a unit fails habitability standards. When a housing authority stops or abates its assistance payments for a failed inspection, the federal program rules and the assistance contract decide what happens; Alabama law does not let you shift the abated amount to the tenant by statute. Under Alabama law the tenant may not withhold rent while in possession, and the tenant's repair remedies are notice-and-termination, damages, and the essential-services remedy. Under the federal voucher rules, the family is not responsible for the housing authority's share of the rent. For assistance contracts signed on or after, or renewed after, June 6, 2024, you also may not end the tenancy because the authority withheld or abated its payments, and the authority does not pay you for the abated period once you make the repairs. So do not charge the tenant any amount the housing authority stopped paying; fix failed items within the federal deadlines (24 hours for life-threatening items, 30 days for others, unless the housing authority allows longer).

title: Repair and Demolition Orders; No Housing Receivership in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no receivership program for substandard rental buildings. Instead, local governments and the State Fire Marshal use repair, closure and demolition orders. Cities may adopt housing ordinances that set minimum standards, compel owners to repair or alter dwellings, and bar occupancy until the work is done. Cities, and counties for unincorporated areas, may order an unsafe building repaired or demolished after notice and charge the cost as a lien on the property. A fire official may order a fire hazard fixed, and if a court order is not obeyed the court may have the work done at the owner's expense, with a lien for the cost. A court can also close a building used for a drug nuisance and appoint a receiver to sell the owner's furnishings and fixtures. Respond promptly to any notice, and give the tenant written notice of any work that needs entry.

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Are Not Made
bodyText: If you fail to make repairs Alabama requires, the tenant's remedies are: (1) a written notice ending the lease on a date at least 14 days after you receive it unless you fix the problem first, for a material breach of the lease or a breach of your maintenance duties that materially affects health and safety; (2) a lawsuit for actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees and a court order to make repairs; (3) if you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service after notice, either a 14-day written termination notice or damages for the reduced rental value; and (4) a counterclaim if you sue for possession or rent. Alabama has no repair-and-deduct remedy and no rent escrow program, and a tenant in possession may not withhold rent. When you sue a tenant who is still in possession and the tenant counterclaims, the tenant must pay the rent that has come due, and keep paying it as it comes due, into court; the court decides who gets the money, and if the tenant's counterclaim is without merit and not in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees. None of these remedies arises for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused. For the full list of your repair duties see `edu-landlord-repair-duties-al`.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule on the temperature setting of a water heater in a rental, and no duty to set or check it before a new tenant moves in. You must supply reasonable amounts of hot water at all times unless the unit's hot water comes from equipment the tenant alone controls on a direct utility connection, and you must keep supplied water heaters in good and safe working order. Separately, the state boiler law requires certificate inspections of hot water supply boilers, but it exempts directly fired units of 120 gallons or less, 200,000 BTU per hour or less, and water at 210 degrees Fahrenheit or less, which covers ordinary residential water heaters; heating boilers in private homes or apartment houses with fewer than six units are also exempt from the inspection and certificate rules. A scald-safe setting is good practice, but it is not set by Alabama law.

title: No Waterbed Statute in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals. You may ban them, require your consent, or set conditions in the lease, such as a proper frame and liner and the tenant's insurance; the library's optional clause `waterbed-mn` does this. The tenant is responsible for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes. If you take extra security for the risk, it counts as a security deposit; Alabama's one-month cap on deposits has an exception for increased liability risks to you or the premises, and the deposit must be returned or accounted for within 60 days after the tenancy ends.

title: No Window Guard Rule in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires window guards or window-fall devices in rentals or a lease notice about them, or regulates burglar or security bars or their release mechanisms (the model codes the State Fire Marshal adopts by rule were not read for this). Your general duties still apply: comply with applicable building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, which can include emergency escape openings in bedrooms, and keep the premises habitable and common areas safe. If you install security bars on bedroom windows, make sure they can be opened from inside for escape and check the local building code.

title: Agreed Notice Methods in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule that lets you and the tenant agree on an extra way of giving a notice the law requires, such as a text message. The Alabama landlord-tenant act says a person is notified when the sender takes steps reasonably calculated to inform the other person in the ordinary course, even if the person never actually learns of it. A tenant receives a notice when it is handed to the tenant, or three days after it is mailed with postage prepaid to the tenant's last known residence. You receive a tenant's notice when it is delivered at your place of business or mailed to a place you have designated for receiving notices, so name that address in the lease. These rules do not apply to a notice ending a tenancy or starting an eviction. Alabama's electronic-transactions law works only where both sides have agreed to deal electronically, and it does not reach notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's primary residence. So give every termination, default and cure notice on paper, by hand delivery or mail. For routine messages the law does not require, such as reminders, you may use e-mail or text if the tenant agrees, but keep a paper copy of anything important. The library offers no clause adding an electronic notice method in Alabama.

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property faces a foreclosure, condemnation, lawsuit, code-enforcement order or other proceeding that could affect the tenancy. Some proceedings reach the tenant directly instead. When a city building official finds a building unsafe enough to be a public nuisance, the notice to repair or demolish goes to the owner by certified or registered mail and a copy is posted near an entrance of the building. When a Class 2 municipality forecloses its code-enforcement lien in court, it mails the petition to the property addressed to the occupants and posts a notice on the property. When a state agency acquires property for a public project, it must try to schedule the work so that no lawful occupant has to move out of a home without at least 90 days' written notice of the move-out date. A Fire Marshal's repair order is served on the owner or the occupant. Because papers may arrive at the rental rather than at your address, the library's lease clause asking the tenant to pass on any notice of a proceeding to recover the property (`tenant-forward-proceedings-ca`) applies in Alabama. For foreclosure of a mortgage on the rental, see `edu-foreclosure-al`.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no law regulating automatic-renewal terms in residential leases: no general consumer auto-renewal statute, no bold-type or opt-in rule, no required reminder before a lease renews, and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to renew. A lease may renew itself, or roll into a month-to-month tenancy, if it says so, because the parties may set the term of the agreement. Without a renewal term, a fixed-term lease simply ends on its last day. If the tenant then stays without your consent, you may sue for possession, and a willful, bad-faith holdover can cost the tenant up to three months' rent or your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes week-to-week or month-to-month, and either side may end it by written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date (weekly) or at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (monthly). The library's optional Automatic Renewal clause (`automatic-renewal-ks`) works in Alabama: put the whole renewal mechanism in the signed lease, give a clear deadline for a non-renewal notice, and tell the tenant in writing before renewal of any rent change.

title: Cold-Weather Notice Before Vacating in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no cold-weather rule for tenants: no statute requires a tenant to warn you before leaving a unit empty in freezing weather, to keep the heat at a minimum temperature, or to winterize the unit, and none bars a winter move-out or eviction. What the law does give you is an absence-notice term: the lease may require the tenant to tell you of any expected absence of more than 14 days, no later than the fifth day of the absence. If the lease has that term and the tenant willfully fails to give the notice, you may recover your actual damages, and during any absence of more than 14 days you may enter the unit at times reasonably necessary. The library's Alabama clause for this is `extended-absence-notice-al`. Remember that you must keep the heating and plumbing in good working order and supply reasonable heat and hot water unless the tenant controls them, so a freeze caused by a heating failure you were told about is your responsibility, not the tenant's. A tenant still must use the heating and plumbing reasonably and not negligently damage the unit, and is responsible for freeze damage caused by the tenant's own neglect.

title: Criminal Activity at an Alabama Rental
bodyText: Alabama law reaches criminal activity at a rental in four ways. First, the lease: certain acts by a tenant or occupant are a default the tenant has no right to cure unless you agree, and you may end the lease on a seven-day notice: making, growing, bringing in, moving, possessing, furnishing, giving or using illegal drugs in the unit or common areas; illegal use, possession or discharge of a firearm or ammunition on the rental property (self-defense and other lawful uses excepted); and criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property (self-defense excepted). Other crimes are handled as an ordinary material breach, which the tenant may cure within seven business days after receiving your written notice. Second, drug nuisance suits: the Attorney General, a district attorney, a county or city attorney, a county resident (including a tenant of the property) or a community group may sue in circuit court to abate a drug-related nuisance, and you as owner may ask in that same case for the tenant's eviction (`edu-drug-nuisance-al`). Third, prostitution nuisance suits: the Attorney General, a district attorney or any citizen may sue to close a place used for lewdness, assignation or prostitution; the owner, agent and lessee are all treated as maintaining the nuisance, and the court may close the place for a year. Knowingly providing premises for prostitution is itself a crime (advancing prostitution). Fourth, screening: the fair-housing law does not bar refusing a person convicted of illegally making or distributing a controlled substance, and your application may ask about such convictions for anyone who will live there. Alabama has no crime-free lease statute, no rule making you evict for crime, no fast-track criminal eviction procedure, and no requirement that the lease state your right to end it for criminal use. The library's optional Criminal Activity clause (`criminal-activity-ky`) works in Alabama as a lease term.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has two notice-and-cure tracks and one no-cure track. Unpaid rent: give a written notice stating the rent and any late fees owed and that the lease will end on a date at least seven business days after the tenant receives it; if the tenant does not pay in that time, the lease ends. Other breaches: for a material noncompliance with the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, give a written notice describing the breach and naming a termination date at least seven business days after receipt; if the tenant fixes the breach before that date, the lease does not end. If both kinds of breach exist, the nonpayment notice period governs. No cure: an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the lease or application cannot be cured, and illegal drugs, illegal firearm use, criminal assault on the property, and a repeat of substantially the same breach within six months of a cured one are noncurable defaults you may end on a seven-day notice. No breach may be cured more than twice in 12 months without your written consent. The lease may give the tenant more time to cure than the law does, but do not shorten the statutory periods. Alabama's law does not say whether the lease can decide which terms are material; that is for the court, so describe in the notice why the breach matters and do not rely on a lease label alone. The library's Alabama default clause (`default-by-tenant-al`) carries these rules; the full eviction process is in `edu-eviction-process-al`.

title: Renting the Same Home Twice in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute deals with double letting as such: nothing forbids renting part of a room to more than one household, and nothing sets a special remedy when the same home is leased to two tenants for the same period. The general rules on delivering possession apply instead. At the start of the term you must deliver possession to the tenant. If you do not, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may end the lease by written notice (you then have five days to return all prepaid rent and the deposit) or demand performance and sue whoever is wrongfully in possession, recovering actual damages. If the failure is willful and not in good faith, the person responsible owes up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. So never sign a second lease for a unit until the first tenancy has ended and the first tenant has left. Renting out property you have no authority to lease is a separate crime (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-al`). Which of two competing tenants has the better right is a question of case law and the recording rules, which this library has not reviewed. See also `edu-possession-delay-al`.

title: Drug-Free Lease Terms in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires, prescribes or limits a drug-free housing addendum in a private lease. You may include a drug-free term, and the library's optional Criminal Activity clause (`criminal-activity-ky`), which applies in Alabama, already makes the illegal manufacture, sale, distribution or possession of a controlled substance on the property a breach. You do not need an addendum to act on drug activity: making, growing, bringing in, moving, possessing, furnishing, giving or using illegal drugs in the unit or common areas by a tenant or occupant is a default the tenant cannot cure unless you agree, and you may end the lease on a seven-day notice. Drug activity can also expose the property to a drug-related nuisance suit, in which you may ask for the tenant's eviction (`edu-drug-nuisance-al`, `edu-criminal-activity-al`). Alabama's medical cannabis law says nothing about leases; whether a registered patient's use counts as illegal drugs under the no-cure rule is not settled by statute, so if you want to bar it, say so in the lease and treat a violation as an ordinary breach the tenant may cure. Federal rules for subsidized housing are not covered here.

title: Eminent Domain and Leased Property in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute says what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the rented property is taken by eminent domain, and none lets the condemnation court cancel a lease or defers to what the lease says. The Constitution requires just compensation, paid before the taking, to the owner of property taken for public use, and the Eminent Domain Code compensates everyone with an interest in the property. The court first fixes the total compensation for the property and then, in a later proceeding, divides it among the people claiming an interest, which can include a tenant. A tenant who owns a building or other improvement on the land is paid for it separately. If the condemnor lets a former owner or tenant stay on for a short term after acquiring the property, the rent may not exceed fair rental value, and a state agency must try to give a lawful occupant at least 90 days' written notice before requiring a move from a dwelling. Because the law does not settle how the lease ends or who gets the leasehold's share of the award, say so in the lease. The library's optional Condemnation clause (`eminent-domain-vi`) applies in Alabama: it ends the lease on a total or near-total taking, reduces rent on a partial one, keeps the award for you, and leaves the tenant any relocation payment. Casualty rules (fire and similar damage) do not cover a taking.

title: Company Landlords in Alabama Courts
bodyText: In Alabama a statute, not only a court rule, speaks to this, but only for the small claims docket. District court cases worth $6,000 or less (not counting interest and costs) go on the small claims docket, and there an individual, partnership or corporation may appear with or without a lawyer. A partnership that appears without a lawyer must be represented by a partner or employee, and a corporation by an officer or full-time employee. A party without a licensed attorney cannot get a judgment on the small claims docket that includes attorney's fees, so a landlord who wants the attorney's fees the Act allows needs a lawyer. Outside the small claims docket, only licensed lawyers may practice law, and appearing for someone else in court is the practice of law; a business may attend to its own claims, but whether a non-lawyer officer may appear for a company in an eviction case on the regular district or circuit court docket, and whether an LLC is treated like a corporation, is left to the court rules and case law, which this library has not read. Cautious course: if your rental is owned by an LLC, corporation or other entity, use a licensed Alabama attorney for eviction cases, and for any appeal to circuit court.

title: Delays and Stays in an Alabama Eviction
bodyText: No Alabama statute lets a court postpone a tenant's removal because of hardship, such as illness, age, children, weather or trouble finding new housing. The delays Alabama law does provide are fixed. After an eviction judgment for you, the writ of possession is automatically stayed for seven days, and then issues on your application. Either side may appeal to circuit court within seven days, and a timely post-judgment motion suspends that deadline; but a tenant's appeal does not stop the writ unless the tenant pays into court all rent due under the lease since you filed and keeps paying rent as it comes due, and if the tenant misses a payment the court, on your motion, issues the writ. Under the older unlawful detainer article, a trial may be postponed for good cause for no more than 15 days, at the cost of the party asking. A tenant who re-enters without just cause after removal can be held in contempt. Federal law can also stop or delay an eviction (a tenant's bankruptcy filing, and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act), and any court may manage its own docket under the court rules, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Who Is Served With Alabama Eviction Papers
bodyText: Alabama law sets who is served in an eviction case, and the lease cannot change it. Court papers are served under the Alabama Rules of Civil Procedure: normally by personal service on the tenant. If the sheriff, constable or process server cannot serve the tenant personally, the papers may be handed to any competent adult living at the unit, or, if after reasonable effort no one is found living there, posted on the door; on the day of posting or by the close of the next business day, a copy must also be mailed first class to the tenant at the unit's mailing address (or, if the unit has none, the tenant's last known address), and service by posting is complete on the date of mailing. No Alabama statute lets a lease name another person to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and the library offers no such clause for Alabama; whether a tenant may appoint an agent for service under the court rules is a court-rule question not reviewed here. Alabama has no address-confidentiality program in its Code. On your side, you must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and business address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for service of process and notices (`landlord-disclosure-al`); a manager who fails to do so becomes your agent for service.

title: Eviction for Criminal Activity in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no separate fast-track eviction procedure for drug or violent crime, and no rule letting police, prosecutors, neighbors or a tenant group bring an eviction for you. Two features make removal quicker anyway. First, illegal drugs in the unit or common areas, illegal firearm use, and criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property are noncurable defaults: you may end the lease on a seven-day notice, and the tenant has no right to cure unless you agree. Second, every eviction case in Alabama is entitled to precedence in scheduling over all other civil cases, and the ordinary eviction steps then apply (`edu-eviction-process-al`). Separately, when a drug-related nuisance suit is brought about the property by a public attorney, a county resident, a tenant or a community group, you as owner may ask in that same case for the eviction of the tenant who maintains the nuisance; and a prostitution nuisance suit takes precedence over all other cases except injunctions. See `edu-criminal-activity-al`.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Rule in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to tell a new or current tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that you have received a notice of default, or that a foreclosure sale has been advertised. The only disclosure the Alabama landlord-tenant act requires at the start of a tenancy is the name and business address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for service of process and notices, kept current. Even so, think carefully before signing a new lease on a property you expect to lose: a foreclosure sale can cut short the tenant's stay (subject to the federal 90-day notice and lease-term protections in `edu-foreclosure-al`), and misleading a tenant about the property can raise fraud or misrepresentation claims under general law. The library offers no foreclosure-disclosure clause for Alabama.

title: Foreclosure of a Rented Home in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no state statute protecting tenants when a rented home is foreclosed: no rule that the lease survives, no state notice-to-vacate period, no rule sending rent to the buyer, and no equity-skimming or sale-leaseback statute. Most Alabama mortgages are foreclosed out of court under a power of sale, after the sale is advertised once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper; tenants get no separate notice, and the foreclosure deed passes legal title to the buyer. Federal law fills the gap. Under the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, the immediate successor after a foreclosure of a dwelling takes the property subject to the rights of any bona fide tenant: the successor must give at least 90 days' notice to vacate, and a tenant with a bona fide lease made before the foreclosure may stay to the end of the lease term, unless the successor sells the unit to a buyer who will live there, who may end the lease on the date of sale after the 90-day notice. A month-to-month tenant, or one with no lease, also gets the 90 days. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant is not the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, the deal was at arm's length, and the rent is not substantially below market (unless subsidized). If a lender has a receiver appointed during foreclosure, the receiver generally may not reject the lease of a tenant who lives in the home as a primary residence. Until the foreclosure deed, you remain the landlord and the tenant still owes you rent. The library's tagged clause asking tenants to forward notices of proceedings (`tenant-forward-proceedings-ca`) helps you learn of a foreclosure filing. Redemption after foreclosure is covered separately.

title: Lease Guarantors in Alabama
bodyText: A guarantor's promise to pay a tenant's rent is a promise to answer for another person's debt, so under Alabama's statute of frauds it is void unless it, or a note of it, is in writing, states the consideration, and is signed by the guarantor. Having the guarantor sign the lease, with a guaranty that says it is given in consideration of your entering into the lease, meets that rule; the library's Alabama clause is `guaranty-al`. No Alabama statute limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, or makes a continuing guaranty revocable, so the guaranty itself should say whether it covers renewals, extensions and month-to-month continuations, and how much the guarantor can owe. Alabama's suretyship statute lets a surety on a contract to pay money give the creditor written notice to sue the principal debtor, and discharges the surety if no suit is brought within three months; whether that applies to a lease guarantor is unsettled, so if a guarantor sends such a notice, take it to a lawyer promptly. Any cash you take from a guarantor as security for the tenant's obligations counts toward the one-month deposit cap (`edu-security-deposit-rules-al`), on the cautious reading of the cap, which limits money received "as security" without saying from whom.

title: No Health or Care-Facility Termination Right in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute lets a tenant end a fixed-term lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or a relative's care, and no Alabama rule says that a tenant's incapacity ends a tenancy.
