A tenant in that position stays bound by the lease unless you agree otherwise or the lease gives an early-termination right; a week-to-week or month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy by the ordinary written notice, given at least 7 days before the termination date (weekly) or at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (monthly). If the tenant leaves early, you must still make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit at a fair rental (though you may first rent your other vacant units), and the lease ends when a new tenancy begins. A tenant's death does not end a lease either (`edu-no-tenant-death-termination-al`). If a guardian or conservator has been appointed for the tenant, deal with that person. Federal law may still apply: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (`edu-servicemember-rights-al`) and, for a tenant with a disability, a reasonable accommodation under fair-housing law (`edu-fair-housing-al`).

title: Settling Lease Disputes Before Court in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires, authorizes or limits a lease term asking the parties to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court. Such a term is a contract choice. The Alabama landlord-tenant act says that a claim or right under the act or the lease, if disputed in good faith, may be settled by agreement, though a court may refuse to enforce a settlement that was unconscionable when made. Keep any such term non-binding and out of the way of possession cases: a lease may not make the tenant waive rights under the law of unlawful detainer, and enforcing a known prohibited term carries a penalty. The library's optional Informal Dispute Resolution clause (`informal-dispute-resolution-or`) applies in Alabama: it asks each side to give written notice and offer to meet within 10 days before suing, leaves out possession actions and emergency relief, and does not delay any notice, deadline or remedy. An agreement to arbitrate is a separate question (Alabama law does not let a court order specific performance of one, and federal arbitration law may apply), covered in the library's arbitration rows.

title: No Landlord Lien on a Tenant's Belongings in Alabama
bodyText: An Alabama residential landlord has no usable lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. A lien or security interest for the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable unless it was perfected before January 1, 2007, and distraint for rent (seizing a tenant's goods to collect rent) is abolished. So do not put a lien or security-interest clause in the lease, and never take, lock up or sell a tenant's property to collect rent; recover rent through the court and collect a money judgment by the ordinary process. Older Alabama statutes still give a landlord of a storehouse or other building a lien on the tenant's goods enforced by court attachment, and a landlord of farmland a lien on the crop; the crop lien belongs to agricultural leases, which the residential act does not cover, and whether the building lien reaches anything a residential tenant owns beyond household goods is not settled by statute, so do not rely on it for a home. Property a tenant leaves behind is handled under the abandonment rules (`abandoned-property-al`), and a tenant's waiver of personal-property exemptions is covered separately (`exemption-waiver-al`).

title: Lease Length Limits and Formalities in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama limits how long a lease may run and adds formalities for long ones. No leasehold may be created for more than 99 years, and a lease for more than 20 years is void for the part beyond 20 years unless the lease, or a memorandum of it, is acknowledged or approved as the law requires for deeds and recorded with the probate judge of the county where the property is within one year after it is signed. A residential lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed (see `edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-term-al`). Alabama is not a community-property state, and no statute requires both spouses to sign an ordinary lease. One caution: a mortgage, deed or other conveyance of a married owner's homestead is not valid without the other spouse's voluntary signature and assent, shown by acknowledgment before an officer; no statute says whether a lease of the homestead counts as a conveyance, so if you lease out a home you or your spouse claim as a homestead for a long term, have both spouses sign and acknowledge it. Leasing a homestead for a time does not by itself abandon a filed homestead exemption. Leases by state agencies for more than one year need the Governor's written approval, which does not affect private landlords.

title: Time Limits for Rent and Damage Claims in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's general time limits apply to landlord claims; there is no special limit for rent. Most claims on a residential lease must be brought within six years: claims on a written promise not under seal (an ordinary written lease), claims for rent owed under an oral lease, claims for the use and occupation of land, claims for trespass or damage to real or personal property, and claims on any other simple contract. A claim on a contract under seal, and a suit to recover land or its possession, has ten years. A tenant's partial payment on the debt before the time runs out, or the tenant's unconditional written promise to pay, signed by the tenant, restarts the clock; nothing else does, so an oral promise to pay will not. A separate rule bars an eviction action under the unlawful detainer article against someone who has occupied the property without interruption for three full years before the complaint, if that person's estate has not been determined (that is, has not ended); it does not bar an action against a tenant whose tenancy has ended. Personal-injury and other tort claims have their own, shorter periods, which this row does not cover.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in Alabama
bodyText: No. An Alabama landlord may not lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even with advance notice, a lease clause or key access on request. The law bars a landlord from recovering or taking possession of the unit by action or otherwise, including by willfully cutting off heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except where the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit or the act permits it. A tenant who is unlawfully locked out or removed, or whose essential services are willfully interrupted, may recover possession or end the lease and, either way, recover up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees, and the return of the deposit and unearned prepaid rent if the lease ends. For unpaid rent, give the written seven-business-day notice and, if the rent is not paid, file an eviction case (`edu-eviction-process-al`). The library offers no lockout clause for Alabama; see `edu-self-help-eviction-al`.

title: Minors and 18-Year-Olds as Tenants in Alabama
bodyText: In Alabama the age of majority is 19, not 18. Since 2019, though, an unemancipated 18-year-old of sound mind may enter into a binding contract as if of full age, and cannot later cancel it because of minority; so an 18-year-old may sign a lease as a tenant and be held to it. A person under 18 generally cannot be bound by a lease in his or her own name (whether a court would hold a younger minor to a lease for necessaries is case law, not reviewed here). So have only tenants aged 18 or older sign the lease, list younger children as occupants, and if a 16- or 17-year-old must live there without a parent, have a parent or guardian sign as tenant or guarantor. A juvenile court may relieve a minor over 18 of the disabilities of nonage on a petition. No Alabama statute bars naming a minor in an eviction case or sets a special procedure for one; who must be named and how a minor is served are court-rule questions not reviewed here, so name the adult tenants who signed the lease.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent in Alabama
bodyText: Before you can evict an Alabama tenant for unpaid rent, you must deliver a written notice stating the amount of rent and any late fees owed to remedy the breach and that the lease will end on a date at least seven business days after the tenant receives it. If the tenant does not pay within those seven business days, the lease ends and you may file for eviction. If the tenant is also in breach of another term, the nonpayment notice period governs. The tenant's right to cure by paying is limited: no breach may be cured more than twice in 12 months without your written consent, and a repeat of substantially the same breach within six months of a cured one is a noncurable default. The Act prescribes no statutory wording or form for the notice and no particular delivery method, and the general notice rules in the Act (including the three-days-after-mailing rule) do not apply to a termination notice; because the period runs from the tenant's receipt, hand delivery is the safest proof. The notice must be on paper, since Alabama's electronic-transactions law does not cover default or eviction notices for a primary residence. No statute lets the lease shorten or waive this notice, and no statute requires a state-agency form or a mediation program with it. Arrangements outside the Act (such as farm leases) follow the older ten-day notice to quit. See `default-by-tenant-al` and `edu-eviction-process-al`.

title: No Notice-Service Fee in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute authorizes, caps or bans a fee charged to a tenant for preparing or serving a notice, such as the seven-business-day notice for unpaid rent or a breach notice. But an Alabama lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney's fees or cost of collection, and such a term is unenforceable; if you try to enforce a lease term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees. A fee for serving a notice you must give before you can collect or evict looks like a cost of collection, and a fixed charge for it could also be treated as a penalty under case law. Cautious course: do not charge a notice fee, and do not add one to the amount demanded in a nonpayment notice, which should list only the rent and any late fees owed. Recover your costs through the statutes that award them, such as the actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees allowed after a tenant's breach. The library offers no notice-service fee clause for Alabama.

title: While a Notice to Vacate Is Pending in Alabama
bodyText: No general Alabama statute limits what you may do to the unit or the tenancy while a notice ending the tenancy is running, and none governs a move-out or notice-to-vacate form that adds terms. Your ordinary duties continue until the tenancy ends: you must keep the unit habitable and the facilities working, you may not willfully cut off heat, water, electricity, gas or another essential service, and you may not lock the tenant out (doing so lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or actual damages, plus attorney's fees). So schedule renovation that would make the unit hard to live in for after the tenant leaves, and enter only on the usual notice. One special rule applies to condominium conversions: the declarant must give each residential tenant at least 60 days' notice of the conversion before requiring the tenant to vacate, may not require a tenant to leave on less notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants, and may not change the terms of the tenancy during that period; failure to give the notice is a defense to a possession case. Keep any move-out form you ask a tenant to sign to the facts (the address and the move-out date); a form cannot add lease terms the tenant has not agreed to.

title: Owner Move-In Terminations in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute gives a landlord the right to end a lease early so that the owner or a family member can move in, and none sets a minimum ownership period, special notice or relocation payment for doing so. For a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy you do not need a reason: either side may end it by written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date (weekly) or at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (monthly) (`edu-no-for-cause-eviction-al`). For a fixed-term lease, the right to end early for owner occupancy exists only if the lease reserves it; a lease that is silent binds you to the full term. The library's optional Owner Occupancy clause (`owner-occupancy-termination-ar`) works in Alabama: it reserves the right for a fixed term, names the person who will move in, requires written notice of at least the number of days you choose (not less than 30) ending on the last day of a monthly rental period, refunds rent paid for later days, and requires a court eviction if the tenant does not leave. Do not use it to retaliate against a tenant for a code complaint, a repair request or joining a tenants' union.

title: No Possession Bond in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no possession bond: no statute lets you require a tenant to post a bond, or sign a confessed judgment, to secure giving up possession when the lease ends, and the library offers none. A lease term letting anyone confess judgment on a claim under the lease is prohibited and unenforceable, and Alabama law separately voids any pre-suit agreement to confess judgment (`edu-confession-of-judgment-al`). Money you hold to secure the tenant's obligations is a security deposit, capped at one month's periodic rent with limited exceptions (`edu-security-deposit-rules-al`). The bonds Alabama law knows arise inside a possession case: a tenant who appeals an eviction keeps possession only by paying the rent due into court as it comes due, and in the older unlawful detainer procedure a judgment against an appellant who gave a supersedeas bond is entered against the bond's sureties for the rent pending the appeal.

title: Rent for a Defective Unit in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute forbids you to demand or collect rent while the unit is cited for code violations or is substandard. The tenant, for its part, may not withhold rent while in possession to enforce its rights under the landlord-tenant act. The tenant's remedies run another way: for a material breach of the lease or of your repair duties materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give a 14-day notice and end the lease if you do not fix it, and may recover actual damages and attorney's fees; if you willfully or negligently fail to provide heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service after notice, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' notice or recover damages based on the drop in the unit's fair rental value; and in an eviction or rent case the tenant may counterclaim, paying rent into court, and wins possession if no rent remains due after the court nets the claims (`edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-al`). Rent is payable without demand or notice when due, unless the lease says otherwise. Do not bring or threaten an eviction because the tenant complained to a code agency or to you about repairs (`edu-retaliation-al`).

title: Rent Collection and Repair Duties in Alabama
bodyText: Some states say that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Alabama's version of the uniform landlord-tenant act left that rule out, and we found no Alabama statute like it. Two rules come close. First, if you or your agent fail to give the tenant, in writing at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and business address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for notices and service, the person who failed becomes the landlord's agent for performing the landlord's duties under the act and the lease, and must spend or make available for that purpose all rent collected from the premises. Second, your repair duties are set by statute and cannot be waived in the lease, and a buyer or successor landlord is bound by the disclosure and deposit rules. A separate question, whether accepting rent with knowledge of a default waives your right to end the lease for that breach, is covered in the library's waiver-by-acceptance row (Ala. Code § 35-9A-424).

title: Seasonal Rentals in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute creates a special seasonal or vacation tenancy, such as one that ends automatically at the end of a season without notice or skips the eviction process. A lease for a season is an ordinary lease with an agreed term: state exact start and end dates, because a fixed term simply ends on its last day, and a tenant who stays on without your consent is holding over and can be removed only through the court (`edu-holdover-remedies-al`). If the rental is really transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings, the Alabama landlord-tenant act does not govern it at all, unless the arrangement was set up to avoid the act; whether a particular short stay is transient occupancy depends on the facts, and short-term rentals are outside this library's scope. Transient occupancy is subject to the state lodgings tax and local lodging taxes, which this row does not cover.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a court to postpone a nonpayment eviction, gives the tenant a defense, or reinstates the tenancy because a Social Security payment, other government benefit or housing-voucher payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply: the written seven-business-day notice to pay, then an eviction case. If the tenant pays all the rent and any late fees stated in the notice within the seven business days, the lease does not end, but a tenant may cure only twice in 12 months without your written consent. You may agree to accept rent late, or set a due date that matches the tenant's benefit date, in writing; be careful, because accepting rent with knowledge of a default can waive your right to end the lease for that breach (see the library's waiver-by-acceptance row). Federal rules for voucher and other subsidized tenancies (including the housing authority's share of the rent) are not covered here.

title: When an Alabama Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Alabama's writing threshold for leases is one year. Under the statute of frauds, a contract for the sale of land or of any interest in it is void unless it, or a note of it stating the consideration, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged, except leases for a term of not more than one year; an agreement that by its terms cannot be performed within one year must be in writing too. So a lease for more than one year must be written and signed (by the person you would enforce it against, or an agent authorized in writing), while a lease of one year or less may be oral, unless it cannot be completed within a year of being made (for example a one-year lease agreed now to start next month), which the one-year rule may require to be in writing. The Alabama landlord-tenant act covers oral as well as written rental agreements, and it adds a safety valve: if one side never signs a written lease but the landlord accepts rent without reservation, or the tenant takes possession and pays rent without reservation, the lease takes effect as if signed, but a term longer than one year is effective for only one year. Leases for more than 20 years must also be acknowledged and recorded within a year to be valid beyond 20 years (`edu-lease-term-limits-al`). Have every adult tenant and every guarantor sign.

title: When an Alabama Tenant May End a Lease Early
bodyText: Alabama law lets a tenant end a lease early only for the landlord's own failures or for damage to the unit, not for personal reasons. The tenant may end the lease: (1) for a material breach of the lease, or a breach of your repair duties materially affecting health and safety, by a written notice naming a date at least 14 days after you receive it, unless you fix the breach before then; (2) if you willfully or negligently fail, after notice, to provide heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, by a written notice naming a date at least 14 days after you receive it, on moving out; (3) if you fail to deliver possession at the start of the term, by written notice, with prepaid rent and deposit returned within five days; (4) if fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs the unit, by moving out and notifying you in writing within 14 days; (5) if you unlawfully remove, lock out or cut off services to the tenant; and (6) if you make unlawful or harassing entries. In each case you must return the deposit and unearned prepaid rent as the act provides. Alabama has no state statute releasing a tenant because of domestic violence, illness, age or a job move (`edu-no-dv-termination-al`, `edu-no-infirmity-termination-al`), no special rule for a landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation (general fraud law applies), and no rule forfeiting rent because a statement was left out of the lease. Servicemembers have federal rights (`edu-servicemember-rights-al`).

title: Renting to Students in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no student-housing statute for private landlords: nothing on student leases, parental guarantees, roommate matching, academic-year terms or disclosures to student tenants. A lease to a student in a private building is an ordinary lease under the Alabama landlord-tenant act. Two rules touch the subject. First, the act does not govern residence at an institution, public or private, if it is incidental to the institution's educational or similar services, so a college's own dormitory housing falls outside it (unless an arrangement is set up to avoid the act); privately owned or leased student apartments are covered like any other rental. Second, the fair-housing law's ban on sex discrimination does not apply to renting dwellings in a single-sex dormitory property. Students under 19 are minors in Alabama, but an 18-year-old may sign a binding lease (`edu-minor-tenants-al`); for younger students, or if you want extra security, have a parent sign as guarantor (`guaranty-al`).

title: Tenancies Without a Fixed Term in Alabama
bodyText: For a home rented under the Alabama landlord-tenant act, a tenancy with no definite term is not a tenancy at will: it is week-to-week if the tenant pays weekly rent and otherwise month-to-month, and either side ends it by written notice of at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice (month-to-month) (`edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-al`). An older Alabama statute still says that where no time is fixed a tenancy runs from December 1 to December 1, and that an express tenancy at will may be ended by either party on 10 days' written notice; how that rule fits tenancies under the act is not settled by statute, so for a residential rental give at least the act's 7- or 30-day notice and never less than 10 days. A person who stays on by your mere sufferance (for example after a tenancy ends) owes a reasonable payment for use and occupation, and if a tenant holds over without consent after 30 days' notice, the older statute speaks of double the customary rent (see `edu-holdover-remedies-al`). Either way, possession is recovered only through the court.

title: When an Alabama Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Bankruptcy is federal law, and Alabama adds almost nothing for residential tenancies. Under the federal Bankruptcy Code, a tenant's bankruptcy filing operates as an automatic stay of most actions against the tenant, including starting or continuing a court case and any act to obtain possession of property of the estate, so stop collection and eviction steps when you learn of a filing until you have the bankruptcy court's permission or an exception applies. Two exceptions matter for landlords: the stay does not stop you continuing an eviction for a home where you obtained a judgment for possession before the filing (subject to a 30-day period if the tenant certifies a right to cure and deposits rent), and it does not stop an eviction based on the tenant's endangering the property or illegal drug use there if you file and serve the required certification. Alabama law does not say whether a writ of possession may be enforced after you learn of a tenant's bankruptcy, does not make bankruptcy a ground for ending a lease, and does not regulate a lease clause that treats bankruptcy as a default (federal law generally makes such clauses unenforceable against the trustee, a point not reviewed here). The only Alabama rule naming a tenant's bankruptcy limits the old building lien on a tenant's goods to six months' rent against the trustee; that lien does not reach a residential tenant's household goods (`edu-landlord-lien-al`). Get legal advice before taking any step against a tenant in bankruptcy.

title: Changing the Terms of a Periodic Tenancy in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act sets no special notice period for changing the terms of a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, whether the change is to rent, to a fee the lease already provides, or to another term (`edu-no-rent-increase-notice-al`). Because a lease term cannot be changed without the tenant's agreement, the lawful route for a change the tenant will not sign is to end the periodic tenancy by the ordinary written notice (at least 7 days for week-to-week, at least 30 days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month) and offer a new tenancy on the new terms. Rules and regulations are different: you may adopt a rule from time to time, and it binds the tenant if it meets the statutory tests and the tenant has notice of it when adopted, but a rule adopted after the lease is signed that substantially modifies the tenant's use of the unit is not valid unless the tenant consents in writing, and the lease controls over any conflicting rule (`edu-rules-and-regulations-al`). During a fixed term you may change terms only as the lease allows or with the tenant's signed agreement. A change may not be retaliatory, and during a declared state of emergency a rent increase can be unlawful unconscionable pricing (see `edu-disaster-duties-al`).

title: Barring Non-Tenants From Alabama Rental Property
bodyText: Alabama's criminal trespass law lets you, as owner or as a person authorized by the owner, bar a non-tenant from areas you control, such as common areas, grounds and parking. A person commits criminal trespass in the third degree (a violation) by knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on premises, and in the second degree (a misdemeanor) by doing so in a building, or on land fenced or enclosed to keep intruders out. A person enters or remains unlawfully when not licensed, invited or privileged to be there. Someone on premises open to the public is there by license unless he defies a lawful order not to enter or remain, personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person, so give the barring order in person (and keep a written record). A license to be in the public part of a building does not extend to its private parts. A tenant's invited guest is on the tenant's unit with the tenant's license, so you cannot bar a guest from the tenant's own unit by a trespass warning alone; to keep a dangerous person out of the unit, use a lease covenant. The library's Barred Persons clause (`barred-person-covenant-ne`) applies in Alabama: after your written notice, the tenant must not admit a person barred for dangerous conduct or property damage, with exceptions for emergency help, court-ordered access and domestic-violence situations. Squatters are handled under a separate procedure (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-al`).

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Charges in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama law supplies interest on money owed under a contract without any lease term: every contract for the payment of money bears interest from the day the money should have been paid. The statute does not state the rate for that implied interest; the general legal ceiling on interest for a loan or forbearance is 6 percent a year without a written contract and 8 percent a year by written contract (higher rates are allowed only for loans, forbearances and credit sales of $2,000 or more). Whether a landlord's charge on overdue rent is a "forbearance" under those caps is not settled by statute, so the cautious course is to set any lease interest rate at no more than 8 percent a year, simple interest, and to keep it separate from any late fee. After a court enters a money judgment on a contract, the judgment bears interest at the rate stated in the contract (7.5 percent a year for other judgments). The library's optional Alabama clause is `unpaid-amounts-interest-al`.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act requires writing for the notices and consents that matter most. Landlord notices: the notice ending the lease for unpaid rent (stating the rent and late fees owed, at least seven business days) or for another breach (at least seven business days, describing the breach); the notice ending a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy (at least 7 days, or 30 days before the periodic rental date); the notice asking the tenant to fix a condition affecting health and safety before you do the work and bill it (seven days, except in an emergency); the disclosure, at or before the start of the tenancy, of the manager's and owner's (or owner's agent's) names and business addresses; and the notice to the tenant that you have sold the property or that a manager's role has ended. Tenant notices: the 14-day notice of your breach or of a failure to provide essential services; the notice ending the lease when you fail to deliver possession; the notice, within 14 days after moving out, that a fire or casualty has ended the lease; and the forwarding address at move-out for the deposit. Consents in writing: a rule adopted after the lease that substantially changes the tenant's use of the unit needs the tenant's written consent; a third cure in 12 months needs your express written consent; and the chore split for a single-family residence must be in writing (separate signed writing for other dwellings, `tenant-repair-agreement-al`). Showing entries need a general notice signed by the tenant separate from the lease. Give termination, default and cure notices on paper (`edu-electronic-notices-al`).

title: Construction Liens and Tenant Work in Alabama
bodyText: Under Alabama's mechanics' and materialmen's lien law, a lien for work or materials attaches to the interest of the owner or proprietor who contracted for the work, directly or through an agent, contractor or subcontractor. When a tenant in possession contracts for a building or improvement and the work does not violate the lease, the lien attaches to that improvement and to the remaining term of the lease, not to your ownership of the land. The lienholder may keep the lease alive by paying the rent, and a buyer at a lien sale may take over the rest of the term or remove the improvement; you may pay off the lien before a sale, or pay the buyer the improvement's value afterward, and then the improvement becomes yours. Two cautions. The law's owner or proprietor includes anyone for whose use or benefit the improvement is made, so work done for your benefit, or that you request or approve as your own project, can expose your interest. And a supplier who gives you written notice before furnishing material for the tenant's contractor may claim a lien for the full price unless you object, or tell the supplier in writing before the material is used that you will not be responsible for it. Alabama has no recorded notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure and no statute making a lease no-lien clause bind contractors. So require your written consent for alterations, keep the tenant responsible for paying for the tenant's own work (`no-liens-al`), and answer any supplier's notice in writing at once.

title: No Electric Submetering Disclosure in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama requires no special disclosure when you submeter or rebill electricity to a tenant. The limits that matter are in `edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-al`: for electricity from a Public Service Commission-regulated utility, a multi-unit building begun on or after January 1, 1981 generally must have a utility meter for each unit, so landlord submetering of electricity is mostly limited to older buildings and the listed exceptions. No Alabama statute or Commission rule says whether reselling electricity to tenants by meter makes you a regulated utility; Alabama's definition covers anyone who sells or furnishes electricity to or for the public. The cautious course is to bill only your actual cost, with no markup or billing fee, to state the method in the lease, and to check with the Commission or your provider first.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy or water usage data to the building owner, and no building energy-benchmarking law. Whether a utility will release a tenant's account data to you is up to the utility; most will do so only with the account holder's authorization. You may include that authorization in the lease; the library's optional clause `energy-data-release-wy` does this, limits your use of the data, and lets the tenant withdraw it. Alabama's new consumer data-privacy law takes effect May 1, 2027. It reaches only businesses that control or process the personal data of more than 25,000 Alabama consumers, or that earn more than 25 percent of gross revenue from selling personal data. If your business is that large, note that the law does not treat agreeing to a broad document that mixes data terms with unrelated terms as consent; the cautious course is to get the tenant's authorization on a separate signed page.

title: No EV Charger Removal Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends. Decide it in the lease: either the tenant removes the charger and repairs any damage, or it stays and becomes yours. The library's optional clause `ev-charger-installation-hi` makes you choose one. Whether equipment a tenant attached to the property became a fixture that stays with it, when the lease is silent, is a question for the courts, so do not leave it unstated. At move-out the tenant must leave the premises in the condition the law requires and is responsible for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes, which you may deduct from the security deposit with an itemized list within 60 days.

title: No EV Charging Rules for Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on electric vehicle charging at rental property: no tenant right to install a charger (`edu-no-ev-charging-right-al`), no registration or safety rules for a tenant's charger, and no weights-and-measures or price-posting rule for a landlord who lets tenants charge for a fee. Whether you allow a charger, and on what terms, is a matter for the lease. The library's optional clause `ev-charger-installation-hi` lets a tenant install a charger only with your written consent, by a licensed contractor under codes and permits, with association rules followed, the electricity reimbursed and removal or surrender agreed. Bill charging electricity at your actual cost: no Alabama statute or Public Service Commission rule says whether reselling electricity makes a landlord a regulated utility. Owners of multifamily buildings with five or more units may finance charging equipment through a local property-assessed financing program where one exists.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rules in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on electric vehicle chargers in shared parking areas, on reserving a charging space, or on who is responsible for damage to a charger in a common area. Set any of this by lease or by a rule. A parking or charging rule adopted for common areas binds tenants only if it is reasonable, applies fairly to all tenants, is explicit, and the tenant has notice of it; a rule adopted mid-lease that substantially changes the tenant's use of the premises needs the tenant's written consent. If you let a tenant install a charger, use `ev-charger-installation-hi` and name the space; any fee for reserving the space is your figure, since Alabama sets no limit. A lease term binds only the tenant who signs it, so put any duty about the charger in each later tenant's own lease.

title: No Rental Fee Transparency Law in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law. Nothing requires you to state rent as one figure that includes every mandatory fee, to list fees on the lease's first page, or to use prescribed wording. Two general rules still apply. Every payment the tenant owes you under the lease counts as rent, so a fee is collectible only if the lease provides for it. And Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches leasing and renting, including a catch-all against any unconscionable, false, misleading or deceptive act; advertising a rent figure while hiding mandatory fees risks that rule. The cautious course is to list every fee, with its amount and when it is due, in one place in the lease (`fees-and-charges-vi`) and to show mandatory fees wherever you advertise the rent.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no landlord-tenant statute on charging a fee for a service or amenity you do not actually provide. General law covers it. A fee in the lease is part of the rent the tenant agreed to pay, but if you charge for a service and then do not furnish it, the tenant may claim breach of the lease. Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches leasing and renting, makes it unlawful, after receiving payment for services, to fail to furnish them within the time represented, or within 30 days if no time was stated, unless you offer a refund or a new date; it also bars any other unconscionable, false, misleading or deceptive practice. Charge only for services and amenities that exist and that you will provide, describe them in the lease, and refund or credit a fee when the service stops.

title: No Government Fee Pass-Through Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on passing a government fee, such as a rental registration or licensing fee, through to the tenant. Such fees are rare in Alabama because counties and cities may not adopt ordinances about residential landlords or rental housing codes. The main exception is the 2026 law letting Class 1 cities adopt vacant-property registration, which applies to vacant property, not to occupied rentals. If a local government does charge you a fee for the property, the tenant pays a share only if the lease says so. Write any such share into the rent the lease states (for example a stated monthly amount), not as a promise to reimburse you for the fee, because an Alabama lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for a liability the law places on you. Amounts the tenant owes you under the lease count as rent.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that bars or allows passing a government fine to the tenant, and no nuisance statute that makes the tenant liable to you for abatement costs unless the lease says otherwise. A fine or abatement charge a city imposes on you as owner is your liability under the law, and an Alabama lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for liability you have under the law. Some cities may also turn unpaid code fines and abatement costs into a lien on the property. What you may do is hold the tenant to the tenant's own duties: to comply with code obligations placed on tenants, not to damage the premises, and to keep guests from disturbing neighbors. If a tenant's breach of those duties or of the lease causes a fine, the amount is your actual damages for that breach. The library's optional clause `tenant-caused-fines-oh` is written that way and excludes conditions you are responsible for.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, and counties and cities may not impose one through a rental registration or licensing ordinance, because local ordinances about residential landlords and rental housing are barred. Carrying liability and property coverage is still prudent: your liability for injuries and for failing to keep the premises safe cannot be shifted to the tenant by the lease.

title: No Late Fee Limit in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama sets no cap on residential late fees and no grace period; see `edu-no-late-fee-cap-al`. That holds for manufactured homes and lots too: a dwelling unit under Alabama's Act includes a manufactured home, and Alabama has no separate manufactured-home community statute capping late fees or utility charges. Alabama's manufactured-dwelling law deals only with abandoned homes. Set the late fee in the lease (`late-fee-ne`). Late fees may be demanded in the seven-business-day nonpayment notice. Whether a large fee is an unenforceable penalty is for the courts, so keep it reasonable in relation to your actual cost of late payment.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no meter conservation charge and no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a utility account carries a charge for energy-efficiency improvements, or to reduce rent for one. Alabama's property-assessed financing program for energy, water and resilience improvements is a different thing: the owner consents to an assessment and lien recorded against the property, and nothing in that law puts the assessment on the tenant's utility bill or requires a tenant notice. If you want the tenant to pay toward an efficiency charge or financing cost, say so in the lease as a stated amount; amounts the tenant owes you under the lease count as rent. Alabama also has no statute on landlord-submetered water charges like Kansas's; see `edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-al`.

title: No Lien for a Tenant's Utility Bills in Alabama
bodyText: If a utility account is in the tenant's name, Alabama law protects your property from the tenant's unpaid bill. Statewide, a sewer bill received in a tenant's name is the tenant's sole responsibility and is not a lien on the property. More broadly, a provider of goods or services, including a utility, may not make a landlord or owner pay a tenant's delinquent bill for an account in the tenant's name, and has no lien on the real property for it. In Jefferson County, the state constitution adds the same rule for residential garbage service from the county, a city or another local government. These protections depend on the account being in the tenant's name, so have the tenant open each account in the tenant's own name (`utilities-responsibility`). No affidavit or filing is needed. Alabama has no general statute putting a tenant's unpaid garbage fees on the owner's property tax bill. Two practical limits remain: a city may cut off water service to premises to collect unpaid city sewer charges, and some water and sewer districts may require a deposit from the owner, tenant or occupant before serving the property.

title: Parking Rules and Notice in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no parking-specific rule on delivering parking or towing rules before signing, prescribed headings, the vehicle information you may ask for, or permits that must last as long as the lease. Parking rules are ordinary landlord rules. A rule binds the tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property or fairly shares facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies fairly to all tenants; is clear enough to follow; is not a way to avoid your own duties; and the tenant had notice of it when signing or when it was adopted. A rule adopted mid-lease that substantially changes the tenant's use of the premises needs the tenant's written consent, and if a rule conflicts with the lease, the lease wins. Give tenants the parking rules with the lease, and keep assigned-space terms in the lease itself (`assigned-parking-space`, `parking-vehicle-rules`). If you let tenants or the public drive and park on your lot, traffic-control devices there must follow local rules and the Alabama traffic-control manual. Towing follows `edu-towing-al`.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Rent in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama's only statute on pet money is the security-deposit cap. You may not take more than one month's rent as security, except for pets, changes to the premises, or increased liability risks. So a refundable pet deposit may be charged on top of the one-month deposit. It is still security: apply it only to unpaid rent and damage the tenant caused, and return it, or send an itemized list of what you kept, within 60 days after the tenancy ends and you get possession back, or you owe double the original deposit. Alabama has no statute on monthly pet rent or a one-time nonrefundable pet fee. Both are payments to you under the lease and so count as rent; state them in the lease (`pet-policy-al`). A fee labeled nonrefundable that really secures against pet damage may be treated as a deposit, so label each charge for what it is. No pet deposit, fee or rent may be charged for a service animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it does; for other assistance animals, check federal fair-housing rules, which this row does not review.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no renter's property-tax credit and no duty to give a tenant a statement of the share of rent attributable to property tax, whether annually, on a rent change or on request. Nothing is required here. If a tenant asks for a statement to support a tax claim in another state, you may give one voluntarily.

title: No Rent Concession Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on rent concessions, free-rent periods or move-in specials, and no rule on how a concession must be stated or whether it can be recaptured if the tenant leaves early. If you give one, write it into the lease: the amount, the months it covers, and any condition. The library's optional clause `rent-concession-wi` does this. Any condition that takes the concession back if the tenant breaks the lease works like liquidated damages; whether a given recapture term is an unenforceable penalty is for the courts, so tie it to the value actually given.

title: Rent Escalation in Alabama Leases
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on rent escalation clauses. Rent is whatever the lease sets, so a fixed-term lease may raise rent during the term only if the lease itself provides for it, by stating the new amounts and dates or an index formula. The library's optional clause `rent-escalation-la` does this. Without such a term, rent changes only by agreement or on renewal, and for a periodic tenancy, after proper termination notice (`edu-no-rent-increase-notice-al`). Two limits apply to any increase. You may not raise rent as retaliation for a tenant's complaint to a code agency, a complaint to you about repairs, or joining a tenants' organization. And during a declared state of emergency, Alabama's price-gouging law reaches rent: an increase of 25 percent or more over the average in the area for the 30 days before the declaration, not explained by your added costs, is presumed unconscionable. Alabama has no retaliation safe harbor that depends on the lease's wording.

title: Rent Installments in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama lets the lease set when and how rent is paid. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is payable at the dwelling unit, periodic rent for a term of one month or less is due at the start of the term, longer terms are paid in equal monthly installments at the start of each month, and rent is apportioned day by day. You may agree to a different schedule, such as two payments a month; the library's optional clause `rent-installments-or` states the installments and says that paying on that schedule is not a partial payment. Accepting late or partial rent with knowledge of a default can waive your right to end the lease for that default unless you agree otherwise after the breach, so a written installment schedule protects you.

title: No Rent Reporting Law in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rent-reporting law. Nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, lets a tenant opt out of a state program, or requires written notice before you report late rent. If you report rent payments, federal credit-reporting law also applies to what you furnish; this row does not review it. If you plan to report, say so in the lease, state whether you will report on-time payments, late payments or both, and report only accurate amounts that are actually owed under the lease.

title: Taxes on Rent in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama does not tax ordinary residential rent. The state sales tax reaches sales of tangible goods, and its definition of taxable gross proceeds leaves out rentals of real estate. The state rental tax applies to leases of tangible personal property such as furniture or equipment, not to the dwelling itself. Short stays are different. The state lodgings tax is a 4 percent tax (5 percent in the 16 north Alabama mountain-lakes counties) on anyone in the business of renting rooms, lodging or accommodations to transients, and it does not apply to accommodations supplied for 180 continuous days or more. Many counties and cities add their own lodging taxes by local law. So a furnished or short-term rental of less than 180 days can owe lodging taxes, and transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings is also outside Alabama's landlord-tenant act. If you furnish the unit, check whether the furniture rental is taxed separately. Alabama has no statute barring a landlord from passing a repealed local tax on to tenants.

title: No Renter Insurance Rules in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on renter's insurance. You may require it in the lease, set a minimum liability amount, and ask for proof; the library's clause `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca` does this. Nothing requires you to let the tenant choose the carrier (though you should), to give a written statement that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, or to give a flood or insurance notice before signing. Two cautions. If you buy a policy for a tenant who fails to and charge the cost, that charge is rent only if the lease provides for it, and any fee on top is your figure, so keep it to cost. And no insurance term may limit your own liability under the law or make the tenant indemnify you for it.

title: No Required-Fee Listing Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama does not require the lease to list fees, set a notice period for adding one, cap markups on third-party services, or bar common-area maintenance fees. Because every payment the tenant owes you under the lease counts as rent, a fee you want to collect must be in the lease. The library's optional clause `fees-and-charges-vi` lists every fee and charge in one place and promises no new fee during the term without the tenant's written agreement. Limits that do apply: no fee may shift your attorney's fees or collection costs to the tenant, and no fee may operate as an unenforceable penalty, which is a question for the courts. A new rule adopted during the lease that substantially changes the tenant's use of the premises needs the tenant's written consent.

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Tenancies in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on late fees for subsidized tenancies. Federal rules control. Under the Housing Choice Voucher program, the housing authority's payment is credited toward the rent, the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, and you may not demand or accept more from the tenant than the rent minus that payment. So you may not charge the tenant a late fee because the housing authority's payment was late. The housing assistance payments contract must instead provide for late-payment penalties against the housing authority, but only if they follow local practice for late rent, you charge them to assisted and unassisted tenants alike, and you charge the tenant late fees for the family's own share. Any late fee on the tenant's share must follow the lease and the HUD tenancy addendum.

title: No Tax Escalation Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on passing property-tax or insurance increases to a residential tenant, and none requiring a stated share or a refund of abatements. A lease may provide for it; the library's optional clause `tax-insurance-escalation-la` sets the tenant's percentage share of any increase over a base year and requires a copy of the bill and the calculation. Without such a term you may not add tax increases during a fixed term. Amounts the tenant owes under that clause count as rent. The retaliation and emergency price-gouging limits on rent increases apply to these increases too (`edu-no-rent-escalation-rule-al`).

title: No Tenant Insurance Claims Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on tenant insurance claims: none requires a tenant to claim first under the tenant's own policy, governs a landlord's claim against the tenant's insurer, or addresses waivers of subrogation in residential leases. Keep insurance terms to what the tenant must carry and prove. Do not use a term that makes the tenant look only to the tenant's own insurance for losses you cause, or that waives the tenant's or the tenant's insurer's claims against you: that limits your liability under the law and is prohibited in an Alabama lease, with a penalty if you knowingly try to enforce it. The tenant remains liable for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no unbundled-parking law: nothing requires you to rent parking separately from the dwelling, or bars you from doing so. You may include parking in the rent or charge a separate parking fee, stated in the lease. A parking fee the tenant owes you under the lease counts as rent. Local governments may still set off-street parking requirements in zoning and building rules, which this library does not cover.

title: No Utility Charge Cap in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility, requires you to pass on only the amount the provider actually billed, or regulates a utility allowance. You may agree in the lease that you pay a utility up to a set monthly amount and the tenant reimburses the excess; the library's optional clause `utility-allowance-cap-co` does this, with a copy of the provider's bill as support. Alabama's Act counts every payment the tenant owes you under the lease as rent, but that clause has you agree not to treat the reimbursement as rent for late fees or eviction remedies; that is your choice to limit your own remedies, which the law allows. Because no Alabama law says whether reselling utility service makes a landlord a regulated utility, the cautious course is never to bill more than the provider charged you.

title: Apportioning Shared Utilities in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on apportioning shared-meter utility costs among tenants, and no rule that makes a lease term unenforceable because it makes the tenant pay for a utility not separately metered to the unit. You may agree in the lease that the tenant pays a share of a utility billed to you, measured by a submeter or by a stated formula such as square footage or number of occupants. The library's optional clause `utility-billing-wv` does this: it lists the utilities and the method, requires a written bill showing the calculation, and adds no administrative fee. Two cautions. For electricity from a Public Service Commission-regulated utility, multi-unit buildings begun on or after January 1, 1981 generally must be metered unit by unit, so apportioning electricity is mostly limited to older buildings and the listed exceptions (`edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-al`). And because no Alabama law says whether reselling utility service makes a landlord a regulated utility, charge only your actual cost. Utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease count as rent, so unpaid amounts may be included in a nonpayment notice and applied against the security deposit at the end of the tenancy.

title: Utility Deposits in Alabama
bodyText: Utility deposits the tenant pays a utility are between the tenant and the utility. For a utility regulated by the Public Service Commission, the deposit may not exceed an estimated bill for two billing periods, earns 7 percent interest a year credited each December, must be refunded with interest after 24 months if the account is in good standing, and on final disconnection is applied to the final bill with any balance refunded. A waterworks board in a Class 1 city must pay interest on customer security deposits at the federal funds rate. Electric cooperatives, other city utility boards, and water, sewer and gas districts set their own deposit rules; some districts may require a deposit from the owner, tenant or occupant and pay no interest on it. If you collect a deposit yourself to cover utilities billed to you, it is security for the tenant's obligations under the lease. It counts toward Alabama's one-month cap on security deposits and must be returned or accounted for in writing within 60 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives up possession, or you owe double the original deposit.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama requires no utility disclosure form or attachment with the lease: no statement of average utility costs, of which utilities are separately metered, or of whether water and power are available. The only general written disclosure Alabama's Act requires is the name and business address of the property manager and of an owner or agent for notices and service of process, given at or before the start of the tenancy. Because you are not responsible for paying utilities unless the lease says so, state clearly in the lease which utilities you provide and which the tenant arranges and pays (`utilities-paid-by-landlord`, `utilities-responsibility`), and how any utility you bill to the tenant is measured (`edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-al`).

title: No Shutoff-Notice Designation Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute or Public Service Commission rule that lets a tenant name you, or requires a utility to let a tenant name you, to receive copies of shutoff notices on the tenant's account. Under the Commission's rules, a regulated utility gives its disconnection notice to the customer: it is left with the customer, left at the premises, or mailed to the customer's last known address. Some utilities run their own third-party notice programs; whether yours does is a matter for that utility. Because nothing in Alabama law forbids it, you may ask the tenant in the lease to authorize each provider to list you as an additional contact for the tenant's account. The library's optional clause `utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co` does this. It does not make you responsible for the tenant's bill: a provider may not make a landlord pay a tenant's delinquent bill for an account in the tenant's name, or claim a lien on the property for it.

title: No Right to Cut Off Submetered Utilities in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no rule that lets a landlord who submeters or rebills a utility cut off that service when the tenant doesn't pay. The general rule controls: you may not interrupt or cause the interruption of a tenant's heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service to force payment or possession. If you do it willfully, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. Utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease count as rent, so the remedy for nonpayment is the written notice for unpaid rent and, if it is not cured, an eviction case. A short interruption you need for repairs is a different matter: give the tenant as much notice as you can and restore service promptly.

title: No Special Rule for Landlord-Held Utility Accounts in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no special statute for utilities billed in your name. Tenants get no right to pay your utility bill and deduct it from rent, the utility need not warn each unit before cutting off service on your account, and there is no receivership for unpaid utilities. The tenant's protection comes from the lease and the landlord-tenant act instead. If the lease makes a utility your responsibility, or the law requires you to supply running water, hot water and reasonable heat, and after the tenant's notice you willfully or negligently fail to make heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service available, the tenant may end the lease on at least 14 days' written notice or recover damages for the reduced rental value. If you willfully cut off or cause the loss of an essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant may not withhold rent while staying in the unit to enforce these rights. Under the Public Service Commission's rules, a regulated utility gives its shutoff notice to the account holder, which may include leaving it at the premises; nothing requires it to notify each tenant. Keep accounts in your name paid, and say clearly in the lease which utilities you provide.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that stops a utility from cutting off service in winter, in hot weather or during a declared emergency, and no statute on utility shutoffs at rental homes. The shutoff rules come from the Public Service Commission and bind only the utilities it regulates (mainly investor-owned electric, gas and water companies). Under those rules a bill becomes delinquent 10 days after its due date; the utility must then give the customer at least five days' written notice before cutting off service; it may not cut off for nonpayment after 3:30 p.m. on a day before its office is closed; and it may not disconnect residential electric or natural gas service for nonpayment on a day when the National Weather Service forecasts 32 degrees Fahrenheit or below at that location. Each regulated utility must also follow its own approved rules for cases where a shutoff may threaten life or health, or where the customer's age or disability calls for special consideration. Electric cooperatives, municipal utility boards, waterworks boards and public gas districts are outside the Commission's jurisdiction and follow their own rules; a city that runs the sewer system may also cut off water service to collect unpaid sewer charges. A utility may rely on a writ of possession when deciding whether to discontinue service at a dwelling. As landlord, you may never interrupt or cause the interruption of a tenant's heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service to force the tenant out. If you do, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Submetering and Utility Billing in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on submetering, ratio billing or other ways of charging tenants for utilities that are billed to you, and no required lease disclosure for them. For electricity from a utility regulated by the Public Service Commission, master metering is not allowed in a building with more than one unit if construction began on or after January 1, 1981: the utility must meter each unit separately. The exceptions are buildings whose units are usually rented for less than 30 days, a single-family house divided into units, buildings whose units have no individual electric heating, cooling or water-heating appliances, student housing, buildings where tenants must be at least 60, and others the Commission allows by order. Mobile home parks opened after June 1, 1981 also need separate meters unless spaces are usually rented for under 30 days. Electric cooperatives, city utilities, waterworks boards and gas districts set their own rules. No Alabama statute or Commission rule says whether a landlord who resells metered electricity, gas or water to tenants becomes a regulated utility. The cautious course is to charge tenants only your actual cost, with no markup or billing fee, and to ask the Commission or your provider before reselling metered service. If you bill any utility to the tenant, put the utilities, the method (submeter or formula) and the due date in the lease; the library's optional clause `utility-billing-wv` does this. Amounts the tenant owes you under the lease count as rent under Alabama's Act. Tampering with a utility meter to divert gas, electricity or water is a crime.

title: No Utility Transfer Cutoff Rule in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no statute setting a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name, and none that lets you cut off service in your name if the tenant doesn't transfer it. Do not shut off or ask a provider to discontinue service to an occupied unit to force a transfer: willfully interrupting a tenant's electricity, gas, water or other essential service exposes you to the tenant's claim for up to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. You may require the transfer in the lease and have the tenant reimburse you for service billed to you until it happens; the library's optional clause `utility-transfer-nj` does this without any cutoff. Getting accounts into the tenant's name also matters because Alabama protects your property only from bills for accounts in the tenant's name. A tenant's failure to transfer is a lease breach you can address with the written breach notice.

title: No Alabama Accessory Dwelling Unit Statute
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on accessory dwelling units (a second, smaller home on the same lot, such as a garage apartment, backyard cottage or in-law suite). No state law requires a city or county to allow one, protects your right to rent one out, bars an owner-occupancy requirement, or sets a minimum or maximum rental term for one. Whether you may build, convert or rent a second unit is a local zoning question: cities may divide their land into residential and other districts and regulate the use of buildings, lot coverage and population density. Before you build, convert a garage or outbuilding, or rent a second unit, check the zoning district with the city or county planning office and get any building permit and occupancy approval the local building code requires. State law bars local ordinances about residential landlords and landlord-tenant rights, but keeps local building codes, health codes and other general laws that apply equally to owner-occupied homes. No statute says whether that bar reaches a local zoning rule that applies only to rented second units, so follow the local zoning rule unless a lawyer advises otherwise. Once rented, an accessory unit is a dwelling unit like any other, and the rest of this library applies to it. One point to watch: an accessory unit that shares heating, hot water or another essential service with the main house, or has no direct street access, is not a single-family residence under Alabama's landlord-tenant act, so maintenance duties can move to the tenant only by a separate signed agreement, not by the lease.

title: No Alabama Landlord Asbestos Disclosure or Notice Rule
bodyText: No Alabama statute or rule requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, disclose asbestos to an applicant or tenant, or give tenants notice before work that may disturb it. Alabama regulates asbestos only as an abatement-work and air-pollution matter. Anyone who inspects for asbestos or designs or carries out asbestos response work in a covered building must be accredited through the state's Safe-State Program, and the owner or operator of an asbestos removal project that must be reported under the federal Clean Air Act rules must use certified removal contractors. Those federal and state air rules cover renovation and demolition of apartment buildings and other residential buildings with five or more units; a residential building with four or fewer units is outside them. The federal accreditation rules for building inspections cover apartment buildings of 10 or more units. What to do: if an older building may contain asbestos (old floor tile, pipe or boiler insulation, popcorn ceilings, cement siding), have suspect material tested before any renovation, repair or demolition that could disturb it, use accredited and certified contractors where the rules require them, keep tenants out of work areas, and tell tenants about planned work that could disturb asbestos. Don't hide a known asbestos hazard from a tenant; damaged asbestos that endangers occupants is a repair you should make, as part of your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable.

title: No Alabama Association Disclosure Rule for Leases
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a homeowners' association to disclose the association's obligations, attach the declaration, bylaws or rules, or carry a statement by you or the tenant about the condominium law or the association's rules, and none requires you to file the lease with the association's board. The Condominium Act's disclosure documents (the offering statement a developer gives buyers and the resale certificate an owner gives a buyer on request) apply to sales, not to ordinary leases: a lease for less than 20 years does not make the tenant a purchaser. Even so, the association's rules bind your tenant in practice, and a homeowners' association may act directly against a tenant who breaks them, so give the tenant the declaration's use and leasing restrictions and the current rules before signing and have the tenant acknowledge them. Check the declaration and bylaws themselves: they may require registration of leases, copies to the board, minimum terms or association approval. See the condominium and HOA rules row for details.

title: No Alabama Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the dwelling has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or bars rent for a period when the building lacked one. Certificates of occupancy in Alabama come from local building codes, which cities and counties adopt and enforce; state law mentions them only in passing (for example, a builder must give the city an updated list of subcontractors before it issues one). Your duty to keep the premises in line with applicable building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety still applies, so before you rent a newly built, converted or substantially renovated unit (a garage apartment, a basement unit, an addition), confirm with the local building official that any required certificate of occupancy or final inspection has been issued, and keep a copy in your property file. Renting space the local code says may not be occupied can expose you to code enforcement and to the tenant's remedies for a code violation that affects health and safety.

title: Special Land Tenure and Lease Approval in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no communal, native or customary land system, and no state statute requires a government officer to approve a private residential lease before it is valid. Three special land arrangements carry their own lease rules, so check the land's status before you sign. (1) Indian trust land: federal law, not state law, governs restricted Indian lands held for a tribe or its members, and a lease of them is valid only with the approval of the U.S. Secretary of the Interior. If the property is on tribal trust land, work through the tribe and the Bureau of Indian Affairs before renting. (2) Single-tax colony land (Fairhope): a single-tax corporation's land leases must let the lessee object in writing to the rent claimed, and the rent is then fixed by a binding three-arbitrator panel. If your house stands on single-tax land, you are the corporation's lessee, not its lessor; your right to rent the house to a tenant, and any rent or transfer terms, come from your own lease with the corporation, so read it before you sublet. (3) Community land trust land (Class 1 municipalities, from October 1, 2026): a community land trust may lease its land only for affordable housing, under a recorded ground lease of up to 99 years that sets occupancy requirements, resale limits and the trust's and city's purchase options. If you hold a home under such a ground lease, renting it out must fit the ground lease's occupancy rules.

title: Alabama Confirmed Absences (Disclosures and Lease Form)
bodyText: Rules found in some other states for which Alabama has no statute, each explained with what Alabama does have nearby in its own row of this library: no accessory dwelling unit statute; no landlord asbestos disclosure or notice rule; no association-document disclosure in leases; no certificate of occupancy disclosure; no special district statement; no defective drywall disclosure; no emergency contact rule; no code or condemnation order disclosure; no minimum type size, initialing rule, translation duty or plain-language statement for leases; no military zone, ordnance, demolition or shared-meter disclosure; no recycling notice; no chemical (Proposition 65-style) warning; no shoreline access disclosure; no lease-type parity rule; no single-family rental disclosure; no stigmatized property statute; no state tenant rights guide or statement; and no truth-in-renting law. Where Alabama law is silent, the lease, the landlord-tenant act's general duties (habitability, disclosure of owner and manager, prohibited terms), the fraud and deceptive trade practices statutes, and case law fill the gap.

title: No Alabama Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a landlord to disclose defective or corrosive (often called "Chinese") drywall, or sets any standard for it in rental housing. Drywall appears in Alabama law only as a construction step for new homes and as part of a condominium unit's boundaries. General law still matters. Hiding a material fact you are obliged to disclose, or misstating one, can be fraud, and a real estate licensee who leases for you must disclose any significant latent defect the licensee knows about to a prospective tenant. Corrosive drywall can damage wiring, plumbing and air-conditioning coils and cause odors, so it can also fall under your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable. If you know or suspect defective drywall (sulfur odor, blackened copper wiring or pipes, repeated air-conditioner coil failures), have it inspected, fix it, and tell a prospective tenant in writing before signing about any condition you have not yet corrected.

title: No Alabama Emergency Contact Rule for Tenancies
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour contact number, to collect an emergency contact from each tenant, or to put a management website or social-services hotline notice in the lease, and none says what a named contact may do. What Alabama does require is the written disclosure, at or before the start of the tenancy, of the name and business address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for notices and service of process, kept current; the library's owner and manager disclosure clause covers it. You may ask a tenant to name an emergency contact. Naming one should give that person no right to occupy the home or remove belongings, and you should not let a contact into the unit or hand over the tenant's property without the tenant's consent or a court order. If the tenant dies, deal with the personal representative or heirs.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute says whether a tenant of rented land has hunting or fishing rights unless the owner grants them in writing; the lease decides, and if it is silent the question is left to case law. Two Alabama rules make the lease worth writing carefully. First, hunting on the lands of another without the written permission of, or being accompanied by, the landowner or the person in possession or control of the land is a crime, so a tenant in possession can lawfully let other people hunt on the land unless the lease takes that right away. Second, a tenant (and the tenant's immediate family) who lives on the leased land may hunt there without a hunting license. If you rent rural or agricultural property and want to keep control of hunting, fishing and trapping, use the optional sporting-rights clause, which reserves those rights to you and bars the tenant from giving permission without your written agreement. Liability: an owner, lessee or occupant who lets someone hunt or fish does not by that permission promise the land is safe, but the protection does not cover willful or malicious failure to warn of a danger or permission given as a business for profit; a landowner who leases land for hunting or fishing must still warn the lessee of a hidden dangerous condition the landowner knows about.

title: Alabama Foreign Principal Property Restriction
bodyText: Alabama's Property Protection Act bars a foreign principal from acquiring title to, or a controlling interest in, agricultural or forest property, or any real property on or within 10 miles of a military installation (at least 10 contiguous acres) or a critical infrastructure facility (such as a refinery, power plant, water or wastewater plant, seaport facility, airport or aerospace site), for acquisitions on or after August 1, 2023. A foreign principal is the government or a government official of China, Iran, North Korea or Russia (not Taiwan), a political party of one of those countries or its members, or a country or government on a U.S. Treasury sanctions list. Private individuals and businesses from those countries are not named. The Act speaks of acquiring title or a controlling interest; it does not mention leases, has no lease-duration carve-out, and puts no duty on a landlord to find out whether an applicant is a foreign principal. Whether an ordinary residential lease could be a controlling interest is unsettled; the cautious course is not to lease property covered by the Act to a foreign government, its officials or a sanctioned government without legal advice. Otherwise, Alabama lets any alien, resident or nonresident, take and hold property like a citizen, and the Constitution gives resident foreigners the same property rights as native-born citizens. There is no state requirement to record or state a nonresident alien's name and address in a lease, and no government approval of leases to corporations. Separately, a 2012 law makes it unlawful to rent to a person you know, or recklessly disregard, is unlawfully present in the United States; see the immigration rental row. Don't screen applicants by national origin or citizenship as a proxy for any of these rules.
