title: Contaminated Property Disclosure in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has one lease-content rule for contaminated property. If the property is listed on the state's Voluntary Cleanup Properties Inventory as cleaned up only to a standard less strict than unrestricted residential use, the owner must put a prescribed notice in every lease or rental agreement; use the voluntary cleanup notice clause. The inventory is kept in the probate court's deed-records room, and the Alabama Department of Environmental Management can tell you whether your property is listed. Apart from that, no Alabama statute requires a landlord to disclose contamination, a past release of hazardous substances, or a recorded environmental covenant to a tenant, and none puts a notice duty on a residential tenant who learns of a release. When an environmental covenant (a recorded limit on how a cleaned-up site may be used) is created, a copy must go to each person in possession of the property, which includes a tenant then living there. The covenant runs with the land, so read any covenant recorded on your property and make sure the tenant's use complies with it. General law still applies: hiding a material fact you are obliged to disclose can be fraud, a real estate licensee who leases for you must disclose known significant latent defects, and contamination that makes the home unsafe falls under your duty to keep it fit and habitable. If you know of contamination that could affect a tenant's health (a leaking fuel tank, a former drug lab, a dry-cleaning solvent plume), fix it or tell the applicant in writing before signing.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules That Reach Alabama Tenants
bodyText: If your rental is a condominium unit or a home in a development with a homeowners' association, the association's recorded declaration, bylaws and rules govern how the property may be used and rented, and they reach your tenant. Condominiums: the declaration must state any restrictions on use, occupancy or leasing of units. The association may adopt rules and, after notice and a chance to be heard, fine unit owners for violations, and assessments and fines are a lien on your unit. If the declaration gives tenants the vote on specified matters, your tenant votes on those matters instead of you and gets notice of meetings and access to records for them. Homeowners' associations under the Alabama Homeowners' Association Act (developments whose declaration was recorded on or after January 1, 2016, and older associations whose members voted to come under the Act; condominiums and cooperatives are excluded): if your tenant breaks the declaration or rules, the board may, to the extent the governing documents allow, act directly against the tenant as well as you. It may suspend the tenant's use of association facilities (but not access to the lot), assess a penalty after notice to you and the tenant and a chance to be heard, and enforce any right you as landlord could have used under the lease. A penalty counts as an assessment and can become a lien on your lot. No Alabama statute caps an association's lease-approval or application fee, regulates an association-held tenant deposit, lets an association collect rent from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments, limits a new rental restriction to later buyers, limits the tenant information an association may demand, or protects home child care against association rules. Those points come only from the declaration and bylaws. Before you rent, read the declaration, bylaws, rules and any amendments for leasing limits, minimum terms, approval and registration requirements; give the tenant the rules that bind occupants; and if the documents require the association to approve the lease, use the association approval clause.

title: No Alabama Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about an outstanding inspection report, code-violation notice, repair or demolition order, or condemnation of the building. The state's unsafe-building laws send notice to the owner who last assessed the property for taxes and to mortgagees, and require a copy of the order to be posted at or within three feet of an entrance to the building, so a tenant may see it there; they give tenants no notice of their own. Local housing codes may have their own notice and vacate procedures. General law still applies: hiding a material fact you are obliged to disclose can be fraud, a real estate licensee who leases for you must disclose known significant defects, and a building under an unsafe-structure order will usually fall short of your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable. Don't rent a unit under an order that bars occupancy. If an order is pending, tell the applicant in writing before signing, and don't retaliate against a tenant who reports a code violation to the authorities.

title: What an Alabama Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Alabama does not require a residential lease to contain any particular terms or to put the start and end dates, or anything else, on its first page. The parties may include any terms the landlord-tenant act or other law does not prohibit. If the lease is silent, the law fills in: the tenant pays the fair rental value; rent is due without demand at the dwelling unit, monthly at the start of each month (or at the start of a term of one month or less), and apportions day to day; and with no definite term the tenancy is week-to-week for weekly rent and otherwise month-to-month. What must be given in writing at or before the start of the tenancy is the name and business address of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices (the owner and manager disclosure clause). Other required content applies only in particular cases: the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978, and the voluntary cleanup notice for listed properties. State the start date, end date, rent, due date and deposit clearly near the top of the lease anyway, and fill in every blank before signing.

title: Lease Copies and Signing in Alabama
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a self-managing landlord to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and a missing copy is not a statutory defense to enforcing the lease. A real estate licensee who leases for you is different: a licensee can be disciplined for failing to voluntarily furnish a copy of each lease and other document to each party who signs it with reasonable promptness. Signing and delivery also matter under the landlord-tenant act: if one side signs and delivers a written lease and the other does not sign it, the lease still takes effect when the landlord accepts rent without reservation, or when the tenant takes possession and pays rent without reservation, but a lease given effect that way runs for no more than one year. Give every tenant a fully signed copy promptly after signing, and keep proof that you did; the optional lease-copy acknowledgment clause records it.

title: No Alabama Lease Initialing Requirement
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a tenant to initial any lease clause or notice, or makes a clause unenforceable because it was not initialed. Alabama's initialing rules are for other documents (pawn tickets, a power of attorney form, the agency disclosure clause in a real estate purchase offer). You may ask the tenant to initial key terms (late fees, pets, smoking, any optional addendum) as evidence the tenant saw them, but initials do not make a prohibited term enforceable.

title: No Alabama Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: No Alabama statute bars terms or rent that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant (or the reverse), or caps the rent difference between lease types. The landlord-tenant act only sets defaults: with no definite term, a tenancy is week-to-week for weekly rent and otherwise month-to-month, and either side may end a periodic tenancy with written notice (7 days for week-to-week, 30 days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month). You may price month-to-month and fixed-term leases differently; apply the same terms to every applicant offered the same lease type so the difference cannot look discriminatory.

title: No Alabama Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: No Alabama statute sets a minimum type size for a residential lease or for any notice in it, and none makes small print inadmissible or unenforceable. Alabama's type-size rules reach other documents, such as rental-purchase agreements for merchandise, towing notices, cottage-food labels and private transfer fee notices, not dwelling leases. Use a readable type size anyway (10 or 12 point for body text) and make important terms conspicuous: a court can refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and tiny print hurts any later argument that the tenant agreed to it.

title: No Alabama Military Zone Lease Disclosure
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a lease disclosure for property in a military air installation noise or accident-potential zone, near a military installation, or in a military impact district, and none gives a tenant a right to end the lease on learning of one. Alabama's military-compatibility law runs between governments: a city or county within two miles of a military installation must notify the installation's commander of local impact issues, and must follow a review process before approving tall structures or wind energy facilities. If your rental is near a base or under a flight path, telling applicants about aircraft noise is good practice, and don't misstate it if asked.

title: Optional Lease Terms and Purchase Options in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama leaves most lease terms to the parties: a lease may include any terms the landlord-tenant act or other law does not prohibit, and the act's defaults (rent due at the unit at the start of each month, day-to-day apportionment, month-to-month tenancy with no definite term) apply only if the lease does not change them. Options to purchase: an option in favor of a tenant that must be exercised by the end of the lease term (or an extension or renewal) is not cut off by the 20-year limit on options to buy land, and an option with no stated duration otherwise expires after two years. No Alabama statute requires a seller's property-condition disclosure, so granting a tenant an option to buy does not trigger one; Alabama has no lease-option statute setting contract terms, cancellation rights or recording duties. Careful: the landlord-tenant act does not cover occupancy under a contract of sale when the occupant is the purchaser, so a lease-option that operates as a sale (for example, rent credited toward a price the tenant is bound to pay) may fall outside the act and under the older landlord-tenant chapter and general contract law. Whether a particular lease-option is a contract of sale is case law; keep the option separate, optional and clearly priced, and get legal advice before using a rent-to-own structure.

title: No Alabama Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosure
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a former military ordnance or munitions site, that a demolition permit is pending, or that utilities are on a shared or master meter. The only master-meter rule found is a gas pipeline safety inspection fee the meter operator pays per unit served. If utilities are master-metered or shared, say in the lease how they are billed and divided, because any utility charge the lease requires the tenant to pay you is rent; and if you plan to demolish or substantially renovate, tell an applicant before signing.

title: No Alabama Plain-Language Consumer Statement
bodyText: Alabama has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers or restrictions, no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms, and no dollar exclusion. The library's existing plain-language row says the same. Write the lease in plain English anyway. Alabama's deceptive trade practices act reaches residential leasing, a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and prohibited terms (waivers of the landlord's repair, deposit and utility duties, confessions of judgment, attorney's-fee shifting and exculpation) are unenforceable however clearly they are written, with a penalty for knowingly enforcing them.

title: Alabama Rules That Turn on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act has no small-landlord exemption: its duties apply whether you rent one unit or a thousand. A few other rules turn on numbers. (1) Fair housing: the state discrimination rules do not apply to rooms or units in a building of up to four families where the owner lives in one of them, or to a single-family house rented by a private owner who owns no more than three such houses and rents without a broker or discriminatory advertising; the advertising ban still applies, and federal law has its own exemptions. (2) Real estate licensing: an owner managing his or her own property (or a spouse's, child's or parent's), and a person acting as manager of an apartment building or complex, need no real estate license, however many units are involved; condominium on-site managers are not covered by that exemption. (3) Asbestos rules for renovation and demolition cover residential buildings with five or more units, and federal inspector-accreditation rules cover apartment buildings of 10 or more units. (4) A condominium of four or fewer units may be created under the older condominium statute. Read two-part exemptions as requiring both parts.

title: No Alabama Chemical Warning Rule for Rentals
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 does not apply in Alabama, and no Alabama statute requires a landlord to post or give a warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Alabama law mentions carcinogens only in firefighter and employee health programs. Federal lead-based paint disclosure still applies to housing built before 1978, and the asbestos and contamination rows cover the other environmental rules.

title: Lease Forfeiture for Unlawful Liquor Use in Alabama
bodyText: One old Alabama statute lets a landlord treat a lease as forfeited because of how the premises are used: the unlawful manufacture, sale, keeping for sale or giving away of prohibited liquors, or carrying on an unlicensed liquor, beer, brewing or distilling business, on the premises by the tenant (or by the tenant's agent or employee with the tenant's knowledge) works a forfeiture of the tenant's rights under the lease, at the landlord's option. No Alabama statute makes a residential lease void because the premises are used for gambling, prostitution or other unlawful purposes. For a residential tenancy the practical tools are the landlord-tenant act's: the manufacture, possession or use of illegal drugs in the unit or common areas, illegal discharge of a firearm, and criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the premises are noncurable defaults that let you end the lease on seven days' written notice, and drug-related nuisance law reaches owners who tolerate drug activity. Even where the liquor-forfeiture statute applies, recover possession only through the court eviction process.

title: No Alabama Recycling Notice Duty
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a landlord to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to provide recycling at multifamily property. Alabama's solid waste law encourages recycling through local and regional planning, and counties and cities may run their own programs. If your property has recycling, say in the rules where it goes and what is accepted.

title: Alabama Required Lease Disclosures at a Glance
bodyText: What an Alabama landlord must disclose, and when: (1) Always: in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and business address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices, kept current (owner and manager disclosure clause). (2) Housing built before 1978: the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet before the lease is signed (lead-based paint clause). (3) Property on the state's Voluntary Cleanup Properties Inventory that was cleaned only to a non-residential standard: the prescribed cleanup notice in the lease (voluntary cleanup notice clause). (4) In Jefferson County (including Birmingham) and Morgan County, an optional tenant statement protects you from the sex-offender clustering penalty. (5) If a real estate licensee leases for you, the licensee must disclose known significant latent defects to the prospective tenant and give each signer a copy of the lease. Alabama has no state lease form or first-page form, no notice about rent control or just-cause eviction (local rent control is barred), no seller property-condition disclosure (so a purchase option in a lease triggers none), and no statute on disclosing mold, bed bugs, radon, flooding, asbestos, drywall, deaths or crimes, military zones, special districts or certificates of occupancy; the separate rows in this library explain each. Don't misstate any material fact you do disclose.

title: No Alabama Tenant Rights Guide Requirement
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, at signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. No state agency is charged with publishing such a guide. You may give tenants a plain summary of how rent, repairs, entry, deposits and notices work under the lease and the landlord-tenant act; if you do, make sure it is accurate, because a misleading summary can be used against you.

title: Sex Offender Residence Rules That Reach Alabama Landlords
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a landlord to tell applicants or tenants that a registered sex offender lives on or near the property, or to check the registry, and Alabama's sex offender registration and notification act puts its residence and notification duties on registrants and law enforcement, not on landlords. But in three places a landlord who knowingly lets registered sex offenders cluster faces a $5,000 civil penalty per violation. (1) Jefferson County (including Birmingham): no adult or unrelated juvenile sex offender may live in a residence where another offender on the Jefferson County Sheriff's list lives, and no more than one adult offender on that list may live in an apartment complex unless their residences are at least 100 yards apart. (2) Birmingham (Class 1 city): the same one-residence rule under a general statute. (3) Morgan County: no adult or unrelated juvenile sex offender may live in a residence where another offender on the Morgan County Sheriff's list lives, and adult offenders must live at least 100 yards apart. In each place the owner is protected if the rental application or the lease contains the tenant's signed statement that the tenant is not a convicted sex offender, and a spouse or child of the owner or lessee is excepted. Use the tenant's sex-offender statement clause for property in Jefferson or Morgan County. Elsewhere you may screen applicants under a written criminal-history policy, but don't make public statements about a tenant's registry status.

title: No Alabama Single-Family Rental Disclosure
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a special disclosure, with a set type size or first-page placement, when a single-family house is rented, or a statement about the house's permitted occupancy. Single-family status matters in two other ways. Under the landlord-tenant act, a single-family residence (one that shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility and has direct street access) lets you and the tenant agree in writing, even in the lease, that the tenant takes over trash removal, appliance upkeep and specified repairs and maintenance; and under the state fair housing law, a private owner of no more than three single-family houses who rents without a broker and without discriminatory advertising is exempt from most of the discrimination rules (federal law has a similar exemption, and the advertising ban always applies). Occupancy limits come from local codes; don't set them lower than those codes or fair housing rules allow.

title: No Alabama Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a lease (or a sale) of shoreline or beachfront property to disclose public rights of way or access to the shore. Alabama's coastal and submerged-land statutes run to the state's own lands and to coastal permitting, not to private leases. If a public beach access or easement crosses your property, describe it in the lease so the tenant knows the public may use it.

title: No Alabama Special District Lease Statement
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a lease to state that the property is in a special district (such as an improvement district, cooperative district, community development district or tax increment district) or that the tenant knows about district charges or plans. District assessments fall on the property owner. The one district-related disclosure in Alabama law is for sales: when property carrying an unpaid energy, water-efficiency or resiliency assessment (the property assessed clean energy program) is sold, the seller must give the buyer a written disclosure statement. It does not apply to leases. If your lease passes any district assessment or fee to the tenant, state the amount or how it is figured, because any payment the lease requires the tenant to make to you or for your benefit counts as rent. If your property is in a community development district with its own amenities or rules, give the tenant the rules that apply to occupants.

title: No Alabama Stigmatized Property Statute
bodyText: No Alabama statute addresses stigmatized property: nothing says whether you must, or need not, tell an applicant that a death, suicide, homicide or other crime occurred at the property, or that a prior occupant had HIV or another illness, and no statute protects a landlord who stays silent. Nor does any statute require a landlord to answer an applicant's question about nearby registered sex offenders; the registry is public through law enforcement. General law applies instead. Don't make false statements: a misrepresentation of a material fact can be fraud, and staying silent can be fraud where the circumstances create a duty to speak. A real estate licensee must not misrepresent or fail to disclose significant known defects to a prospective tenant. Never disclose or ask about a person's HIV status or other disability; fair housing law protects a person with a handicap, which includes a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, a record of one, or being regarded as having one. If an applicant asks directly about a death or crime on the property, answer truthfully or decline to answer, but don't lie.

title: No Alabama Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires a state-agency statement of tenant rights, attached to the lease or given separately, with the tenant's signed acknowledgment, and none bars an eviction suit until such a statement is given. Nothing requires a summary as the first page of every lease or renewal, or each tenant's signature on each page. The writings Alabama does require are the owner and manager disclosure at the start of the tenancy and, where they apply, the federal lead disclosure and the voluntary cleanup notice. The library's guide and truth-in-renting rows say the same for related rules.

title: No Alabama Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: No Alabama statute requires you to translate a lease, to give a lease in the language you advertised or negotiated in, or to give a translated copy to a tenant who sells a home and rents it back, and no statute prescribes lease wording or type size with a translation duty. English is the official language of the state under the Alabama Constitution; that provision governs the state's own role and does not regulate private leases. If you negotiate with a tenant in another language, a translated copy marked as a courtesy translation, with a statement that the English version controls, helps show the tenant understood the terms. Federal fair housing law bars discrimination on national origin, so don't refuse to rent or set different terms because of the language a person speaks.

title: No Alabama Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Alabama has no truth-in-renting law: no rule that voids or penalizes lease terms just because they misstate the tenant's legal rights, and no required statement of rights. What Alabama does have: prohibited lease terms (waivers of the landlord's repair, deposit and utility duties and of eviction procedure, confessions of judgment, attorney's-fee and collection-cost shifting, and exculpation) are unenforceable, and a landlord who tries to enforce a lease known to contain one owes actual damages plus up to one month's periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. The deceptive trade practices act reaches residential leasing, a material misrepresentation can be fraud, and a real estate licensee renting property must not misrepresent. Keep lease language accurate about the law; don't include terms you know are prohibited.

title: Leasing When You Hold Only a Life Estate in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama property law is common law and has no usufruct, so the civil-law rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise. The closest Alabama interest is a life estate, and it limits what a lease can give. If you hold the property only for your life, you can lease no more than you hold: a lease that claims to run longer passes only your life interest, so the tenancy can end when you die even if the lease term has not run out. Rent is then split: if you die on or after a rent day, your estate collects the whole rent then due; if you die before a rent day, your estate gets the part that built up before your death and the remainder owner gets the rest. Any warranty you give does not bind the people who take the property after you. So if you hold a life estate (or any other limited interest), tell the tenant in writing before signing, and have the remainder owners sign the lease if it may run past your life. If you are married and the property is your homestead, for example a room or unit in the home you live in, have your spouse sign the lease too: a conveyance of the homestead is not valid without the spouse's signature and acknowledgment, and whether that reaches a lease is a point for a lawyer.

title: No Special Right to Enter for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: Alabama gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal. You may enter without the tenant's consent only in an emergency, under a court order, during an absence of more than 14 days at times reasonably necessary, to do maintenance the tenant failed to do after notice, to show the unit under a separate signed notice, or when you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the unit. Otherwise you need consent or at least two days' notice, unless notice is impracticable. An animal left without food or water while the tenant is hospitalized or detained may well be an emergency, but that is a judgment call. The safer course is the tenant's own arrangement: the optional clause `animal-care-access-al` has the tenant name a caretaker you may let in. If no caretaker can be reached, call animal control or law enforcement. Do not sell, give away or destroy a tenant's animal, and do not treat an animal as abandoned property to dispose of; cruel neglect of an animal in a person's custody is a crime.

title: Cannabis and Medical Cannabis in Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has medical cannabis only, and only in limited forms: tablets, capsules, tinctures, certain gel cubes or lozenges, topical preparations, suppositories, patches, nebulizers and inhaler liquids bought from a licensed dispensary by a registered patient or caregiver with a medical cannabis card. Raw plant material, anything smoked, burned or vaped, and edibles such as cookies or candies are not medical cannabis, and only licensed facilities may grow cannabis; a patient may not grow it at home. All other marijuana possession and use remains a crime. The medical cannabis law gives cardholders no housing protection. It does not bar a landlord from refusing to rent to a cardholder, and it does not limit lease rules on cannabis. So your lease may ban smoking, vaping and growing marijuana, and may also ban possessing or using it in any form, including medical cannabis; the optional clause `cannabis-restrictions-ak` lets you choose. Lawful card possession is not by itself grounds to search a person or home, and the card does not affect the cardholder's constitutional rights. Two cautions. First, a tenant whose disability is treated with medical cannabis may ask for an accommodation; whether Alabama's Fair Housing Law could require one for lawful non-smoked use is untested, so handle any such request individually and in writing rather than by rote denial. Second, Alabama's indoor smoking law covers tobacco and electronic nicotine products, not cannabis, so cannabis smoke is controlled by your lease, not by that law.

title: Children and Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Alabama does not require your lease to say anything about children, and it has no landlord-tenant rule of its own on a tenant who has a child during the tenancy. The Fair Housing Law decides the question. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or otherwise make a unit unavailable because a household includes children under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian or the custodian's written designee. The same protection covers a person who is pregnant or is in the process of getting legal custody of a child. That includes ending or refusing to renew a tenancy because a child is born or joins the household. You may set reasonable occupancy and safety standards based on things like the number and size of bedrooms and the overall size of the unit, as long as they do not violate local, state or federal limits; apply them the same way to adults and children. Your application may ask the number, age, sex and family relationship of the applicants and everyone who will live in the unit, and you may consider those facts in deciding how utilities are paid. The familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons (62 and over, or 55 and over meeting the statutory test), and the state exemptions for small owner-occupied buildings and for a private owner of up to three single-family houses apply here too. List every occupant, including children, in `permitted-occupants`.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Alabama's Fair Housing Law makes it discrimination to refuse a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services when one may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. It also makes it discrimination to refuse a reasonable modification of the unit, at the tenant's expense, that is necessary for the person's full enjoyment of the premises. These duties cover the tenant, anyone living or about to live in the unit, and anyone associated with them. Current illegal drug use is not a protected disability. You need not rent to a person whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. For a modification, you may, where reasonable, make your permission conditional on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and you may ask for a description of the work and assurance that it will be done properly with any required permits. Alabama law does not require this restoration condition to be written into the lease; set it when the tenant asks, in writing. The optional clause `disability-modification-restoration-mn` states it in the lease. Alabama has no statute on a restoration deposit. Although Alabama's deposit cap allows extra security for changes to the premises, federal rules bar you from raising the usual deposit because of a disability; where truly needed to make sure restoration money will be there, you may negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, over a reasonable time and no more than the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. Owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, and single-family houses rented by a private owner of no more than three houses without a broker or discriminatory advertising, are exempt from these state duties, though federal law and the advertising ban may still apply. Assistance-animal requests follow `assistance-animal-accommodation-al`.

title: Background Checks on Apartment Employees
bodyText: Alabama does not require you to run background checks on apartment employees such as leasing agents, maintenance staff or on-site managers, and it sets no screening standard for them. An apartment manager does not need a real estate license, so the state's licensing background check does not reach that job; a real estate broker or salesperson who leases or manages property for others does go through state and national criminal history checks to get licensed. If you choose to screen, Alabama's state background check service, run by the Alabama State Law Enforcement Agency since October 1, 2026, is open to any employer screening a prospective employee or contractor. The person must give express permission first, and you must keep that permission, on paper or digitally, for three years or for as long as the person works with you, whichever is longer. You may not pass the report on to anyone else. Using a report for an unauthorized purpose, or running one without a required release, is a crime. A check on someone under 18 needs a parent's consent. If you use a private screening company instead, federal consumer-reporting rules apply; they are outside this row.

title: No Tenant Right to Run a Family Child Care Home
bodyText: Alabama does not require a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, and it has no rule on a landlord's conditions for one, such as proof of liability insurance or a liability waiver. A lease may bar child care for pay or require your written consent; the AL-tagged `residential-use-only` clause already bars commercial use. A tenant who cares for children who are not related to the tenant generally needs a state child-care license from the Department of Human Resources (day care homes and group day care homes are licensed categories), with exemptions such as some church-run programs; whether a particular arrangement needs a license is for the tenant and the department. If you consent, you may require the tenant to show the license and carry liability insurance naming you as an interested party, but do not make the tenant release you from liability the law places on you, which an Alabama lease cannot do.

title: Firearms in Alabama Rentals
bodyText: Alabama has no statute that bars or limits a private landlord's lease rules on firearms, and none that protects a tenant's right to keep firearms in a rental. A private lease may therefore restrict firearms, and the library's optional clause `firearm-rules-ks` bars discharging a firearm at the property except in lawful defense of persons and requires safe storage. Alabama law already treats illegal use, possession or discharge of a firearm or ammunition on the rental premises by a tenant or occupant as a noncurable default: you may end the lease on seven days' notice and the tenant has no right to cure, except for use or discharge in self-defense, defense of a third party or other lawful use of defensive force. Two related rules. As an employer, you may not stop your own employees, such as on-site managers or maintenance staff, from keeping a lawfully possessed pistol locked out of sight in their own vehicles in the parking area, and similar rules cover hunting firearms during hunting season; that law protects employees, not tenants. And counties and cities may not regulate firearms except as a state statute expressly allows, so a local rule on firearms in rental housing would be void; whether that limit reaches a public housing authority's lease is not settled by the statute.

title: No Statutory Guest-Access Rights
bodyText: Alabama has no statute giving a tenant's guests, caregivers or service providers a right to enter a rental building, barring guest fees, or making guest access unwaivable. Guests come in under the tenant's right to occupy and the lease's guest terms (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`, both tagged for Alabama). The tenant must make sure people on the premises with the tenant's consent do not disturb the neighbors, and criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the premises is a noncurable default. A guest who stays past the lease's limit can be treated as an unauthorized occupant under the lease. Limits still apply: guest rules must be reasonable, clear, disclosed and applied fairly to all tenants; you must make reasonable accommodations, such as allowing a live-in or visiting caregiver a tenant with a disability needs; and you may not apply guest rules differently because of a protected trait. A guest fee is part of rent under Alabama's broad rent definition, so state any fee in the lease.

title: No Home-Based Business Statute
bodyText: Alabama has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a residence or limiting what a lease may say about one; the phrases "home-based business" and "home occupation" do not appear in the state Code. Whether a tenant may work from home is a matter of the lease and of local zoning. The AL-tagged `residential-use-only` clause limits the property to residential use and bars commercial use; if you want to allow quiet home offices, say so in writing, for example by consenting to work done entirely inside the unit with no customer traffic, signs, employees on site or stored inventory. A tenant's business use may also need a local business license and may affect your insurance. County and city zoning rules on home occupations are local ordinances outside this library; they apply because they govern all residences, not because of the lease.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: In Alabama you need the tenant's consent or at least two days' notice to enter for repairs, maintenance, pest control or other services. The other states' rule that a conspicuous lease clause can allow no-notice entry for scheduled services does not work here: Alabama lets you skip the per-visit notice only if you give the tenant, separately from the lease, a general notice or an advance schedule more than two days ahead, either for a specific time or a stated window. Once that separate notice or schedule is given, no further notice is needed for those entries. Write the notice as its own paper, not as a lease section; the library's form is `scheduled-services-notice-al`. The notice covers only repairs, maintenance, pest control and services relating to health or safety. Enter at reasonable times, do not use scheduled entries to harass the tenant, and give fresh notice for any visit outside the schedule. The tenant may also agree to shorter notice for a particular visit.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: Alabama requires no fact sheet, notice or lease disclosure about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and there is no state publication to hand over. Pet terms are a matter of the lease (`pet-policy-al`); service and assistance animals are not pets (`assistance-animal-accommodation-al`). If an eviction leaves an animal behind, do not abandon, harm or neglect it: cruel neglect of an animal in a person's custody is a crime. Contact the tenant first, and if no one takes the animal, call local animal control or law enforcement rather than disposing of it yourself.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Access Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no statute giving candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators a right to enter apartment buildings or gated communities to canvass, and none that requires you to let tenants hold political events in common areas or that limits a lease rule on political signs. The only political-sign laws are county local acts banning campaign signs on highway rights-of-way. You may set neutral rules for access to common areas and for signs, enforced the same way for every candidate and cause, but the rule standards for building rules apply. A tenant may still invite a canvasser into the tenant's own unit as a guest. Do not punish a tenant for political activity in a way that singles out a protected class, and remember that tenants who organize or join a tenants' union are protected from retaliation (`edu-tenant-right-to-organize-al`).

title: No Tenant Right to a Window Air Conditioner
bodyText: Alabama gives tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner and requires no lease disclosure about cooling-device restrictions; nor is there a mobile-home or association cooling right that could carry over to ordinary tenants. You are not required to supply air conditioning. If you do supply it, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the tenant must use it reasonably. A lease may restrict or require consent for window units, for example to protect windows, prevent leaks or water damage, and keep electrical loads safe, but state the rule clearly in the lease or in rules that meet Alabama's rule standards, and apply it to all tenants. Consider allowing a tenant with a disability-related need for cooling to install a unit as a reasonable accommodation.

title: No Tenant Right to Portable Solar
bodyText: Alabama gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, has no statute voiding lease, deed or association restrictions on solar equipment, and has no utility rule letting a tenant connect such a device without the utility's approval. A lease may therefore require your written consent before a tenant installs any solar device, or bar such devices. If you allow one, require that it be safety-certified, plugged into a standard outlet rather than wired into the building, kept off roofs and common areas, and removed with any damage repaired at move-out. Whether a plug-in device may feed power into the building's circuits is a matter for the electric utility's rules and the electrical code, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Questions About Protected Traits
bodyText: Alabama has no separate rule that bars asking about, or keeping records of, an applicant's protected traits. What it bans is discrimination itself, plus any notice, statement or advertisement about renting that shows a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. A question on an application or in an interview can be such a statement, and asking it invites the claim that you used the answer, so do not ask about race, color, religion, national origin or disability. Alabama expressly lets your application ask the number, age, sex and family relationship of the applicants and everyone who will live in the unit, and whether any intended occupant has been convicted of illegally making or distributing a controlled substance. Use those answers only for occupancy standards, utility arrangements and the drug-conviction screen the law allows, never to turn away families with children. Federal fair housing rules go further for disability: you may not ask whether an applicant or household member has a disability, or how severe it is. You may ask every applicant, alike, whether they can meet the tenancy requirements, whether they qualify for housing or a priority reserved for people with disabilities, whether they currently use illegal drugs, and about drug manufacturing or distribution convictions. Keep any disability information you receive for an accommodation request confidential.

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Alabama has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah, wreath or prayer flag, on a door or in a unit, and none that limits a lease rule on them. Your general display and decoration rules still apply, but the Fair Housing Law bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion or national origin, so a rule must be neutral and enforced the same way for every kind of display. Refusing a small door-frame item for religious reasons while allowing other door decorations invites a discrimination claim. Building rules bind tenants only if they meet Alabama's rule standards (reasonable purpose, fair application, clear terms and notice; written consent for a later rule that substantially changes the tenant's use). The cautious practice is to allow small religious items on the entry door or frame and require only that the tenant repair any damage at move-out.

title: No Work-Card Rule for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Alabama has no work-card, permit or background-check requirement for people who work in housing for older persons, such as 55-and-over or 62-and-over communities. What Alabama does have is the definition of housing for older persons: housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rules only if it qualifies, either as housing under a state or federal elderly program, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit, with at least 80 percent of units so occupied, published age policies that you follow, and suitable facilities and services. If you operate an assisted-living or other licensed care facility rather than ordinary rental housing, the licensing rules for that facility apply instead and are outside this library.

title: No Specific Penalty for Refusing a Service Animal in Housing
bodyText: Alabama has no criminal or civil penalty aimed at a landlord who refuses a service or assistance animal in rental housing. The duty is still real: a person with a disability who has a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to rental housing, cannot be charged extra for the animal, and remains liable for any damage it causes; you may ask for proof of vaccinations. For other assistance animals, refusing a reasonable accommodation is housing discrimination, enforced by a complaint to ADECA or a lawsuit for actual and punitive damages, and under federal fair housing law. Two older public-access penalty laws use public-accommodation lists that do not name residential rentals. A small misdemeanor fine applies to an owner, lessee, manager or employee of a place of public accommodation, such as an inn or hotel, who refuses a guide dog accompanying a blind person; and the general service-animal access law covers hotels, lodging places and other places open to the general public. A leasing office or model unit open to the public could arguably be a place of public accommodation, so let service animals in there too. Housing access itself is governed by the separate housing section described above. Allergies or fear of animals are not grounds for refusing a service animal in a public accommodation, and the same approach is the safe course in housing.

title: Misrepresenting a Service or Assistance Animal
bodyText: Alabama makes misrepresenting a service or assistance animal for housing an offense, and the statute is written for housing, not only for public places. A person commits it by intentionally telling someone that a person has a disability or a disability-related need for an animal in housing, by making materially false statements to get documentation for one, by creating or giving someone a document falsely calling an animal a service or assistance animal for use in housing, or by putting a vest, harness, collar or sign on a pet to pass it off as one. A first offense carries a $500 civil penalty or is a Class C misdemeanor; a repeat is a Class B misdemeanor. A separate public-access law makes it a Class C misdemeanor, with 100 hours of community service, to knowingly and willfully misrepresent oneself as using a qualified service animal or as its trainer, rising to a Class B misdemeanor and a $100 fine for a repeat. These laws do not change your accommodation duties. Where a disability or need is not obvious or known, you may ask for reliable documentation from the person's medical provider and must keep it confidential; you may not refuse an animal because you suspect fraud without that process. If you believe a document is false, report it to law enforcement rather than acting on your own, and do not threaten a tenant with prosecution to make them give up a request.

title: Showing Notice: Shortening or Waiving It
bodyText: Before asking whether a tenant can give up showing notice, start with the default: you must give at least two days' notice before entering to show the unit and may enter only at reasonable times. A note posted on the main entry door, stating the time and purpose, is enough notice. The tenant must not unreasonably refuse consent to a showing. You may show the unit without the tenant's consent only within the last four months before the lease expires, only with the prospective tenant or buyer present, still on two days' notice, and only if the tenant has signed a general notice allowing it that you gave separately from the lease; give that notice within those four months, since the Act can be read to require it then, not at signing. The library's form is `showing-access-notice-al`. The tenant may agree to less than two days' notice. The Act does not say whether that agreement can be given in advance in the lease, and a court could treat a lease term cutting the notice period as ineffective. The cautious course is to keep two days' notice in the lease and ask for shorter notice for a particular showing when you need it, by text, e-mail or in person, letting the tenant say no. Never use showings to harass the tenant.

title: Smoke in Common Areas and Smoke Drift
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on smoke drifting between units and none that lets a tenant waive, or makes a landlord answer for, smoke that seeps in from a neighbor. What it does have is the Clean Indoor Air Act (now the Vivian Davis Figures Clean Indoor Air Act). In lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, senior residences and other multiple-unit residential buildings, no one may smoke and you may not designate a smoking area unless the area is enclosed and well ventilated. Since October 1, 2026, vaping with an electronic nicotine device counts as smoking. A private residence, including a tenant's own unit, is not covered. You must post "No Smoking" signs where the Act bans smoking, and you may make the whole building nonsmoking. The Act covers tobacco and electronic nicotine products, not cannabis; the lease controls cannabis smoke (`smoking-policy`, `cannabis-restrictions-ak`). The Act reaches apartment common areas directly, so you do not need to ask whether building staff make a hallway a workplace. Do not put a smoke-drift waiver in the lease. A term in which the tenant accepts drifting smoke and gives up any claim about it could limit your liability under law, or waive the tenant's rights under your duties to keep the premises fit and comply with codes, and Alabama makes both kinds of term unenforceable, with a penalty if you knowingly try to enforce one. Use the smoking-policy clause to control smoking instead, and treat drift complaints as a maintenance and rules matter.

title: Cable, Satellite and Antenna Access
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on cable, satellite or internet access to rental buildings: nothing gives a provider a right to wire your building, gives tenants a right to the provider of their choice, or bars different rent for subscribers. Federal law does reach leases. Under the FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule, a lease term may not impair a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or fixed-wireless antenna one meter or less in diameter, or a television antenna, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony, patio or yard the tenant alone uses. A rule impairs if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation, unreasonably increases cost, or prevents an acceptable signal. Safety and historic-preservation rules are allowed if clearly stated, no more burdensome than necessary, and applied evenly. The rule does not give tenants a right to install on roofs, exterior walls or other common areas you control. You may require notice and good workmanship and make the tenant repair damage, using the optional clause `telecom-access-mn`, which yields to the federal rule.

title: No General Tenant-Information Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alabama has no general statute barring a landlord from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, and none setting a consent form for doing so. Several specific rules do limit what you share. A state background check report you obtain on an applicant or resident may not be passed to anyone else, and misusing it is a crime. Medical documentation you receive for an assistance-animal request must be kept confidential. Intentionally and maliciously revealing the contents of an expunged criminal file is a crime. Records containing sensitive identifying information, such as Social Security, driver's license or bank account numbers, must be protected with reasonable security and disposed of securely. The cautious practice is to share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent, with your own agents and service providers who need it, in response to legal process, or to answer a reference request with facts you can document. Starting May 1, 2027, a consumer data privacy law adds duties, but only for large data handlers (more than 25,000 consumers' personal data, payment-only data excluded, or a business built on selling data).

title: Flags, Signs and Displays
bodyText: Alabama protects one display right that can reach a lease: notwithstanding any covenant, contract or restriction, a person may display a current United States flag, no larger than 40 square feet, on his or her property, and any contract term that prohibits it is void. The statute speaks of the person's own property and does not say whether a tenant's leased home counts; the cautious course is to treat it as applying and not to forbid a tenant's U.S. flag of that size on the tenant's own unit, porch, balcony or yard. A separate statute bars condominium, homeowners' and unit owners' associations from stopping members from displaying the Alabama state flag where they own or have exclusive use, subject to reasonable time, place and manner rules; it binds associations and their members, not landlords. Otherwise Alabama has no statute on tenant signs, banners or decorations. You may set display rules in the lease or as building rules, but a rule binds the tenant only if it serves tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or protects the property, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies to all tenants fairly, is clear, and was disclosed; a rule adopted later that substantially changes how the tenant uses the unit needs the tenant's written consent. Apply display rules evenly: enforcing them only against religious or national-origin displays could be housing discrimination. See also `edu-religious-cultural-display-al` and `edu-no-political-access-rule-al`.

title: Housing for Employees
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act does not cover housing that an employee occupies only because of a job in and about the premises, such as an on-site manager or maintenance worker whose right to live there ends with the job. That arrangement falls back on the older landlord-tenant chapter and the general law, and the act's notice, deposit and repair rules do not automatically apply. The exclusion does not apply if the arrangement is set up to avoid the act. Alabama has no statute requiring a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating employer housing, no requirement to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, no eviction statute that expressly names caretakers, and no filing or sponsor-liability rule for housing guest workers. The cautious course is to put the arrangement in a separate written employee-housing agreement that states the housing is a condition of employment, what the employee pays or how housing is valued as pay, and how much time the employee has to move out after the job ends. If the employee stays after the job ends, use a court eviction; do not lock out or remove belongings yourself. If the employee pays rent under an ordinary lease that does not depend on the job, the act applies in full.

title: Online Portals for Payments and Signatures
bodyText: Alabama has no statute on tenant portals: nothing requires you to offer one, forbids one, or limits what a portal may require. Two rules shape how far a lease can push tenants onto one. First, Alabama's electronic-transactions law applies only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, and a party who agreed may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically; that right cannot be waived by agreement. So a lease may invite e-signatures and online notices, but cannot lock the tenant into portal-only signing or notices for every future document. Keep a paper route available. Second, notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence fall outside the electronic-transactions law (`edu-electronic-notices-al`), so serve those on paper whatever the portal says. For payments, the lease may list accepted methods, including an online portal (`acceptable-payment-methods`), but a portal fee is part of rent under Alabama's broad rent definition (`edu-fees-as-rent-al`), so state it in the lease.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: Alabama has no rent-ledger rule: you need not keep a ledger in a set form, give one on request, or attach one to a notice, and you need not give rent receipts (`edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-al`). The one statutory content rule is that a notice ending the lease for unpaid rent must state the amount of rent and any late fees owed, so keep records good enough to state that figure accurately. Alabama's Data Breach Notification Act applies to any person or business that acquires or uses sensitive personally identifying information, which includes landlords holding applicants' or tenants' Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, financial account numbers with access codes, or health information. You must keep reasonable security measures in place (scaled to your size and resources: someone responsible, a risk review, safeguards, service providers bound by contract, and periodic review), dispose of such records by shredding or erasing them when you no longer need them, and, if a breach is reasonably likely to cause substantial harm, notify each affected Alabama resident within 45 days. If you use the state background check service, keep each applicant's or resident's written permission for three years or the length of the tenancy, whichever is longer. A broader consumer data privacy law takes effect May 1, 2027, but it reaches only businesses handling the personal data of more than 25,000 consumers (not counting data used only to complete payments) or earning more than a quarter of revenue from selling data; most landlords will fall outside it.

title: Tenant Organizing in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama protects a tenant's choice to organize or join a tenants' union or similar group: you may not retaliate by raising rent in a discriminatory way, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant organized or joined one. A tenant who is retaliated against has the remedies for an unlawful ouster and a defense to the eviction. You may still evict for unpaid rent or another material lease violation, and the retaliation bar does not give the tenant a separate right to use common areas, post notices or canvass other units. Alabama has no statute that gives tenants in private housing a right to meet on the property, distribute flyers or go door to door. If your property is a HUD-insured or HUD-assisted multifamily project covered by the federal tenant-participation rules (for example, project-based Section 8, Section 202 or Section 811 housing), federal rules require you to let tenants and organizers distribute leaflets, post on bulletin boards, survey tenants door to door and hold independent meetings in an on-site space, without asking your permission first. Do not put a lease term or rule in place that bars or penalizes joining a tenant organization.

title: Tenant Screening in Alabama
bodyText: Alabama has no general tenant-screening statute. It does not require a conditional offer before a criminal-history check, set look-back periods, limit minimum-income or income-to-rent tests, cap application fees, or offer certificates that lift a conviction-based housing bar. The rules that do apply come from several laws. Fair housing: screen everyone the same way, on criteria unrelated to race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. You may refuse an applicant convicted of illegally making or distributing a controlled substance, and your application may ask about such convictions for any intended occupant. State background checks: since October 1, 2026, a landlord or housing authority may get a state criminal background check from the Alabama State Law Enforcement Agency on a prospective or current resident. Get the person's express permission first and keep it, on paper or digitally, for three years or the length of the tenancy, whichever is longer. Do not share the report with anyone else; misusing it, or running a check without a required release, is a crime. A check on a minor needs a parent's consent. Expunged records: an applicant whose record was expunged does not have to disclose it on a rental application, and the case is treated as never having happened; do not ask about or rely on expunged matters. If you rent to someone without knowing of a record because it was expunged, you are immune from civil liability for damages that person causes, unless your own conduct was unreasonable, wanton, willful or intentional. Consumer reports: if you deny an application, require a co-signer or larger deposit, or otherwise act against an applicant based on a consumer report from a screening company, federal law requires an adverse action notice naming the company, stating that it did not make the decision, and explaining the applicant's right to a free report and to dispute it. Local sex-offender rules: in Birmingham, throughout Jefferson County and in Morgan County, an owner who knowingly lets two registered offenders live together (and, in Jefferson County, two within 100 yards in an apartment complex) faces a $5,000 civil penalty per violation; a signed statement in the application or lease that the tenant is not a convicted sex offender protects you (`sex-offender-statement-al`).

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Alabama offers no tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee, vacancy relief or other incentive to a private landlord for renting to a veteran, and it does not require or regulate a veterans' preference or discount in private rental housing. The closest state program is the Alabama Housing Trust Fund, run by ADECA, which funds affordable-housing projects through a competitive process and must address the housing needs of several groups, including veterans; it supports projects, not individual leases. Federal programs such as HUD-VASH vouchers are outside this library. If you accept a veteran's voucher, follow the program's own lease addendum. You may offer a veterans' discount if you choose, but keep in mind that Alabama protects servicemembers in some lease situations (see `edu-servicemember-rights-al`).

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Alabama follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Ala. Code § 7-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Ala. Code § 7-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Alabama's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Ala. Code § 35-9A-142). That binds you and the tenant alike. Alabama's version also covers every agreement under the chapter, and 'good faith' means honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction concerned (Ala. Code § 35-9A-141(6)). In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
